name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico State Land Office finalizes increased bonding requirements for oil and gas operators
description: The New Mexico State Land Office on Monday announced that it had finalized higher bonding requirements for oil and gas companies that lease state Trust lands.
text:
The New Mexico State Land Office on Sept. 28, 2026, finalized rules requiring oil and gas operators to greatly increase the amount of financial assurances they provide before receiving extraction leases on state Trust land. Above: Oil derricks pictured in Hobbs on Aug. 18, 2026. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
The New Mexico State Land Office on Monday announced that it had finalized higher bonding requirements for oil and gas companies that lease state Trust lands. 
The rule goes into effect Monday, marking the end of a months-long process aimed at ensuring New Mexico taxpayers and the beneficiaries of state Trust lands do not bear the cost of oil and gas contamination or wastewater spills.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The rule increases the financial assurance levels for oil and gas operators for the first time in 40 years. The prior rule enabled operators to post between $10,000 and $25,000 to cover potentially hundreds of wells. 
Those “nominal” bonds, the State Land Office said in a news release Monday, “provided no real protection for damage to state lands,” because plugging a single abandoned well, for example, tends to cost at least $100,000. 
The new rule raises the minimum bond for oil and gas lessees to $150,000, an amount that can increase if a company has a demonstrated track record of failing to address spills or other regulatory violations, according to the State Land Office. 
“New Mexicans should never have to foot the bill to clean up messes on state lands,” New Mexico Commissioner of Public Lands Stephanie Garcia Richard, a Democratic lieutenant governor candidate in the Nov. 3 election, said in a statement. “This new rule puts much stronger financial assurances in place in the event there are unaddressed spills or a company goes belly-up and is unable to plug its wells.”
Industry groups including the New Mexico Oil and Gas Association and the Independent Petroleum Association of New Mexico previously announced their opposition to the rule during public hearings in May. The groups argued that the State Land Office does not have adequate authority to implement it. 
New Mexico Election 2026: Commissioner of public lands

Anticipating a lawsuit over the new bonding rule, the State Land Office on Monday filed a lawsuit in First Judicial District Court in Santa Fe seeking a judicial declaratory judgment affirming that the State Land Office, which manages mineral rights to more than 9 million surface acres statewide, has adequate authority to increase the bonding minimums. 
“We will not be intimidated by threats from oil and gas corporations to challenge my statutory and constitutional authority to do my job on behalf of New Mexicans,” Garcia Richard said in the statement. 
Even with the new bonding requirements, the state still faces a huge potential cost associated with plugging abandoned wells. The state Legislative Finance Committee in a 2025 report found that plugging an identified 1,400 wells could cost the state between $700 million and $1.6 billion.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA wildfire home damage totals at least $188M, Ferguson says
description: Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson on Monday asked President Donald Trump for tens of millions of dollars in federal aid to help communities recover from devastating wildfires this summer. Across the state, 649 primary residences were destroyed, mostly in Spokane County, according to the governor’s office. More than 2,500 more were damaged to some extent. The […]
text:
Damaged structures in the aftermath of the Spokane fires that began on Aug. 1. Some officials and consumer advocates fear the wildfire could lead to property insurance rate hikes and policy cancellations.
(Photo courtesy of Spokane Valley Fire Department)Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson on Monday asked President Donald Trump for tens of millions of dollars in federal aid to help communities recover from devastating wildfires this summer.
Across the state, 649 primary residences were destroyed, mostly in Spokane County, according to the governor’s office. More than 2,500 more were damaged to some extent. The financial toll of this damage exceeds $188 million, Ferguson said. In all, the total damage is estimated to be hundreds of millions dollars more.
Ferguson announced the ask in Spokane, where a trio of blazes in early August forced tens of thousands of residents to evacuate and destroyed hundreds of homes and other buildings. The complex of fires is considered the worst disaster the region has seen in years. He also unveiled ideas to help residents rebuild their homes.
“We’re in for the long haul on this,” Ferguson said. “This is going to take a long time to dig out from this and to get folks the help that they need.”
The Trump administration granted Ferguson’s earlier request for immediate help from federal agencies during the fires. The state’s new entreaty is meant to help the communities recover.
The money sought under Monday’s request for a major disaster declaration would help individuals, nonprofits and state, tribal and local governments. This could include grants for temporary housing, home repairs and low-cost loans to cover those recovering, and cost-sharing for emergency work public agencies undertook during the fires. 
The individual assistance is for residents of Spokane, Benton, Stevens and Okanogan counties, as well as the Spokane Tribe of Indians. Ferguson estimated the feds could provide at least $11 million for this purpose. The maximum aid this program can provide is $42,500 per person. Yakama Nation and the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation are pursuing their own similar requests, separate from the state’s. 
About 70% of homes affected across these four counties and one tribal reservation are insured. But insurance won’t fully cover the recovery costs.
“That is why federal resources we are requesting today are absolutely essential,” Ferguson said.
Separate federal aid for local, state and tribal governments that Ferguson is asking for could cover costs in Asotin, Chelan, Columbia, Douglas, Ferry, Grant, Okanogan, Spokane, Stevens, Whitman and Yakima counties. The state estimates it qualifies for over $117 million in this funding. 
The state is specifically seeking funding to help with debris removal and recover costs for emergency protective measures, like hundreds of generators that were deployed. More requests are forthcoming dealing with damaged roads and other needs. 
More than 900,000 acres have burned in Washington this year, making 2026 one of the worst wildfire years in recent memory. While the peak of the fire season appears to be over, several large blazes continue to burn.
At least two people have died in the wildfires, one in the Chelan Hills Fire in July and the other in the Upriver Fire in June in the Spokane area.
It will take weeks before the state gets an answer from the White House on Monday’s request for what is called a major disaster declaration. 
“What we need right now is the federal government to move very, very, very quickly,” Ferguson said. “We need the federal government to step up and help out folks right here in our community who are really, really hurt and need that help.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Since Trump retook office last year, concerns have festered about his politicization of disaster aid, favoring Republican-led states while shutting out states run by Democrats. Washington saw this with Trump’s denial of aid for the 2024 bomb cyclone windstorm.
The president did OK a disaster declaration for the historic flooding that hit the state in December. This resulted in the distribution of upward of $14 million in federal assistance.
Ferguson, a Democrat, and U.S. Rep. Michael Baumgartner, R-Spokane, asked last month to meet with the president to discuss the then-forthcoming request. They haven’t heard back, Ferguson said Monday, though the governor noted federal officials have so far been “tremendously helpful.”
Baumgartner said he spoke with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Monday morning. Mullin’s agency oversees the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Baumgartner is confident Trump will approve the state’s request.
“This has just been a unified effort across the board,” Baumgartner said, “and that has been great to see.”
Washington’s 12-member congressional delegation penned a letter to Trump on Monday urging him to approve the state’s funding request.
Speeding up the rebuild
Sherry Merritt lost her home of 45 years in the Spokane fires. Her family evacuated with nothing but their medicine, she said.
“I pray that all of us will recover, both mentally, spiritually, physically, and financially,” Merritt said in a press conference alongside Ferguson and other elected officials.
Ferguson tasked Lt. Gov. Denny Heck with providing recommendations that would help homeowners like Merritt rebuild faster.
For one, Ferguson said Monday that he is pushing the state Building Code Council to allow those whose homes burned down to rebuild with older energy standards to make it cheaper. Homes built before 2015 would be rebuilt to 2015 standards, and those built later would be rebuilt based on the code when the home was originally constructed, under the governor’s proposal. 
The governor will also push legislation to offer rebates on state and local sales and use taxes for costs stemming from efforts to rebuild after a disaster. He’ll also waive the state fee on building permits in wildfire-affected counties.
The state has distributed $1 million of its own individual assistance to more than 600 households. Applications are still open.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas judge weighing future of lawsuit challenging state’s abortion ban
description: A Pulaski County circuit judge is considering whether to dismiss the constitutional challenge to Arkansas’ abortion ban after hearing arguments from the plaintiffs and the state in a two-hour hearing Monday. Circuit Judge Cara Connors did not say when she expected to rule regarding the lawsuit filed earlier this year by six women and an […]
text:
Attorneys Maria Victoria Abut (second from right) and Molly Duane (right) leave the Pulaski County Circuit Courthouse on Sept. 28, 2026 after a hearing over Arkansas' abortion ban. Abut and Duane represent seven plaintiffs, including Theresa Van (second from left), pictured with her daughter, Camille (left). (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)A Pulaski County circuit judge is considering whether to dismiss the constitutional challenge to Arkansas’ abortion ban after hearing arguments from the plaintiffs and the state in a two-hour hearing Monday.
Circuit Judge Cara Connors did not say when she expected to rule regarding the lawsuit filed earlier this year by six women and an obstetrician-gynecologist challenging Arkansas’ abortion law.
Arkansas has among the nation’s strictest abortion bans, and the challenge against it is the first filed by Amplify Legal, the litigation arm of Abortion in America, an abortion-rights advocacy group co-founded by the late Planned Parenthood President Cecile Richards.
The challenged law bans the procedure with a narrow exception to save the life of a pregnant person in an emergency. It went into effect in 2022 when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the federal right to abortion, leaving the matter up to the states.
The case has drawn national attention to the fact that Arkansas’ abortion ban puts decisions about treating miscarriages and nonviable pregnancies in the hands of lawyers rather than doctors.
Connors dismissed the case in April under a 2025 state law regarding how circuit courts handle constitutional challenges, but she revived the case in May because the state Supreme Court had previously struck down the relevant law.
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Attorney General Tim Griffin, three state prosecuting attorneys and the full Arkansas State Medical Board are defendants in the case.
The lawsuit faces an uphill battle if it eventually winds up before Arkansas’ Supreme Court, where five of the seven justices have Republican ties.
2 women join lawsuit challenging Arkansas’ near-total abortion ban

 Protected liberties

Arkansas Solicitor General Autumn Hamit Patterson argued that the case should be dismissed because the state has sovereign immunity, meaning it cannot be sued in its own courts, and because “all the plaintiffs’ legal theories are flawed.”
Molly Duane, the plaintiffs’ lead attorney, said the ban infringes on the state’s constitutional rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
“Those rights do not disappear the moment an Arkansan becomes pregnant,” Duane said. 
Duane was the lead attorney for Amanda Zurawski, a Texas woman who sued the state in 2023 after being unable to obtain an abortion for a nonviable pregnancy that threatened her life. The Texas Supreme Court upheld the state’s abortion ban.
Unlike the Arkansas and United States constitutions, Texas’ constitution does not have language protecting life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
Patterson argued that the constitution’s life and liberty provision “has never been interpreted that broadly” and that it should not include abortion.
Duane told reporters after the hearing that the court should take the cited language seriously, especially since judges and attorneys “spend a lot of time worrying over other words in constitutions.”
“The fact that these constitutional provisions aren’t cited that often [in abortion litigation] doesn’t make them any less fundamental and important,” Duane said.
 ‘Reasonable medical judgment’

Duane also argued that the ban’s exception allowing abortion to save a pregnant person’s life is unconstitutionally vague. Arkansas law makes it a felony punishable by a maximum prison sentence of 10 years, a maximum fine of $100,000 or both for a medical professional who performs an abortion.
A bipartisan 2025 state law clarifies that doctors can perform abortions to save a pregnant Arkansan’s life within “reasonable medical judgment.” Duane argued that the 2025 law did not serve its stated purpose when two Fort Smith hospitals denied care to plaintiff Leitaea Lowrimore for her ectopic pregnancy in February.
Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Have Nearly Doubled. It’s Worse in States With Abortion Bans.

Fearing a misdiagnosis and potential prison time, medical professionals declined to confirm that Lowrimore had an ectopic pregnancy, Duane said.
Patterson acknowledged that ending an ectopic pregnancy saves a pregnant person’s life and is not considered abortion in the eyes of the state.
She also said the abortion ban is not vague and instead presents “a reasonable, ascertainable standard” for its exception. Connors disagreed.
“If physicians are not performing abortions they are legally allowed to perform, how is [the law] not vague?” Connors asked.
Roughly 2,600 Arkansans traveled to Illinois or Kansas to receive abortion care in 2024, according to data from the Guttmacher Institute, a reproductive rights policy and advocacy group. Five of the six women plaintiffs, including Lowrimore, received abortions in those states between 2022 and 2026, according to court documents.
The sixth woman, Theresa Van, continued her nonviable pregnancy for weeks after being denied an abortion, and she began planning her funeral in case she did not survive, according to court documents.
The plaintiffs have asked Connors to block enforcement of the law, which would require a separate hearing.
Both sides can immediately appeal Connors’ ruling on the dismissal motion. Duane told the Advocate that an appeal from the state could prevent the plaintiffs from testifying in court, so she hopes Connors conducts the preliminary injunction hearing before ruling on the state’s motion to dismiss.
Connors said she was “not convinced” that she should hold the injunction hearing first. She previously granted the state’s request to block the gathering of evidence in the case.

name: VTDigger
title: Mental health urgent care center coming to Brattleboro
description:
Health Care & Rehabilitation Services will receive $3.6 million from the Vermont Department of Mental Health to develop the center.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Mental health urgent care center coming to Brattleboro.
text:
In 2023, Health Care & Rehabilitation Services opened its Youth Stabilization Program building on Canal Street in Brattleboro. File photo by Brattleboro Reformer

This story by Chris Mays was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Sept. 24, 2026. 
Starting in January, 24/7 walk-in services at a new mental health urgent care center are expected to be offered at a location in Brattleboro. 
Health Care & Rehabilitation Services will receive $3.6 million in grant funding from the Vermont Department of Mental Health to develop the center, an announcement states. The services provider said the project will create “a much-needed community-based option for adults and youth experiencing mental health, substance use and co-occurring crises.”
Plans are underway to start offering the services in January. Additional components will come online “as implementation progresses,” according to the announcement. 
The project also will expand residential stabilization capacity for children and youth, with four short-term residential beds planned.
“Expanding access to urgent mental health care for Vermonters is essential,” Mental Health Commissioner Emily Hawes said in a statement, “and this work goes beyond just expanding access as it opens options for those most in need at times when they are most in need.”
Health Care & Rehabilitation Services said the new center will address “a critical gap in southeastern Vermont’s crisis continuum: a therapeutic place for people to go when they need more support than can be provided through Mobile Crisis, but emergency department or inpatient care may not be necessary.”
“For years, we have worked to ensure that people experiencing a mental health or substance use crisis have a place to call and someone who can respond,” CEO Anne Bilodeau said in a statement. “This new funding allows us to build the next critical piece — a safe, therapeutic place to go when someone needs more support. We are incredibly excited about what this will mean for individuals and families throughout southeastern Vermont. It gives our communities another option for helping people receive the right care, in the right setting, at the right time.”
The Mental Health Urgent Care Center will provide adults and youth with peer support, crisis intervention and stabilization, medical support, care coordination, assessment and connection to ongoing services. Also, the center will support individuals experiencing co-occurring mental health and substance use conditions.
The project was discussed Friday morning at the One Brattleboro table, where stakeholders meet to improve community resilience, safety and public health. 
“(T)here was consensus that this initiative will fill an important gap in our ability to make Brattleboro a safe, healthy and thriving community,” Town Manager John Potter told the Reformer.
Potter said the center will “provide an outlet to professionally address crisis mental health needs while reducing the demands for municipal services and impacts to the hospital and other service providers.”
“This will potentially be a very positive program for us,” Brattleboro Police Chief Jeremy Evans told the Reformer. “Mental health concerns have continually been a recurring theme, and offering this new alternative is great to see.”
Evans said the police department looks “forward to continuing our strong collaborations” with Health Care & Rehabilitation Services.
State’s Attorney Steven Brown applauded the service provider for the effort. 
“I am supportive of any initiative that expands access to much needed mental health care in our community,” he told the Reformer. “We have not been asked to collaborate, but I do look forward to exploring opportunities for this initiative to address the intersection of the criminal justice system and mental health.”
Specifically designed for mental health and substance use crisis care, the center isn’t intended to replace emergency medical care for physical health emergencies, according to the announcement. 
“Four short-term crisis stabilization beds will be dedicated to children and youth who need a safe, therapeutic level of support but do not require inpatient psychiatric hospitalization,” the announcement states. “The center will operate in close coordination with 988, HCRS’ Mobile Crisis services, local hospitals, outpatient providers, schools, peer support organizations, first responders, housing providers and other community partners.”
Health Care & Rehabilitation Services said it will “work with regional partners to establish referral pathways, warm handoffs, and coordinated follow-up to help individuals move more seamlessly between levels of care.”
“The initiative responds to needs identified through HCRS’ Community Needs Assessment and regional crisis data, including high emergency department utilization, barriers to timely crisis stabilization, and the need for additional community-based alternatives,” the announcement states. “Southeastern Vermont has experienced particularly high emergency department utilization associated with mental health crises, underscoring the need for another option for individuals who require immediate support but not hospital-level care.”
Health Care & Rehabilitation Services is working to finalize leased space in Brattleboro for the center, according to the announcement. Over the coming months, the organization plans to prepare the facility, recruit and train staff, develop operational workflows and continue coordinating with community partners in preparation for the January launch.
About 34 positions are expected to be created for the new center. A job fair to support recruitment is scheduled for 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Tuesday at Brooks Memorial Library. More information can be found on the career page at hcrs.org. 
Brattleboro Select Board Chair Oscar Heller described mental health as “a core issue affecting our community that feeds into the other challenges we face.”
“It’s a welcome sight to see significant resources flowing towards addressing it, and I look forward to seeing how HCRS develops their new program,” he told the Reformer. 
Selectboard member Isaac Evans-Frantz said he’s “delighted to see this news.”
“Expansion of support in Brattleboro is a critical investment in the people of our community,” he told the Reformer. “With too few places to turn for help, too often our neighbors experiencing mental health and substance abuse crises have depended on our local emergency room for care. This has overburdened the emergency room and emergency personnel, cost much and has resulted in delays in care.”
With the new center being open 24/7, Evanz-Frantz said, the community will be offered “a much-needed alternative.”

outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Trump used impossible foreign labor standards as tariff workaround, small businesses say
text: WASHINGTON — Small businesses will once again challenge President Donald Trump’s tariffs in federal court this week as they continue to feel the squeeze of the administration’s roller coaster policy on import taxes.Spice importer Burlap & Barrel and rare watch importer Collective Horology will argue Wednesday in the Court of International Trade in New York City that the Trump administration did not properly establish forced labor cases against dozens of U.S. trading partners before levying duties on goods that numerous American importers buy.The Office of the United States Trade Representative announced in late July that products from 60 top U.S. trading partners will be tariffed at 10% or 12.5%, depending on whether governments have or have not developed laws meant to combat forced labor. The new tariffs cover 99.4% of all goods imported into the United States, according to the office.The plaintiffs, represented by the legal advocacy nonprofit Liberty Justice Center, allege the administration exceeded its tariff authority delegated by Congress under the forced labor statute, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The plaintiffs also argue the tariffs are “arbitrary and capricious” because U.S. trade officials relied on “generalized assertions” that labor policies in 60 economies imposed concrete economic harm to the U.S.Trade law expert blasts Trump usageAmbassador Alan Wm. Wolff, a former trade official who helped draft the forced labor statute and filed a brief in support of the small business plaintiffs, said Section 301 was “designed for sort of a rifle shot of retaliation against a single foreign country doing some particular act that's been verified.”Wolff served in the Carter and Ford administrations, and later as a deputy director-general at the World Trade Organization.“I sat through the executive sessions of the committees that were drafting the statute,” he said. “No one ever conceived of the idea that you could just create a sort of a fake, bogus test for other countries – 60 of them — that none of them could meet.”Wolff told States Newsroom in an interview Sept. 21 that the statute has never been used in this way.“If the U.S. was serious about forced labor being dealt with in this fashion … it would say, ‘Well, we'll review it every six months, and if you put in a statute that has the following provisions, we would probably lift the tariff,’” he said. “There's none of that because the purpose is to have the tariff, not to combat forced labor,” he continued.The Department of Justice declined to comment Monday on ongoing litigation.The White House and the Office of the United States Trade Representative did not respond Monday.One tariff after anotherThe legal challenge on behalf of small business plaintiffs is not the first one to be brought by the Liberty Justice Center, a nonprofit that focuses on “high-impact cases that defend individual liberty and challenge government overreach,” according to its website.In February, the organization secured a victory against the Trump administration when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the president’s unprecedented executive tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, referred to as IEEPA, were unconstitutional.The organization won the case on behalf of several small business plaintiffs, ranging from an Illinois-based toymaker and New York-based wine importer, to a Utah-based plastics producer and a Pennsylvania-based fishing gear company, among others.Almost immediately after the high court struck down his emergency tariffs, Trump imposed a new wide-reaching 10% tariff on global imports under a separate statute – Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. The statute limited Trump to only 150 days.The administration concurrently opened sweeping trade practice investigations, including under the Section 301 forced labor statute, on nearly all U.S. trading partners. The government announced its forced labor findings just as the earlier tariffs expired at the 150-day mark.New duties ‘blatantly pretextual’Sara Albrecht, the Liberty Justice Center’s CEO, described the administration’s new forced labor tariffs as “blatantly pretextual” to replace duties imposed under Section 122.“And Section 122 was pretextual for the IEEPA tariff that rolled off this year when he lost at the Supreme Court. So we feel like our job wasn't done because we struck down the IEEPA tariff, and then the administration just did it again,” Albrecht said.The organization is again representing small business plaintiffs who allege harm to their bottom line because of the administration’s tariff policy. Burlap & Barrel, a New York-based company with warehouses in Hagerstown, Maryland, and Las Vegas imports spices from 22 countries. The California-based Collective Horology imports high-end mechanical watches from independent makers in six European nations.“They are two individual American small businesses that have been swept up in a political kind of debate. We're arguing this on behalf of every American small business, every American business that is being forced to once again pay illegal tariffs,” Albrecht said.The organization has asked the Court of International Trade for class status.“You have to keep in mind that they're just getting their IEEPA refunds right now, and we're almost done with that. But they had to start paying Section 122 (tariffs), and then when that stopped, they had to pay Section 301 (tariffs). So a lot of these businesses are effectively loaning all of their working capital to the U.S. government while we kind of sort this out in court,” Albrecht said.The Liberty Justice Center had also challenged the Section 122 tariffs on behalf of Burlap & Barrel.U.S. Customs and Border Protection is still in the process of refunding roughly $166 billion worth of tariffs paid by businesses under Trump’s IEEPA import charges.“We're a small nonprofit that is, you know, 12 attorneys trying to again strike down the tariffs, and it would be nice if someone else wanted to jump into the fight,” Albrecht said. “So we're doing the best we can, and I think we've done a good job so far.”Prior to the tariff case win, the organization was most well known for its role in successfully arguing before the U.S. Supreme Court in Janus v. AFSCME, in which its client Mark Janus challenged public sector unions over paying dues.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Water conservation program officials ask New Mexico lawmakers to boost funding amid drought
description: Water conservation officials and farmers briefed New Mexico lawmakers on Monday regarding the success of grant funding aimed at helping farmers and ranchers upgrade water conservation infrastructure to efficiently collect and reuse rainfall water, as the state suffers from record low snowpack and drought conditions.
text:
Administrators, scientists and farmers briefed lawmakers on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee on Sept. 28, 2026, regarding the success of funding aimed at helping farmers and ranchers upgrade water conservation infrastructure, and asked for more money for future funding cycles. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)State funding aimed at helping farmers and ranchers implement water conservation techniques is helping address a variety of drought-related problems, administrators, scientists and farmers told New Mexico lawmakers on Monday. They asked legislators to double the program’s funding next year as the state continues to suffer from record low snowpack and drought conditions.
A presentation in front of the Water and Natural Resources Committee during its meeting in Taos noted that 80% of New Mexico’s water benefits agriculture, and this year’s record low snowpack and ongoing drought conditions have negatively impacted farmers’ and ranchers’ ability to produce crops and raise livestock. 
In addition, much of the water that can be reused from rainfall and flooding becomes “essentially wasted” without the proper collection and irrigation systems, Jon Hupp, owner of Goat Tree Orchard in Taos County, told lawmakers.
To address these issues, the Agricultural Water Resilience Program, administered by the New Mexico Water Resources Research Institute at New Mexico State University, provides grants — up to $300,000 each — for farmers and ranchers to upgrade their infrastructure to collect and save water for agricultural production. The state Legislature appropriated $5 million in fiscal year 2026 for the program and doubled funding to $10 million in FY27. 
The New Mexico Water Research Institute projects more than 938,000,000 gallons of water will be saved as a result of the projects funded in the 2026 cycle.
Hupp received $123,600 from the program to upgrade his irrigation system in order to reuse water,along with flow meters to measure water use and fertilization process. 
“Frankly, it is hard to overstate how important this is,” Hupp said. “Without it, we would probably be wiped out by decreasing water availability which drastically limits our operations,” Hupp said.
Conservation officials said Monday they would like to see the funding for the program increase again in next year’s session. Debbie Hughes, executive director of the New Mexico Association of Conservation Districts, which oversees the 47 soil and water districts in the state, said she hopes to see funding doubled to $20 million to meet demand — a sentiment echoed by Hupp.
“We have to continue to improve the infrastructure so that water can be delivered and collected in a more efficient way,” Hupp said. “I think that if we don’t start doing that now, with the aridification and drought, a lot of people like me are going to disappear.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana ‘making the case’ to host US Space Academy
description: Leaders talked about their bid for the academy before approving $5 million for a separate collaboration with Nvidia.
text:
Airmen from the Grissom Air Reserve Base near Kokomo, Indiana, participate in the military appreciation lap at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway before the Brickyard 400 on July 26, 2026. (Photo by Ben Mota/434th Air Refueling Wing)Indiana has entered the latest space race.
An increasing number of states are jockeying for the honor — and the benefits — of hosting the nation’s first Space Academy.
President Donald Trump established the academy Aug. 28, in an executive order that sought to develop a “professional corps of civically grounded leaders prepared to advance American interests within the space domain.”
Alabama, California, Florida, Ohio, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, New Mexico and Texas are all possibilities, The Hill reported — with officials in some states establishing dedicated leadership teams, filing legislation, writing letters to the and more.
U.S. Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana joined the fray last Thursday, when he penned a letter urging the presidential commission in charge of the academy to consider the Hoosier State’s Grissom Air Reserve Base and Aeroplex.
The site is near Kokomo, spread across Cass and Miami counties.
“Grissom offers a fitting connection between America’s earliest achievements in human spaceflight and the next generation of American space leaders,” Banks wrote.
He touted the site’s lengthy runway and space for classrooms, housing and training infrastructure, plus the state’s low cost of living, nearby research universities, prepared workforce and role in the industry.
Indiana Economic Development Corp. President Josh Richardson, left, Gov. Mike Braun and Commerce Secretary Chuck Goodrich lead an IEDC board meeting on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Gov. Mike Braun underscored the effort on Monday.
“We’re making the case for Indiana to play a major role in new United States Space Academy, partnering with Purdue in building on Indiana’s strengths in aerospace engineering, national security, and advanced manufacturing,” he said at an Indiana Economic Development Corp. board meeting.
But, he told reporters afterward, “There’s been nothing in particular. That’s just out there as something that we’re going to be interested in because we’re leading in all the other arenas as well.”
State bids are due Oct. 26, according to the request for information NASA released earlier this month.
The civilian academy won’t be a military institution like West Point or the Naval Academy. NASA, according to the bid document, wants to prepare “future scientists, engineers, astronauts, pilots, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, warfighters, and other leaders.”
The federal agency hopes to start classes by 2028 with an inaugural class of 300 students at an interim academy location, which would ramp up to 1,200 students by the time a permanent campus is ready in 2031.
The academy should have the room to expand to 4,000 students later.

title: Iowa farmers behind on harvest as wet September comes to close
description: In typical years, according to crop progress and condition reports from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, farmers have harvested about 10% of corn acres and 15% or more of soybean acres by the end of September. The latest USDA report, however, shows just 3% of soybean acres and 5% of corn acres have been harvested […]
text:
Rain over a corn field in late September 2026 near Minburn, Iowa. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) In typical years, according to crop progress and condition reports from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, farmers have harvested about 10% of corn acres and 15% or more of soybean acres by the end of September. The latest USDA report, however, shows just 3% of soybean acres and 5% of corn acres have been harvested in Iowa. 
Farmers have had few days to get out in the field, as the state has had unseasonably wet conditions most of September. Iowa climate data shows this month as being one of the wettest Septembers on record. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The report noted farmers, on average, had just over one day of weather suitable for field work during the Sept. 21 through Sept. 27 reporting period. Between the latest reporting period and the week prior, corn and soybean harvest percentages have increased just 1%.
Corn and soybean maturity is also behind the five-year averages and the 2025 crops. In 2025, 78% of corn had reached maturity by the reporting period, compared to 72% of corn in the stage as of the latest report. Soybeans dropping leaves were reported on 62% of Iowa soybean acres in the latest report, which is significantly behind the 80% reported in 2025 at the same time period and 76% in the five-year average. 
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said in a statement that farmers are “eager to harvest their crops and will be ready to get combines rolling as soon as the fields dry out.”
Corn and soybean crops continue to rate highly, with corn at 75% good to excellent for the reporting period and soybeans at 74% good to excellent. 
According to State Climatologist Justin Glisan, Iowa received a statewide average of 1.26 inches, which is only about half of an inch above the climatological normal. Glisan wrote that, “while rainfall was above normal across Iowa during the reporting period, it was not as unseasonably wet as the previous two weeks” when the state received more than a month’s worth of rain. 
While Iowa had some drought conditions in northwestern portions of the state earlier in the season, the vast majority of the state, 87%, is not experiencing any drought conditions according to the latest map from the U.S. Drought Monitor. 
Glisan said that areas of central and western Iowa, where precipitation totals were highest, received 1-2 inches more than normal during the reporting period. 
The above average precipitation for the month has also meant a larger share of topsoil and subsoil have surplus moisture conditions. According to the report, nearly 40% of topsoil and nearly 30% of subsoil in Iowa had surplus moisture conditions as of the reporting period. 
Glisan also reported that the state was abnormally cool for the week, with some stations reporting averages as much as three degrees below the normal of 60.7 degrees Fahrenheit. The statewide average temperature for the period was nearly 1 degree below the normal.

title: URI trustees seek $20.3 million boost in fiscal 2028 budget request
description: University of Rhode Island (URI) trustees on Friday unanimously approved a request seeking a $20.3 million increase in the university’s 2028 budget amid projections of an $8.1 million shortfall this fiscal year. Rising inflation and missed enrollment targets were among the reasons cited for the school’s request of $139.8 million in state support next year, [[...]
text:
University of Rhode Island President Marc Parlange speaks to lawmakers, students and other URI supporters during URI Day at the Rhode Island State House in April 2025. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)University of Rhode Island (URI) trustees on Friday unanimously approved a request seeking a $20.3 million increase in the university’s 2028 budget amid projections of an $8.1 million shortfall this fiscal year.
Rising inflation and missed enrollment targets were among the reasons cited for the school’s request of $139.8 million in state support next year, a 17% increase in operating support for the school over this year. 
The board’s approval at its first meeting of the fall semester comes ahead of the Sept. 30 deadline for state agencies to submit their budget requests for the upcoming fiscal year. 
The full board’s affirmation follows an initial vetting and a unanimous recommendation of approval from the trustees’ Finance and Facilities Committee on Sept. 14. The school ended fiscal year 2026 on June 30 with a $2.2 million shortfall in its unrestricted budget — an improvement from the $3.8 million gap officials had anticipated.
An estimated $153.4 million is needed for URI’s operating needs in the upcoming fiscal year, according to a presentation by Abby Benson, senior vice president and chief financial officer for the school’s Division of Administration and Finance. That includes the school’s current $119.5 million appropriation for fiscal year 2027, plus the projected $8.1 million shortfall and $25.8 million to maintain the current level of services, which includes employee pay, contract costs, utilities, insurance, and athletics. 
URI expects $13.6 million in additional revenue from tuition and other fees, which is factored into its budget request and reduces the amount of money the school is asking the state to provide.
Benson told trustees fewer students returned for their next year or semester than expected, reducing tuition revenue, though this decline was somewhat offset by revenue gains from online programs.
The university expects to fall short of its fall 2026 enrollment target. While final student census numbers will not be available until October, Benson said financial concerns were the reason most often cited by prospective students who did not enroll.
Reasons for the enrollment troubles included reduced federal aid opportunities, limits on federal loans and competing financial offers or programs from public colleges and universities within and outside Rhode Island. URI lacks a free tuition program comparable to those available at Rhode Island College and the Community College of Rhode Island. 
URI is seeking an additional $8.9 million in its budget request which would be directed toward student aid costs.
The university also plans to cut $5 million through vacancies and tighter hiring practices. Benson said URI is likely to leave some budgeted positions unfilled even though state lawmakers increased the school’s staffing cap by 200 positions earlier this year. 
Benson said the school plans to continue a budgetary review of all positions before they’re filled. 
As for the $25.8 million increase URI says it needs to maintain existing operations, it includes $13 million for employee pay and contracting, $6 million for utilities and insurance, and $2 million for athletics. 
Missing from this year’s funding request is “strategic initiatives,” for which URI requested $14.4 million last year. The money was meant to cover costs for faculty and advisers, IT improvements, and student success programs, Benson said, but the school received nothing for it in the fiscal year 2027 budget.
“We decided not to include them in the budget this year,” Benson told trustees Friday.
Instead, the university wants to focus on its expenses and financial obligations. The strategic initiatives funding tends to get no support from either the governor or the General Assembly. Benson suggested state officials see the school’s  existing “unrestricted pool of general appropriation” as a better source to fund such initiatives.
URI’s fiscal 2028 budget request seeks $139.8 million in state operating support, including money to cover a projected $8.1 million shortfall and $25.8 million more to maintain existing operations amid rising costs. The university is separately seeking $7 million for medical school planning. (University of Rhode Island presentation)
Separate line item for medical school sought
The $139.8 million request does not include the school’s separate ask for $7 million for a second year of planning for a proposed medical school at URI. The General Assembly included $5 million for planning for the medical school in this fiscal year’s budget. 
Trustees said they would like to petition state leaders for a distinct budget line for the medical school, instead of having it bundled into the school’s existing state appropriation. Benson agreed that separating funding for medical school planning into its own budget line item would help avoid distorting year-over-year comparisons of the school’s budget. The university treats the medical school money separately in its internal finances.
URI’s budget request now heads to the state Office of Management and Budget. The governor’s proposed budget takes these requests into consideration and emerges in January, after which the state legislature determines a final version of the budget during the legislative session. Rhode Island’s fiscal year begins July 1 each year.

name: VTDigger
title: New book traces Twin States’ cultural split to the soil itself
description:
“Twin States, Different Paths: The Politics of New Hampshire and Vermont,” by Brian Porto argues that the two states are “fraternal, not identical” twins.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New book traces Twin States’ cultural split to the soil itself.
text:
Brian Porto at his home in Windsor, Vt., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Porto spent the past four years of his retirement writing a book about the politics of Vermont and New Hampshire. “I was expecting differences between the two states, but there really are a lot of similarities,” he said. Alex Driehaus/Valley News

This story by Molly Hughes was first published in the Valley News on Sept. 24, 2026.
New Hampshire puts “Live Free or Die” on its license plates. Vermont’s motto is “Freedom and Unity.”
Brian Porto expected the slogans to be mostly branding. Instead, “I was surprised at how accurate I concluded it was,” said Porto, a professor emeritus at Vermont Law and Graduate School.
Free Staters came to New Hampshire looking for the smallest government and lowest taxes. “When you put a big sign (that) says ‘Live Free or Die,’ that’s probably who you’re going to get,” Porto said. In his new book, he calls the state’s license plates “ubiquitous mobile billboards for a libertarian ethic.”
Vermont’s motto asks for something different, Porto says: “We want to give you freedom to be yourself, but by the same token, we want you to be part of the community.”

Brian Porto’s book “Twin States Different Paths” at his home in Windsor, Vt., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. In writing the book, Porto said he learned just how much the physical landscapes of the two states impacted their development and economies. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

Porto spent four years writing “Twin States, Different Paths: The Politics of New Hampshire and Vermont,” which the University of Massachusetts Press published Thursday.
The book argues the two states are “fraternal, not identical” twins. They look nearly the same on a map but differ sharply in how they view government. In the preface, Porto writes that he hopes to “lend a bit of academic rigor to a favorite topic of dinner-party conversation.”
His explanation starts in the dirt and what he called “a long attenuated process.”
“New Hampshire got cheated when it came to soil,” he said. “It’s the Granite State for a good reason.”
By the mid-1800s, families were abandoning New Hampshire’s rocky farms. “The boys typically went west to find better land, and their sisters went south to work in the mills, either in Nashua or Manchester or Lowell, Massachusetts,” Porto said. Vermont’s richer soil kept it a farm state much longer, while New Hampshire turned its rivers into power for mills along the Merrimack.
That split shaped how each state marketed itself. Vermont set up the nation’s first state publicity service in 1891 and sold itself, in Porto’s words, as “a quiet pastoral place to read and think and paint.” New Hampshire advertised its low property taxes, golf courses and horse racing track.
“Vermont tends to push what it has, which is beautiful scenery, small towns,” Porto said. “New Hampshire tends to push what it doesn’t have, which is taxes.”
Vermont has banned billboards since the 1960s. “Billboards or the lack thereof are a marvelous reflection of the two cultures,” Porto said.
“A large part of what Act 250 has tried to preserve is the traditional Vermont town,” he said: buildings clustered in the village, surrounded by farm fields and forest. On the New Hampshire side of the river, “it’s much easier to build things.”
Vermont’s pitch drew newcomers who helped move the state to the political left starting in the 1950s, Porto said.
“If you really wanted to get back to the land, you went to Vermont rather than to New Hampshire,” he said.
The book lays out a short political history of each state. It then profiles New Hampshire as “the individualistic twin” and Vermont as “the community-minded twin.” Porto tests the theory on two policy fights: land use — closely tied to housing — and school finance.
He said housing made a good case because “things can be different without being starkly different.” School funding is the opposite.
In 1997, both states’ supreme courts found their school funding systems unconstitutional. Vermont passed Act 60 within months, and the state’s share of school costs jumped from about 25% to 84%.
New Hampshire’s share, 8% at the time, has since climbed to about 28%, still the lowest in the country, Porto writes. Last year, the state Supreme Court again found New Hampshire’s school funding unconstitutionally low. When a school funding case recently reached the court, 30 Republican lawmakers filed a brief asking the justices to overturn the Claremont decisions, and House Republicans later made their own attempt to challenge the rulings.
“It’s hard not to see this as shooting the messenger,” Porto said.

Brian Porto at his home in Windsor, Vt., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Porto worked as a professor at Vermont Law and Graduate School and has written several books. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

Housing follows the same pattern, just less dramatically. Vermont has Act 250, its statewide land use law. Its 2023 HOME Act ended single-family-only zoning where towns have municipal water and sewer. New Hampshire has pushed towns to allow more multifamily housing but leaves the final say local.
Porto traces that to a distrust of central power going back to Colonial days. Vermont, he said, has “a much more trusting attitude generally toward government and willingness to let government experiment.”
He doesn’t rank the two. “I didn’t want to say this is good and this is bad,” Porto said. “Here’s why they’re different. That was my main concern.”
Porto grew up in Yonkers, New York. He clerked at the New Hampshire Supreme Court in 1987 and 1988, worked for the New Hampshire Senate and has lived in Vermont since 1990. For about 25 years, he clipped Valley News stories and nonprofit reports comparing the two states.
“I saved it for my retirement,” he said.
He retired in 2022 and spent the first year of work on the book just reading each state’s history.
Porto ends the book with an open question: whether, facing demographic and economic pressures, the Twin States “remain fraternal or become more alike.”
He returned to that question throughout an interview, describing each state as being tested on the very trait that defines it.
“Can New Hampshire continue to be as tight with a buck as it has, and not suffer from that?” he said. For Vermont, it’s the reverse: “Can it continue to fund programs very generously without alienating a significant chunk of its population?”
Vermont has already run into that limit. Act 181, the 2024 land use law, included a rule requiring Act 250 review for private roads longer than 800 feet in much of the state. It drew an outcry from rural landowners, and lawmakers rolled it back this spring.
“Those of us who have a lot of formal education and think we know best maybe don’t know the lives of other people,” Porto said, “and we certainly ought to talk to them before we try to impose this sort of thing.”
New Hampshire is changing too. Being a conservative in the state traditionally meant being an economic conservative, Porto said, not a social one. Now, “that socially conservative stuff is starting to creep into New Hampshire politics, at least in terms of bills being introduced.”
He said Vermont’s race for governor this fall is also “largely about” that tension.
“You’re always looking for that balance between spending enough and being aggressive enough to meet problems, without causing a revolt, where people (are) saying, ‘I can’t afford to live here anymore,’” he said.
“Twin States, Different Paths” is available as of Sept. 24 from the University of Massachusetts Press.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey visits South Coast fire station she’s trying to save
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: Fire Station 9, which covers a portion of the city's North End neighborhood, had been billed for closure this fall as part of a round of city layoffs and program cuts intended to resolve what Mayor Jon Mitchell has said is a $32 million budget deficit for the city.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY looked around New Bedford Fire Station 9 at midday Monday taking stock of the state of the firehouse that was built in 1934. Her assessment wasn’t convincing.
“Yeah, I mean, you know, it’s, yeah, it’s good,” the governor said with firefighters, union officials and the area’s elected state officials surrounding her. “It’s functional, right?”
The 92-year-old fire station had been slated to be closed this fall as New Bedford, like numerous communities all over Massachusetts, contends with a local budget deficit. The governor traveled to the South Coast to highlight the section of the $2.24 billion supplemental budget she filed last week that would provide New Bedford with $1.3 million that the mayor has committed to using to keep the station open instead. 
“If you think about this location, you’ve got four grammar schools, one middle school, a high school – it’s so important. It was really important to me that this station stay open and that it stays staffed,” Healey said. “Public safety is job one in government.”
Fire Station 9, which covers a portion of the city’s North End neighborhood, had been billed for closure this fall as part of a round of city layoffs and program cuts intended to resolve what Mayor Jon Mitchell has said is a $32 million budget deficit for the city. Mitchell had said the city would need to do away with 58 unfilled positions and lay off 34 workers, in addition to closing the fire station.
The New Bedford Light reported that Mitchell’s planned cuts were met with fierce resistance from city firefighters and their union. The outlet said Mitchell wanted the union to agree to reduce staffing levels from four firefighters per truck to three and said the closure would be necessary without such an agreement. Mitchell did not attend Monday’s event with Healey.
In a press release last week, Mitchell said the governor’s inclusion of the $1.3 million request followed weeks of discussions between the city and state.
“To be sure, the long-term financial challenges facing the City, driven by unrestrained pension and employee health insurance costs, remain with us, but my hope is that the additional state aid buys us time for compromise with our local public employee unions, members of the City Council, and Retirement Board,” Mitchell said. “Everyone should take advantage of the opportunity this funding creates for putting City finances on a stronger footing.”
If the Legislature approves Healey’s request, the state money will be used to provide additional local aid to New Bedford through the the Executive Office of Public Safety & Security’s Municipal Public Safety Staffing (MPSS) Program, the city said. Mitchell has committed to using the funds to keep Engine 9 in service for now “with the promise of continued operation of Engine 9 should MPSS grant funding come to be included annually in future state budgets,” the city said.
The mayor’s office said Mitchell has been arguing since at least 2018 that “New Bedford has been unfairly denied access to this important state assistance for local fire and police departments.”
In 2018, Mitchell wrote to the city’s delegation on Beacon Hill to point out that eligibility for the program created in 2010 had been “limited only to localities that had submitted grant applications in past years,” which cut off access to the program for cities like New Bedford that were eligible but had not submitted applications previously. The state has said there are 10 municipalities that are eligible for MPSS funds.
“The stated purpose of the Municipal Public Safety Staffing program is to restore or retain laid-off police officers and/or firefighters, or to provide additional overtime funding for those departments. It is ironic (and inequitable) that wealthy jurisdictions such as Newton and Framingham continue to receive allocations under this grant while others do not,” Mitchell wrote in 2018. He largely repeated the same argument in a letter to the delegation this spring.
Healey said she is “confident they’ll take swift action” when asked about the prospects of the Legislature approving the New Bedford money, which appears in section 168 of the 196-section bill. Joining Healey at the firehouse Monday were state Reps. Antonio Cabral of New Bedford, Mark Sylvia of Fairhaven and Steven Ouellette of Westport.
“The way I look at it is, we’ve got to deal with some short-term funding problems right now, which are real across the state. You know, a lot of our cities and towns are struggling right now with their budgets. The cost of healthcare has gone up across the country … that’s one of the things that’s impacting municipal budgets, along with other things that have raised costs in our economy,” Healey said. “So it’s a short term – what do we need to do right now? To me, it was very important to come up with funds to keep the station open and support the work out of Engine 9, but we’re looking at what are long-term things we need to do to make sure that all of our fire departments across the state are well resourced and well funded.”
The governor said her administration has “increased the amount of funding” for municipal public safety grant awards that will be announced soon, and she also said she wants to develop a financing structure for municipal pubic safety buildings modeled on the Mass. School Building Authority.
“Massachusetts, we’re an old state. We’ve been at this for a long time and some of these stations are as old as Massachusetts, it seems,” she said. “So we got to look at that. Obviously, money doesn’t grow on trees and there’s only so much we’re working with … and that’s why I like the financing mechanism that would allow us, through our bonding capacity, to maybe go out and build more and new public safety facilities around the state.”

title: Hawkeye Community College to lead Workforce Pell program expansion initiative
description: Hawkeye Community College will lead a statewide initiative between community colleges and state organizations to establish short-term training programs and expand Iowa’s Workforce Pell offerings. The Waterloo-based community college announced Monday it has been named the lead institution in a new initiative with the goal of establishing more than 50 Workforc[...]
text:
Hawkeye Community College will lead a $10.8 million grant-funded initiative to develop more Workforce Pell programs in Iowa. (Photo courtesy of Hawkeye Community College)Hawkeye Community College will lead a statewide initiative between community colleges and state organizations to establish short-term training programs and expand Iowa’s Workforce Pell offerings.
The Waterloo-based community college announced Monday it has been named the lead institution in a new initiative with the goal of establishing more than 50 Workforce Pell-eligible programs in Iowa by 2030, funded by a $10.8 million grant from the U.S. Department of Labor.
“The federal investment in Workforce Pell is a huge step in creating a highly skilled workforce our employers need and preparing Iowans for high-demand and high-paying jobs,” said Todd Holcomb, president of Hawkeye Community College, in a news release.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Iowa STRONG, or Iowa Systems, Training, and Resources for Opportunity, Navigation, and Growth, is a collaborative project between Iowa’s community colleges, the Iowa Department of Education and Iowa Workforce Development.
The Workforce Pell programs to be developed under the grant-funded initiative will span advanced manufacturing, construction, other skilled trades and healthcare, according to the college.
Iowa Central Community College was the first institution in the U.S. to receive federal approval for its emergency medical technician program to become Workforce Pell eligible. Workforce Pell allows students in short-term training programs, between eight and 15 weeks, to qualify for federal financial aid, with award amounts prorated based on program length.
Hawkeye Community College serves as the primary recipient and fiscal agent for the four-year grant, Executive Director of Public Relations and Marketing Mary Pat Moore said in an email, and 11 out of the state’s 15 community colleges will also receive direct funding to develop new programs or update existing ones to meet Workforce Pell program requirements.
The community college’s HVAC, CDL, CNC machining, construction and pharmacy technician programs will be its focus for Workforce Pell alignment through the initiative, the release stated.
Iowa Workforce Development will also use grant funds to bolster its wage record reporting infrastructure, connect with employers and “support statewide data integration and outcomes reporting,” the release stated. The Iowa Department of Education will work with community colleges to ensure program compliance for Workforce Pell.
“With the Iowa STRONG project, we are not only expanding short-term pathways into high-demand careers, but also establishing the robust data infrastructure needed to track outcomes, measure success, and ensure our training continues to meet the evolving needs of our workforce,” Holcomb said in the release.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota National Guard leader urges community support for new fighter jets in Sioux Falls
description: SIOUX FALLS – The adjutant general of the South Dakota National Guard encouraged business leaders in Sioux Falls to make a “full-throated” case for bringing newer Air Force jets to the city. The South Dakota Air National Guard’s 114th Fighter Wing is located at Joe Foss Field, near the Sioux Falls Regional Airport. There are […]
text:
Sioux Falls Rotarian Steve Watson, left, leads a discussion with South Dakota National Guard Adjutant General Mark Merrill on Sept. 28, 2026 at a meeting of the Sioux Falls Downtown Rotary Club at the Military Heritage Alliance in Sioux Falls (John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS – The adjutant general of the South Dakota National Guard encouraged business leaders in Sioux Falls to make a “full-throated” case for bringing newer Air Force jets to the city.
The South Dakota Air National Guard’s 114th Fighter Wing is located at Joe Foss Field, near the Sioux Falls Regional Airport. There are 450 full-time and 650 part-time staff stationed there, maintaining and operating a squadron of 18 permanently assigned aircraft.
Those aircraft are F-16 fighter jets, but South Dakota officials want to see those jets,first built in 1988 and 1989, replaced with F-35s.
The craft have been upgraded and are well-maintained, Major General Mark Morrell told the Sioux Falls Downtown Rotary Club during its Monday luncheon at the Military Heritage Alliance, but “you can only bolt so much stuff on them.”
State to help fund Rapid City office building for defense contractor Northrop Grumman

“We’re long overdue for investment,” Morrell said.
The F-35s began rolling out more than a decade ago and are already in service nationally and globally. The Air Force is now in the process of choosing two of the last locations for them from a list of nine possible locations, Morrell said. An initial winnowing of those options will come in December, with a final decision in spring.
The other states in the running are Minnesota, Ohio, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Colorado, Indiana, South Carolina. Washington, D.C. is also a contender
When asked by Rotarian Steve Watson what might happen if South Dakota isn’t selected, Morrell said he doesn’t know exactly, but that the thought makes him “a little bit nervous” about the future of Joe Foss Field Air National Guard Station.
“I’ll say that we’ll do what we have always done, and that’s we’ll deliver combat readiness with the platforms we have with excellence, every single day, until those platforms are no longer viable,” Morrell said.
Selling points for South Dakota
South Dakota has a lot going for it, Morrell said. Ellsworth Air Force Base near Rapid City will soon be home to the B-21 Raider stealth bomber, an aircraft typically escorted by a fighter jet. Morrell said coordination between the two programs would weigh in the state’s favor.
He also pointed to the engineering programs at South Dakota State University and South Dakota Mines, as well as cybersecurity and cyberdefense programs at Dakota State University as valuable sources of local expertise for an F-35 squadron. 
Gov. Larry Rhoden’s establishment of an infrastructure and resilience task force in 2025 and of the South Dakota Defense Institute this summer offer proof, Morrell said, that the state can be “nimble” in responding to military needs.
The task force is meant to “strengthen South Dakota’s resilience by identifying infrastructure vulnerabilities, recommending strategies to improve preparedness, and fostering collaboration among public and private partners,” according to Rhoden’s office. The Rapid City-based defense institute was launched as a “centralized hub for defense collaboration, connecting industry, government, and education to strengthen South Dakota’s contributions” to military  and security operations, according to a Rhoden press release.
The task force and institute each spent money on defense projects in 2026 from the Future Fund, a pool of dollars paid for through unemployment taxes, to support economic development projects in the state. The institute’s founding in April was supported by $6 million from the Future Fund.
Last week, Rhoden announced that the state would contribute $1 million from the fund to support the construction of an office building near Ellsworth for Northrup Grumman, the defense contractor building the B-21s.
Community support to play a role
State providing $6 million to grow national security jobs, governor announces

The Sioux Falls business community has been a solid supporter of the 114th Fighter Wing, according to Mitch Rave, public policy vice president for the Greater Sioux Falls Chamber of Commerce.
Since 2007, Rave said, the chamber has had a group of business and nonprofit leaders that meets monthly to address the needs of service members, and the business community has long supported the state’s National Guard.
The collection of leaders works on“pushing one rock up the hill to get something done,” for veterans and the military community, Rave said.
“And right now that’s the pursuit of this new fighter,” he said.
Rave said his local chamber and the South Dakota Chamber of Commerce and Industry are collecting supportive letters to submit to the state’s Congressional delegation to help them push for the F-35 in Sioux Falls. Rave flashed a QR code on the screen during the talk that linked to a form letter for Rotarians to use, encouraging them to personalize the letters and add anecdotes about business leaders’ experiences with veterans and specific ways they can support the Air Force in the event Sioux Falls is chosen as an F-35 location.
Morrell, who is the adjutant general for the Air National Guard and the Army National Guard in Sioux Falls, said he needs the community to make a strong case to Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink. The secretary is a Lemmon native, and Morrell said he hopes the South Dakota native can be convinced that his home state is the right place for the new fighter jets.
If South Dakota makes it through the first round in the selection process in December, Morrell said, he’d hope that the state can keep up the drumbeat through the spring to earn a final selection. 
“We’ve got to give him a really well-reasoned argument and a full-throated argument from the entire South Dakota citizenry and business community about why he should choose us, and just instantly validate that it was the correct decision,” Morrell said. “That’s what we’re after here.”
