title: One-year contracts won’t help Vermont’s schools
description:
Forcing school boards to hire superintendents on one-year contracts won't build the stability Vermont's education overhaul needs.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  One-year contracts won’t help Vermont’s schools.
text:
Dear Editor,
This time of year, I trade in the cup of coffee for a mug of warm apple cider. The leaves are starting to turn, mornings are colder, and schools are settling into familiar late September rhythms.
It is a beautiful time to be a school leader in Vermont. It is also a strange one.
Vermont is embarking on the widest transformation of its education system in decades. And now we face a new wrinkle: School boards have been instructed by the Agency of Education to hire superintendents on one-year contracts instead of standard multiyear contracts.
So here’s the question. Can Vermont redesign its schools while keeping the people who have to lead the redesign? Because, c’mon, somebody has to do the actual work.
It seems like school leaders are doing it all: explaining a merger to a skeptical community, defending a budget — more than once, sometimes — reassuring a teacher and answering a parent’s 11 p.m. email. And then arriving before sunup the next morning to do it all again.
If Vermont wants school leaders to guide this transformation, it needs to think carefully about what keeps experienced people in the room. It shouldn’t be a surprise that we all do our best work when there is stability. And forcing school boards to issue one-year contracts won’t promote continuity or stability.

READ MORE

So here’s the challenge for state policymakers. If you want experienced leaders to carry Vermont through this transformation, start treating leadership stability as part of the transformation itself. Give superintendents enough time to finish the job.
Don’t just redesign the system. Give school boards the go-ahead to invest in the people who will have to make it work.
Steven Berbeco
Winooski, Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  One-year contracts won’t help Vermont’s schools.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Roger Marshall alleges defamation in new ad about former Kansas patient arrested while in debt
description: TOPEKA — Lawyers for a Kansas Republican U.S. senator running for reelection sent his opponent a cease-and-desist letter demanding the Democrat stop airing an ad featuring one of the senator’s former patients. The lawyers for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, said in a Monday letter that the Rev. Adam Hamilton’s campaign had published and distributed […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, appears on Sept. 12, 2026, at the Kansas State Fair debate. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Lawyers for a Kansas Republican U.S. senator running for reelection sent his opponent a cease-and-desist letter demanding the Democrat stop airing an ad featuring one of the senator’s former patients.
The lawyers for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, said in a Monday letter that the Rev. Adam Hamilton’s campaign had published and distributed ads about Marshall’s medical debt collection practices that were “defamatory.”
The ad begins with Meischa Zimmerman, who said she was arrested while eight months pregnant for missing a $50 payment to Marshall. She was paying roughly $50 a month to account for 18% interest on nearly $3,600 in total debt, according to court records. 
The woman was one of more than 700 patients who Marshall sued while a practicing physician in Great Bend, according to reporting by the New York Times. 
“The unmistakable message to a reasonable viewer is that Senator Marshall caused a pregnant patient to be arrested and jailed for missing a single $50 payment. That message is false in every material respect,” the letter said.
The Hamilton campaign’s ad had been viewed more than one million times on X.
Heartland Regional OBGYN, where Marshall worked, opened a case against the woman in December 2009, according to court documents. Zimmerman was first arrested in 2011. She said in the Hamilton campaign ad that she was handcuffed while pregnant in front of her 2-year-old daughter.
Marshall’s lawyers took issue with three facets of the ad. They said Zimmerman wasn’t arrested for a missed payment but, instead, for failing to appear in court. They said the campaign ad frames the premise of the arrest on a $50 bill rather than the sum of Zimmerman’s debts. They said the arrest wasn’t a surprise, arguing that court records show Zimmerman “was called to court in three different counties by eight different businesses over a multi-year period, including by a different hospital and in an eviction proceeding.”
Zimmerman said in the ad: “Roger Marshall preyed on the low-income families of Kansas.” 
The letter demanded the Hamilton campaign within 24 hours remove the ad, issue a formal retraction and apology and cease further republication or promotion of false claims.
“Falsely accusing a physician of having a pregnant patient arrested over a $50 bill strikes directly at Senator Marshall’s professional integrity as a physician and his fitness for public office, and it has been broadcast to thousands of Kansas voters in the final weeks of an election,” the cease-and-desist letter said.
As of Monday afternoon, the campaign had neither issued an apology nor removed the ad from social media.
Hamilton’s campaign, Hamilton for Kansas, spent at least $7,500 to play the ad to YouTube users between 165,000 and 280,000 times from Friday to Monday, according to Google ad tracking. 
Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for the campaign, said that “not once” did Marshall dispute Meischa’s story “that his lawyers had her arrested in front of her children.” 
“The lies in his letter are blatant and reek of desperation,” Brody said. “The truth is what Roger Marshall did is extreme and hurt Kansans. Voters should know the truth about who their senator is and what he’s done.”
Marshall said in an Instagram post: “This ad is a complete lie and multiple organizations have called for the ad to be pulled from TV.”
Samantha Cantrell, regional press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee, issued a statement calling the ad a “manufactured hit piece by Hamilton and national Democrats” and called for it to be taken down.
“Adam Hamilton knows a Democrat has not won a Senate seat in Kansas in nearly 100 years, so he is deliberately lying about Roger Marshall to deceive voters,” Cantrell said.
The cease-and-desist letter is the latest friction in an increasingly contentious U.S. Senate campaign between the former OB-GYN and the Kansas City-area pastor. What once appeared to national forecasters as a safe Republican win has veered closer into toss-up territory as Hamilton has fundraised and campaigned across the state since winning a crowded Democratic primary in August. 
Hamilton has billed himself as the candidate in the middle, attempting to appeal to moderate Republicans and Democrats and undecided voters while Marshall has leaned into his connections to President Donald Trump’s base.
The two faced a predominantly pro-Hamilton crowd at a state fair debate earlier this month and are set to take the stage together again Oct. 21 on FOX4 in a debate hosted by John Holt.

name: Daily Montanan
title: How many heroes are we deporting?
description: I believe in second chances. I have had more than a few. None deserved. All appreciated. A person’s worst day should not define the rest of their life. Think of a man sitting on death row.  After a six-day trial, he is sentence to hang.  He escapes and finds his way to the United States. He didn’t […]
text:
The statue of Thomas Francis Meagher in front of the stairs of the Montana Capitol (Photo by Eric Seidle for the Daily Montanan).I believe in second chances. I have had more than a few. None deserved. All appreciated.
A person’s worst day should not define the rest of their life.
Think of a man sitting on death row.  After a six-day trial, he is sentence to hang.  He escapes and finds his way to the United States.
He didn’t have a visa. Or a green card. He just came. He reinvented himself. He became a lawyer. He married a woman from a prominent New York family.
Do you know who I’m talking about?
Thomas Francis Meagher.
The British government convicted him of treason in 1848 and he was sentenced to death. He was 25. His sentence was commuted to life in Tasmania. He escaped in 1852 and landed in America. Five years later, he was a citizen.  In 1861, he joined the Union army.  He became the General of the Irish Brigade in our Civil War. In 1865, President Andrew Johnson appointed him Secretary of the Montana Territory. In 1866, he called Montana’s first Constitutional Convention. He died in 1867.
His statue sits in front of our Capitol in Helena.  There is another in Waterford, Ireland. Meagher County is named for him.  There is the Meagher Monument at the Antietam National Battlefield.  During WWII, we named a Liberty Ship after him, the S.S. Thomas F. Meagher.
When Meagher became territorial secretary, the governor was absent. He became our acting governor. Yes, he went from death row to being governor — in only 17 years.  He is not the only criminal we have placed in office.
The story of Thomas Francis Meagher is Montana’s story. It’s America’s story.
An immigrant found a new country and built a new life. He was a convicted criminal, a fugitive from British justice. America looked beyond Meagher’s status as a convict and a fugitive. America gave him a chance to become something more.  He became an American hero. Montana and our country are better because of Meagher and millions like him.
Here’s the hard part: Today, Meagher would not be allowed to immigrate to America.  Think of what we would have lost if America had not welcomed Thomas Francis Meagher to our country.
Our country is going through an unholy purge of immigrants today. Mass deportations. A policy of exclusion.  We hear a constant stream of racist and untrue descriptions. Others claim it’s an invasion of killers, rapists, gangbangers, and animals. Some leaders claim those people are poisoning the blood of our country, or that they’re coming from mental institutions.
History will measure those words by reality and facts.
It’s not true.  Not honest.  ICE data shows that roughly 70 of the people we have deported have absolutely no criminal record. None. Only 3% to 5% of those deported had a criminal record of violence.  The rest? Minor things like traffic violations.
Yes, they want us to believe that they are making people safer by deporting someone who had a burned-out taillight. Really, we are spending billions to protect America from minor traffic violations?
Think of the human cost:  Take a few minutes and really think about what this purge is doing to individuals, children, families and the future of our country, our neighborhoods and our schools. That’s the price of fear.
Consider the irony:  We honor Meagher with a statue in front of our Capitol —  an immigrant, and a convicted criminal.  Yet, we are deporting hundreds of thousands of people who have never been convicted of anything.  We are separating spouses, families, children from parents. These people risked their lives to pursue the American dream.
In 75 years, how will history view our treatment of immigrants?  Our deportations?  How will history understand our Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers? How about our elected leaders spewing vulgar lies? Government agents wearing face masks, assaulting and killing people. Hint: The masks are a sign — of guilt and shame. Masks aren’t righteous.
America has always been a place of second chances.  We judge people for who they are, not for what they did in the past.  A land of new beginnings and opportunity.
How will history judge our government action today?  And, how will it judge those who didn’t speak up about the erosion of our fundamental values?  We are spending roughly $200 billion on mass deportation and border security, while cutting funding for critical safety net programs.
Border security is a legitimate government action.  Securing our borders is not the same as deporting our neighbors and breaking up families.
What will our legacy be for allowing mass removal?  Mass cruelty?  All fueled by hatred, racism, and lies.
We have become a deportation state. It is a retreat from the promise of America. No chance, much less a second chance.
Thomas Francis Meagher could not immigrate to the United States today.  If he tried, he would be arrested, put in an ICE detention center, and deported.
Meagher was a hero.
But, how many heroes are we deporting?

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: CT charges its prisoners — and the financial impact can be life changing
description: Ginny Monk discusses her story, written with Andrew Brown, about a law allowing the state to charge people for the cost of their incarceration.
text:
Readjusting to life after incarceration is challenging. It’s harder when a person owes the state money for the time they spent behind bars.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Ginny Monk to discuss her article written with Andrew Brown, “They served their time in prison. Then the bills arrived.” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read their story here.
WSHU: Hello, Ginny. You and your Connecticut Mirror colleague, Andrew Brown, were inspired to investigate this issue during one of the busiest times of the legislative session, when you came across the story of a man whose daughter, Mimi Torres-Garcia, had died of severe child abuse and starvation in a mother’s care. That case had received prominent media coverage, and he was suing the state on behalf of her estate, but Victor Torres had a prison debt. Could you tell us about that?
GM: Yes, as I was reading through some of the filings in the lawsuit and in the probation case, because this case was filed on behalf of the estate of Mimi Torres, technically making it an inheritance that he would receive if he wins his lawsuit against the state, I came across a filing that didn’t make sense to me from the Department of Administrative Services saying he owed several $1,000 for the cost of his incarceration, and this was just a concept I’d never heard of before.
WSHU: Why was prison debt an issue? How did the law come about?
GM: The state of Connecticut in 1995 passed a law that allowed the Department of Correction to assess a daily fine to everyone who’s incarcerated, and then later charge them for the totality of that incurred cost. So Victor owed, as I said, several $1,000. And what we found through reporting this story was that Connecticut has one of the highest costs of incarceration in the country.
WSHU: Now the reason why they did this at that time, the crime rate was pretty high, and the prison population was expanding. You went back to the arguments that were made to implement this law, and this law was implemented at a time when we had a Republican governor who had campaigned on being tough on crime. So, could you just tell us a little bit about the framing that produced this law?
GM: Right. So we had a Republican governor, as you mentioned at the time, who really during his gubernatorial campaign said, “I’m going to be tough on crime. We’re going to get this under control,” and that was kind of something that we were hearing nationally from politicians. It was very popular to be tough on crime. So as that was happening, Connecticut passed this law. Part of the thought was we can recoup some of the money that we are spending on the cost to incarcerate all of these people, a growing number of people, and part of it was they wanted to teach them personal responsibility.
WSHU: Even at that time, there were warnings that this was not a population that could afford to pay for their incarceration, and yet that was not taken into consideration at the time.
GM: Right, as early as 1990, the Department of Correction commissioner at the time was saying, “We’ve researched this idea, and this population cannot afford to pay. It’s not financially feasible for them. It’s going to be hard to collect this money.” They went ahead with the law anyway, and kind of the results we’re seeing today are some of what people were warned about in 1990 that folks who have been incarcerated can’t afford to pay this debt, that it’s hard to collect, that it takes a lot of time.
WSHU: Now, could you tell us about some of the other cases that you came across. Like Tracy DeSenti, for instance, lost her home because the state went after her for money she owed for being incarcerated.
GM: Tracy DeSenti was one of several people we spoke to who had significant financial loss, and you’re right. She lost her home after her husband passed away. The state came to collect what he owed for the cost of his incarceration. What that meant for Tracy was that she had to sell the house because she wasn’t going to receive enough to pay off his debt without doing so. And now she’s living in a rental where she pays much more in rent than she paid in more in her mortgage.
WSHU: So let’s talk about how much the state has been able to recoup, and in the scheme of things, what that means for the state’s budget.
GM: So on average, since 2020, the state has been able to recoup about $3.3 million a year, which I think to the average person sounds like a lot of money. To the state, it is a tiny fraction of a percent of what they spend annually. And I think the key thing is that to the people they’re collecting it from, it’s life changing amounts of money.
WSHU: It could make the difference between having a home and being homeless.
GM: Right, we saw that in several cases that people lost their homes.
WSHU: And basically they become more dependent on the state.
GM: Yeah, one of the women we spoke to after she had to pay off this debt ended up having to go on SNAP benefits because she was counting on that money to support herself as she aged, and now she can’t afford to.
WSHU: I was kind of interested in a quote from the Department of Administrative Services when you asked them why they were so aggressive in going after the prison debt, and basically their response was: We’re not involved in the policy; we just are the ones that implement the law, and they’re doing their job. So the problem here is a political problem that has to be solved by lawmakers. In the past couple of years, they’ve tried to do some things. What have they tried to do, and why is that not enough?
GM: So, in 2022, they actually set out to repeal the law, and as that made its way through the legislative process, that was sort of watered down until it became sort of minor changes to collections from lawsuits. It was limiting what the state could collect from most of the formerly incarcerated population, with the exception of people who had committed the most serious violent offenses. There were a couple other small tweaks in 2024, but ultimately they haven’t been able to repeal the law like so many other states have.
WSHU: Okay, Ginny, thank you so much.
GM: Thank you.

name: VTDigger
title: Shelter isn’t charity. It’s public safety.
description:
Six years ago, a Vermont nonprofit was asked to open a shelter for the first time. That decision protected the whole of Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Shelter isn’t charity. It’s public safety..
text:
This commentary is by Paul Dragon, the executive director of the Champlain Valley Office of Economic Opportunity.
Six years ago, as Covid-19 tore through Vermont, the Champlain Valley Office of Economic Opportunity was asked to do something we’d never done before: open a shelter. What began as low-barrier, family and recovery shelters quickly became the state’s largest pandemic shelter, welcoming people experiencing homelessness from communities across Vermont.
Our staff worked around the clock under extraordinarily difficult circumstances. They showed up every day to care for people who had nowhere else to go. Alongside emergency responders, healthcare professionals and public safety personnel, they helped protect some of the state’s most vulnerable residents during a moment of profound uncertainty. They were heroes, as were shelter providers, outreach workers and emergency responders across the state. Their work demonstrated that care for vulnerable people is not separate from public health or public safety. It is an essential part of both.
My belief is simple: Moral responsibility, public health and public safety are not mutually exclusive goals when it comes to homelessness and sheltering. They are reinforcing obligations. When we provide safe shelter and services to those experiencing homelessness, we honor human dignity, improve public health outcomes and strengthen our communities.
The discussion about where shelters should be located, how they should operate and who is responsible for homelessness is not new. It is a conversation that has existed for decades and one that will almost certainly continue. We understand that shelters can have impacts on the communities where they are located. That is why we engage with communities, seek input, discuss concerns openly, proceed transparently and then make decisions about where shelters may be developed.
Often, we are balancing competing needs: the immediate needs of individuals experiencing homelessness, the broader needs of our communities and state, and the concerns of the neighborhoods and towns where shelters may be located. These questions are not easy to navigate, and they are questions all of us, as a state, will need to continue addressing together.
The number of people experiencing homelessness in Vermont has grown dramatically in recent years. Much of this increase can be attributed to a lack of affordable housing, rising costs, increasing mental health and substance use challenges, and diminished capacity throughout our mental health, recovery and residential support systems.

READ MORE

When we consider shelter development today, we consider the needs of the entire community and the state. Shelters with integrated services support individuals during some of the most difficult moments of their lives while also helping businesses, emergency services and neighbors who are often most affected by the challenges associated with unsheltered homelessness. Shelters are not only expressions of care and compassion; they are important components of public health and public safety.
As a society, we do not want to see homelessness. That much seems clear. Yet too often our frustration is directed primarily toward those experiencing homelessness themselves and how their struggles appear in our communities. At the same time, we can overlook the broader conditions that contribute to homelessness, including the lack of housing, untreated mental illness, substance use disorders, poverty and the erosion of support systems that once helped people remain stable.
The larger question is whether we believe we are morally responsible for one another, regardless of a person’s circumstances, productivity or perceived success. Are we willing to notice, value and care for those who are most vulnerable? Can we recognize the dignity and worth of every person without tying that worth to our expectations of who they should be? Can we see ourselves in others, understanding that vulnerability is not something that belongs only to someone else?
Ultimately, shelters are about more than beds and buildings. They are about who we choose to be as a community. They represent our willingness to recognize the dignity of every person, protect public health and strengthen public safety. These are not competing values. They are intertwined responsibilities.
I believe Vermont is at its best when we recognize that caring for the most vulnerable among us is not separate from caring for our communities. It is one and the same. The challenge before us is not whether we will choose between moral responsibility, public health and public safety. It is whether we will embrace all three and act with the courage, compassion and shared responsibility that this moment requires.

title: Trump thwarted in hunt for rare noncitizen voters as midterms near
text: Five weeks before Election Day, President Donald Trump’s sprawling effort to identify and remove noncitizen voters hasn’t produced the kind of large purges that could meaningfully affect the midterm elections.Even a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision giving states access to a supercharged Department of Homeland Security computer program to verify voters’ citizenship will have a limited immediate impact, election experts say. As Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, Trump and his allies have spent the past year aggressively seeking to root out noncitizen voting. They have called into question the security of the upcoming elections, following the lead of the president, who has long made spurious claims of voter fraud to dismiss unfavorable results.Those efforts are now colliding with federal law — and the reality long shown by studies and available data that noncitizen voting is rare.Little impact seen from court rulingThe Supreme Court on Sept. 25 ruled in a 6-3 decision that states can access Homeland Security’s SAVE system, which draws upon citizenship information stored across the federal government to scour voter rolls in the hunt for possible noncitizens. A district court judge had blocked the program in June.But the high court’s decision came during a quiet period under the National Voter Registration Act that prohibits most states from conducting mass purges of voters in the 90 days before a federal election. The timing limits election officials to only searching for information on individual voters, even though Homeland Security has touted SAVE to states as a tool that can quickly scan millions of names.The Supreme Court’s conservative majority acknowledged as much, writing in its unsigned opinion that the quiet period “limits the potential impact” of the court’s decision. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, writing for the court’s three liberals, agreed the decision would have minimal short-term effects but argued the possibility of disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighed any risk of harm to the government.David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, in a statement emphasized that voters will continue to experience the same safe, secure and reliable voting process this year as in the past."This decision will not have any significant impact on the 2026 election, as systematic voter list maintenance is prohibited within 90 days of a federal election, which the Supreme Court explicitly confirmed,” Becker said.Post-2026The more significant fallout from the Supreme Court’s decision may come in the weeks and months after the election, when states can once again remove large numbers of voters from their rolls. The Supreme Court is also set to hold oral arguments in December in a case that involves the reach of the National Voter Registration’s Act’s quiet period — leaving open the possibility the justices could give states more leeway to purge voters ahead of elections.But for now, the restrictions remain in place.“Until the Supreme Court says, reinterprets otherwise, the quiet period is still the quiet period,” Aaron Blacksberg, federal policy counsel at the Institute for Responsive Government, said in an interview.Separately, a U.S. district court judge on Monday blocked the Trump administration’s efforts to require states to use SAVE as a condition of receiving some Federal Emergency Management Agency grants. Judge Amir H. Ali, an appointee of President Joe Biden, wrote that FEMA exceeded its authority in imposing election-related requirements.Is the data reliable?SAVE’s critics, which include Democrats and privacy advocates, warn that the system relies on incomplete and sometimes outdated data, resulting in false positives. SAVE was previously used to check whether noncitizens were eligible for various government benefits before the Trump administration last year repurposed it into a tool to check citizenship.When U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, a President Joe Biden appointee for a district court based in Washington, D.C., ruled against the program in June, she highlighted sworn declarations by naturalized citizens that Texas had threatened to revoke their voter registrations because of inaccurate Social Security data in SAVE."SAVE was never designed to verify citizenship: it relies on outdated and inaccurate data that produces false matches, risks disenfranchising eligible voters, and exposes sensitive personal information to misuse and bad actors,” Tim Harper, a project lead focused on elections and democracy at the Center for Democracy & Technology, a nonpartisan organization focused on civil liberties in the digital age, said in a statement.The Trump administration and some Republicans hail SAVE as a powerful tool to ensure the accuracy of voter rolls and identify noncitizens who shouldn’t be registered to vote. They note that its use by states is voluntary.“It’s remarkable that we had to file an emergency petition in the Supreme Court just so we can use government data to stop noncitizens from voting illegally. American elections are for Americans,” James Percival, Homeland Security’s general counsel, said in a statement.In an email to States Newsroom, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis faulted Democrats for not voting for the SAVE America Act, a bill that would require voters to produce documents proving their citizenship before voting. The bill has stalled in the U.S. Senate amid bipartisan opposition.“The American people overwhelmingly support this commonsense legislation that enacts basic election security measures like voter ID and ensures only Americans are electing America’s leaders. President Trump is absolutely right: we fix this now, or we lose our country,” Bis said..How many instances of noncitizen voting?The Trump administration’s intense focus on noncitizen voting — which also includes a legal effort to force states to turn over voter data to the Department of Justice — contrasts with the extremely rare nature of noncitizen voting, according to past studies and election experts.The U.S. Census in August identified about 24,000 instances of noncitizen voting in the 2020 election out of roughly 160 million votes cast, or 0.015% of all votes. One study of the 2016 election placed the prevalence of noncitizen voting at 0.0001% of votes cast.But Homeland Security has suggested large numbers of noncitizens may be registered to vote. In July, the department said it had identified over 250,000 potential noncitizens on the voter rolls in California, New Jersey, Nevada and Pennsylvania.On Monday, U.S. Senate Democrats in a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote that they couldn’t trust those numbers. For instance, DHS initially floated nearly 16,000 possible noncitizen voters in Nevada. In the end, the agency provided state officials with a list of 185 people that officials said were noncitizens. All turned out to be citizens.“Federal law already prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and every eligible voter across America has the right to cast a ballot — and should be able to do so without fear of being wrongly purged from the voting rolls,” Sen. Dick Durbin, an Illinois Democrat, said in a statement following the Supreme Court’s decision.The alleged scale of potential noncitizen voter registration by Homeland Security also doesn’t match the scope of the agency’s law enforcement actions. Earlier in September, Homeland Security Investigations, a DHS agency, reported making 160 recent arrests from 1,600 open voter fraud cases.When noncitizens do end up on voter rolls, administrative errors are sometimes to blame. In July, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, announced that a software glitch caused about 6,600 noncitizens to become registered to vote and that about 400 had cast ballots. And in April, then-Texas Secretary of State Jane Nelson, a Republican, wrote in a letter to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services that some noncitizens had been registered to vote because of a clerical error despite acknowledging on a voter application that they weren’t U.S. citizens.“That is why we urge voter registrars to use all available sources to confirm a person’s citizenship status — including SAVE data and other information about the registrant — when they are investigating whether the person is eligible to be a registered voter,” Nelson wrote in an email obtained by Democracy Forward, a pro-democracy legal organization.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Census changes proposed by Trump administration put accuracy, money for NC at risk, critics say
description: At its core, U.S. census data is about money, government representation, and community visibility.  The Trump administration has proposed changing the census to stop counting noncitizens without green cards, eliminate questions about race and ethnicity, and alter the definition of “usual residence.” The administration also wants to bar questions about gender[...]
text:
(Image: AdobeStock)At its core, U.S. census data is about money, government representation, and community visibility. 
The Trump administration has proposed changing the census to stop counting noncitizens without green cards, eliminate questions about race and ethnicity, and alter the definition of “usual residence.” The administration also wants to bar questions about gender identity. 
NC Counts, a nonprofit organization that, among other things, advocates for an accurate census, co-hosted a video meeting Monday to encourage individuals and groups to submit comments opposing the new rules. 
“We’re talking about proposals that would intentionally leave some people out of the numbers used for representation and remove some of the information that allows us to see who makes up our country,” said Stacey Carless, NC Counts executive director. 
The census is used to allocate congressional seats to each state. States use census data to draw congressional and legislative districts. The federal government uses census information to distribute funds for health, transportation, education, and other uses.  
“A huge amount of federal funding is at risk if there’s an undercount,” said David Heinen, vice president for policy and advocacy at the NC Center for Nonprofits, the other meeting co-host. 
A complete count is essential to North Carolina having full representation in Congress, and to redistricting at the state and local levels, he said. Nonprofits need complete data to know where to commit their limited resources, Heinen said. 
The Census Bureau has already received nearly 14,000 public comments on the proposed changes. 
If the rules are approved, it’s highly likely that they will be challenged in court. 
Attendees at Monday’s meeting were urged to submit comments opposing the changes, with organizers saying they could become part of a lawsuit challenging the rules. The deadline for public comments is Oct. 13.
In describing the changes, the Census Bureau wrote they would “better prioritize and fulfill its Constitutional mandate to count for apportionment the ‘whole number of persons in each State’ based on the concept of ‘usual residence’—a process that factors in an element of allegiance but otherwise should be colorblind and should not be distorted in any way by questions about immaterial personal characteristics, such as race.”
Courts stopped President Donald Trump’s efforts in his first term to add a citizenship question to the census and to exclude unauthorized immigrants from the 2020 count. 
Race and ethnicity questions have been part of the census since it started in 1790. Immigration status has never disqualified people from being part of the count.
Businesses, governments, and private organizations use census data in all kinds of ways, said Nathan Dollar, director of Carolina Demography.
The data is used to measure population health and health disparities, by school districts to plan for growth, and by businesses to help understand their markets, Dollar said. 
“The data are used widely, regardless of political ideology or partisan affiliation,” he said. “These proposed changes really imperil North Carolinians’ access to accurate data.”
John Quinterno, the state data center coordinator and the governor’s census liaison, compared the census to a family photo.  
Limiting the census to only citizens and legal residents means that “certain people would be erased from the picture,” he said. The census proposes to use tax records to determine “usual residence,” though it has not said whether people’s residency would be changed based on tax information, or if they would be cut from the count, Quinterno said. 
Removing questions about race and ethnicity and banning questions about sexual orientation would result in an inaccurate picture, he said. 
The result would be “people in the wrong place, people erased, people photoshopped, and the important rich details being erased or just taken out,” he said.

The first month of the Delaware high school football season concluded with last weekend’s slate of games. Multiple programs finished the month undefeated across all three classifications.
 
The first month of Delaware high school football is in the books and many programs across the state have started their 2026 season on a good note. 11 teams are undefeated through the first four weeks of play and many programs have wins against out-of-state competition showing off the talent within Delaware.
Here’s a quick look at a few teams from each of the DIAA’s three football classifications that you should keep an eye on as the season continues:
Class 3A:
Smyrna Eagles
The Eagles have scored 35 or more points in each of their first three games this season, improving to 3-0 with an overtime win over Cardinal Ohara High School (from Pennsylvania) on September 26. Smyrna’s offense is led by senior quarterback Drew Marks, sophomore runners Terrell Ingram and Norman Berry and junior receiver Mikiah Jackson. Marks has thrown for multiple touchdowns in two of Smyrna’s three games this season with Jackson on the receiving end of five of those scores. Ingram and Berry combined for seven touchdowns this season.
Smyrna will compete in its first Class 3A matchup of the season this Friday, October 2, against Middletown High School. Middletown is 1-2 this season with a couple of out-of-state losses to Cardinal Hayes High School (NY) and Our Lady of Good Counsel High School (MD). Middletown beat Smyrna last season, 33-28.
Appoquinimink Jaguars
Appoquinimink is 3-0 this season with a Class 3A win already under its belt with a victory over Dover on September 18. The Jaguars started their 2026 campaign with a win against George Washington High School (PA) and won a 3-2 matchup against Howard last Thursday to remain undefeated on the season. Appoquinimink’s defense is the backbone of its undefeated start, holding all three of their opponents this season under 10 points. The Jaguars defense has given up only 15 points through three games.
The Jaguars will play St. Georges this Friday at 7:00 p.m. at home in Middletown, Delaware. The Jaguars defeated St. Georges, 35-0, on the road last season. The win sparked a three-game winning streak that helped Appoquinimink finish the regular season with a 7-3 record and trip to the semifinal round of the 2025 DIAA Class 3A Football State Championship tournament. 
Class 2A:
Archmere football lines up on offense at the start of its game against the St. Mark’s Spartans, September 18. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
Archmere Auks
The Auks stand atop the District 1 standings in Class 2A with a 3-0 record and wins against two fellow 2A competitors, St. Mark’s and Delaware Military Academy. Archmere recorded shutouts in each of their first two wins and held DMA without a point until the fourth quarter in their most recent win. The Auks defense has recorded a sack or turnover in every game this season. 
Archmere faces a tough road matchup in its next game traveling to Felton, Delaware, to take on the Lake Forest Spartans. The Spartans are 2-1 this season with a win against Class 3A Dover in their most recent game. Last season, Lake Forest defeated Archmere, 35-13, in the regular season and 38-35 in the quarterfinal round of the DIAA Class 2A Football State Championship tournament.
Milford Buccaneers
The Buccaneers are 3-0 for the first time since 2016 starting their 2026 season with wins over Conrad, Indian River and Woodbridge in the season’s first month. Milford’s offense is averaging over 30 points per game this season led by senior Andrew Sivels. Sivels is having an incredible start to the season scoring four touchdowns in each of Milford’s first three games. Sivels has accounted for eight of the Buccaneers’ last nine touchdowns. The Buccaneers’ three wins tie their season total from a year ago.
The Buccaneers will play their third of four straight home games in a matchup against the 1-2 Delmar Wildcats. Milford defeated Delmar, 22-8, last season and Sivels was a big reason why, scoring two Buccaneer touchdowns. The rematch will be played at 7:00 p.m., Friday night.
Sussex Tech Ravens
The Ravens are the lone undefeated team amongst the District 3 standings in Class 2A. Sussex Tech started the season with a win over Glasgow High School and followed it up with two 2A wins against Tatnall and Mt. Pleasant. The Ravens have outscored their opponents 136-12 this season shutting out two of their first three opponents. Junior Eric Wright-McGlotten leads the team with seven rushing touchdowns through the first three games.
The Ravens next game will be a road contest against Bohemia Manor High School from Maryland. That game will be played in Maryland on October 2, at 7:00 p.m. Following that game, the Ravens will begin district play with a matchup against Lake Forest. Sussex Tech finished last season with a 7-3 overall record and 2-3 district record, which included a loss to Lake Forest.
Class 1A:
Concord Raiders
The Raiders started their 2026 season in a similar fashion to last season with three straight wins against Mt. Pleasant, Early College High School and Delcastle. Concord’s defense has started the year strong allowing 20 points through their first two games and earning their first shutout of the season against Delcastle last weekend. The Raider offense is led by senior Declan McNulty who has thrown or ran for a touchdown in every game this season. McNulty had a defensive touchdown as well in the Raiders win over the Hornets.
The Raiders will be on the road for their next game against Christiana High School. That game will be played on Saturday, October 3, at 11:00 a.m. The Raiders defeated Christiana, 20-8, last season. 
Newark Yellowjackets
The Yellowjackets are tied atop the District 2 standings in Class 1A with a 2-1 record this season — the first under new head coach Angel Guerrero. Newark opened the season with back-to-back wins against fellow 1A competition in AI duPont and Brandywine, before falling to Newark Charter last weekend. The Yellowjackets scored a combined 61 points in their first two wins with key contributions from seniors Jahsir Bryant and William Teel. 
The Yellowjackets will play Tatnall on the road next Saturday before playing their first district game against Delcastle at home. Newark’s game against Tatnall will be at 11:00 a.m. on October 3.
Patriot senior Maxwell Laznik finds a small window of running room against the Odessa defense. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
Newark Charter Patriots
The 2025 DIAA Class 1A Football State Championship runner-ups have started their season with a 4-0 record and multiple wins against Class 2A competition. The Patriots lead all of Class 1A with 118 points this season and their defense is amongst the top allowing only 4.5 points per game. The Patriots defense has two shutout wins this season, both against Class 2A opponents. 
Newark Charter will face Conrad in its next game on Friday, October 2. That game will start at 7:00 p.m. and be played at Robert W. Gore Stadium on Newark Charter’s campus. The Patriots beat Conrad, 20-16, last season.

title: President Donald Trump announces $15 billion steel mill in Iowa
description: President Donald Trump announced Monday the company Mesabi Metallics plans to build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, and said he’ll soon visit the state for a rally ahead of the Nov. 3, 2026, election. Joined by Iowa Republicans, Mesabi Metallics leaders and members of his cabinet, Trump said the project will be the […]
text:
President Donald Trump was joined by officials including U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and U.S. Ashley Hinson at a news conference Sep. 28, 2026 in the Oval Office announcing plans for Mesabi Metallics to build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa. (Photo screenshot via CSPAN)President Donald Trump announced Monday the company Mesabi Metallics plans to build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa, and said he’ll soon visit the state for a rally ahead of the Nov. 3, 2026, election.
Joined by Iowa Republicans, Mesabi Metallics leaders and members of his cabinet, Trump said the project will be the largest steel plant in the U.S., and one of the largest in the world. According to the White House, the mill will create 1,750 permanent jobs paying $49 per hour as well as 6,000 construction jobs as the facility is built in Lee County.
The president linked the company’s decision to build the new facility in Iowa with his tariff policies. Democrats have been critical of Trump’s tariff policies, which they say contribute to rising costs and particularly hurt Iowa’s agriculture economy, but the president argued Monday they encourage businesses to grow the U.S. manufacturing industry.
“Soon after my inauguration, I imposed powerful 50% tariffs on all foreign steel, and now our steel industry is roaring back to life,” Trump said. “Everyone’s building their plant here because they don’t want to pay tariffs. It’s really not that complicated. A lot of people say they don’t understand it, but they do. They just don’t like to give us credit.“
The mill, set to begin steelmaking in 2030, is expected to produce 7.5 million tons of steel per year in its first phase, according to the White House. The facility will process iron ore from a Minnesota mine opened earlier in September by Mesabi Metallics, which is owned by the India-based Essar Group.
It is not yet clear whether local or state tax incentives have been brought forward as part of the construction. Although Iowa state lawmakers have been alerted they may have to return to the Capitol for a special session discussing an incentive package for the steel company, Gov. Kim Reynolds has not yet called for such a session.
When asked Monday if the project was contingent on the approval of tax breaks, U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick responded, “I think this deal is done.”
Reynolds said in a statement the steel mill project is “a transformational opportunity for our country, our state, and American families — one that strengthens national security, creates thousands of high-paying jobs, and provides a reliable supply of high-quality, American-made steel for strategic goods and everyday products.”
“Our commitment in Iowa to fiscal responsibility, tax competitiveness, and long-term economic stability has created one of the nation’s strongest environments for business investment,” Reynolds said. “Now, this opportunity will fundamentally change the economic trajectory of our state and the entire region for decades to come.”
Republicans have a trifecta of control at the Iowa Statehouse. Democrats, like state Rep. Elizabeth Wilson, D-Marion, the ranking member of the state Economic Development Budget Subcommittee, called for the state to ensure public investments for the project are worthwhile for Iowa taxpayers.
“As more details become available after today’s announcement, we also have a responsibility to make sure any state investment is transparent, accountable, and a good deal for Iowa taxpayers,” Wilson said in a statement. “As Iowans continue to struggle, we clearly want this project to succeed in order to deliver lasting economic opportunities for Iowa families and communities for generations to come.”
Trump plans Iowa visit to support GOP candidates ahead of election
The project is set to be built in the 1st Congressional District, represented by U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks. She attended the news conference alongside Trump, thanking the president for his efforts to bring the project to fruition.
“Southeast Iowa, my district, has long had jobs leave, go overseas,” Miller-Meeks said. “It’s heartbreaking when you’re in those communities day after day. So to see the largest steel mill in America being built in Iowa, and in Southeast Iowa … These are families that can make over $100,000, and so it’s just transformational in this area.”
Miller-Meeks’ reelection bid against Democratic challenger Christina Bohannan is expected to be among the most competitive U.S. House races in the country in the 2026 midterms. Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball rates the race as “leans Democratic,” favoring Bohannan, who lost against Miller-Meeks in the 2024 and 2022 elections.
Though Iowa currently has an all-Republican federal delegation, the state is expected to host several highly contentious elections in 2026. The races for Iowa’s 2nd and 3rd Congressional Districts are also rated as “toss-ups” by political forecasters, as is the U.S. Senate race between U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and Iowa Rep. Josh Turek to replace Sen. Joni Ernst, who is not seeking another term. The race for Iowa’s governor seat, currently held by Reynolds, is also rated “leans Democratic” as Democratic Iowa Auditor Rob Sand faces GOP nominee Zach Lahn.
Trump said he planned to come to Iowa to rally with Republicans such as Hinson, and he reflected on his 2024 election win in Iowa, saying, “I think I’m more popular now than I was then.”
“I will say that we’re going to do a great rally, and we’ll all be there together,” Trump said. “We have to get you all elected.”
Further details about Trump visiting Iowa ahead of Nov. 3 have not yet been announced.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: States, FTC secure settlement in suit against Corteva pesticide loyalty programs
description: The agriculture company Corteva, Inc. reached a settlement with the FTC and states in a lawsuit about pesticide competition. (Photo by Lance Cheung/USDA)
text:
A farmer in Texas prays a cotton field. (Photo by Lance Cheung/USDA)The Federal Trade Commission along with state attorneys general, including Iowa’s, have reached a settlement with the seed and pesticide manufacturer Corteva Inc. in a case about pesticide competition.
The lawsuit alleged the company was operating a pesticide loyalty program that violated monopoly laws. In addition to the $35 million settlement, a news release from the FTC says, the agreement will lead to lower pesticide prices for farmers. 
The suit, which was filed in 2022, alleged that Corteva paid distributors to limit the sales of generic, less expensive pesticides and those of rival brands. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A news release from Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said the practice “raised farmers’ costs because it stifled competition by keeping less expensive generic alternatives off the shelves and permitted Corteva to maintain high prices on its products.” 
According to Bird’s office, Iowa will receive approximately $2.4 million from the settlement. 
“This is a great win for Iowa farmers, but also for all Iowans,” Bird said. “Higher input prices for farmers growing our food mean higher prices at the grocery store. Iowa farmers and families deserve a marketplace without inflated prices.” 
The lawsuit, which was filed by attorneys general from California, Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, Oregon, Tennessee, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin, was also against Syngenta Crop Protection, another top pesticide and seed company.
The complaint alleged the companies created loyalty programs to “artificially extend” their pesticide patents, which end after 20 years to allow generic versions of the formulas in the market. According to the complaint, the companies paid distributors via a loyalty program to keep their purchases of generic pesticides below a “very low threshold” which in turn meant the companies did not have to “compete fairly with generics.”
The lawsuit with Syngenta is ongoing and was not part of the $35 million settlement. 
In addition to the financial agreement, the FTC’s settlement with Corteva prohibits the company, for the next 10 years, from implementing loyalty programs based on distributors purchasing higher amounts of pesticide ingredients from Corteva versus other companies. The company is also prohibited from discriminating or threatening customers for refusing to agree to exclusivity or loyalty terms, or for doing business with competitors. 
A spokesperson for Corteva said in a statement Monday that the company is “pleased to reach a resolution in the FTC matter and continues to focus on our business, our customers and our work: delivering groundbreaking innovation and agronomic support to retailers and farmers around the world.”
David Shaw, the principal deputy director of the FTC Bureau of Competition, said in the news release that the settlement will “do away with unfair corporate practices that have hurt farmers by impeding the sales of lower-priced products.” 
“The agreement the FTC and its state partners secured will give farmers better pesticide options at lower prices, enabling farmers to continue to put food on Americans’ tables,” Shaw said. 
The FTC has initiated a number of lawsuits and investigations into anti-competitive behavior in the agriculture industry, including the equipment and fertilizer industries. Farmers say that high input costs are one of the factors making it difficult for many operations to turn a profit the past several years.

title: Delaware artist turns the human body into a ‘living canvas’

text:
Dayesla Ixtli brings Mexican folklore, wearable sculpture and body painting together in a new Mezzanine Gallery exhibition opening Oct. 2 in Wilmington
WILMINGTON, Del. — For Delaware artist Dayesla Ixtli, a canvas doesn’t necessarily hang on a wall.
It can breathe, move and ultimately become part of the artwork.
Ixtli transforms the human body using elaborate handcrafted headpieces, sculpted armor, textured prosthetics, special-effects body paint, costumes and makeup. She then preserves the completed transformation through photography.
That process is at the center of “Diosas & Guerreras: The Living Canvas,” Ixtli’s solo exhibition opening Friday, Oct. 2, at the Delaware Division of the Arts’ Mezzanine Gallery in Wilmington.
The exhibition, whose title translates to “Goddesses & Warriors,” will remain on view through Oct. 30. Admission to the gallery and the opening reception are free.
Women portrayed as goddesses and warriors
Photo courtesy of the Delaware Division of the Arts.
Drawing from ancestral mythology, Mexican folklore and Indigenous and Latin American spiritual traditions, Ixtli creates women who appear as divine protectors, nature deities and warriors.
The imagery intentionally challenges traditional portrayals of women as primarily decorative or fragile.
“My practice as a visual artist is rooted in the transformative use of the human form as a living canvas,” Ixtli said.
The figures she creates are intended to convey what she describes as “raw power, divinity, and autonomy rather than fragile ornamentation.”
Among the featured works is “Mictecacíhuatl: Lady of the Dead,” named for the Aztec goddess associated with the dead. The work combines a sculpted mixed-media headdress, textiles, special-effects body painting and photography.
“Nymph” features a handcrafted floral headpiece, while “Yemayá: Queen of the Waters” centers on an elaborate handcrafted crown and trident.
The timing gives the exhibition additional cultural context. It opens during Hispanic Heritage Month and concludes just before Día de los Muertos, observed Nov. 1 and 2.
Building a character from head to toe
What viewers see in the finished photographs represents only the final stage of Ixtli’s work.
Each character is a complete artistic production.
Ixtli creates or coordinates the headpieces, accessories, props, wardrobe, hair and makeup before bringing the elements together on the model. Special-effects techniques can add texture and dimension to the body itself.
That makes the final assembly particularly demanding.
Ixtli calls it the “anxious final moment,” when all the individual pieces must come together “perfectly as one final product.”
The payoff comes when the transformation works and viewers respond.
She describes that reaction as “a moment of shared wonder that nurtures my inner child.”
An artistic career born during the pandemic
Ixtli’s path to becoming an interdisciplinary artist did not begin in an art school or traditional studio.
She is largely self-taught.
Her work developed as a form of self-care after the birth of her youngest daughter during the COVID-19 pandemic. She began experimenting with artistic makeup and discovered that completing the transformations provided a sense of accomplishment during a difficult period.
“It wasn’t until those difficult times that I was truly able to immerse myself and dedicate myself to this discipline,” Ixtli said.
After developing her artistic practice independently, she pursued formal beauty makeup training to complement the skills she had taught herself.
The Newark-based artist was born in Tenancingo, Estado de México, and incorporates cultural memory, mythology and Indigenous and Latin American spiritual traditions into her work.
Her artist name also reflects that connection. “Ixtli” is the Nahuatl word for “face.”
Delaware fellowship recognizes her work
The exhibition follows Ixtli’s selection as a 2026 Delaware Division of the Arts Individual Artist Fellow in the emerging artist category for interdisciplinary visual arts.
The state fellowship provides both recognition and an opportunity for Ixtli to expand her practice.
She plans to explore body-safe pigments and natural adornments that could make her work more sustainable while maintaining the elaborate visual effects that characterize it.
For Ixtli, the fellowship also represents validation of an artistic career that grew from personal experimentation into public exhibitions and performances.
“Art is always saving lives, whether it is for the artist or the spectator,” she said.
She described the fellowship as an “essential push” to continue developing her work.
From festivals to film
During the past five years, Ixtli’s work has taken her to regional festivals, cultural celebrations, fashion shows and performance-art events.
She has appeared as The Magic Marigold Catrina at the Penn Museum’s Day of the Dead celebration and worked as one of the makeup artists on Alba Martínez’s 2022 short film “La Guagua 47.”
She was featured on the cover of Del Hispano Magazine in October 2025 and also operates a business as a freelance face painter and makeup artist.
The Mezzanine Gallery exhibition gives visitors an opportunity to see the finished photographs and wearable artwork together — revealing how sculpture, makeup, costume, cultural tradition and the human body combine to create a single character.
For Ixtli, however, the body remains at the center of it all: not simply the subject of the artwork, but the canvas itself.
To Go

What: “Diosas & Guerreras: The Living Canvas,” a solo exhibition by Dayesla Ixtli
Where: Mezzanine Gallery, Carvel State Office Building, 820 N. French St., Wilmington
Opening reception: Friday, Oct. 2, 5-7 p.m.
Exhibition dates: Oct. 2-30
Gallery hours: Monday-Friday, 8 a.m.-4:30 p.m.
Admission: Free and open to the public

name: VTDigger
title: New poll shows Gov. Phil Scott leading Amanda Janoo by 10 points
description:
The poll comes after last week’s UNH data showed Scott and Janoo in a “statistical tie.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New poll shows Gov. Phil Scott leading Amanda Janoo by 10 points.
text:
Republican Gov. Phil Scott, left, and Democratic nominee for governor Amanda Janoo. Photos by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Gov. Phil Scott holds a 10-point lead over progressive Democrat Amanda Janoo in a poll released Monday, a striking reversal from a separate survey last week that showed the race in a statistical tie.
Vermont Public’s 2026 Poll reported Scott is leading Janoo by 10 points, 42% to 32%. These results reflect a 16-point swing from Friday’s Green Mountain State Poll by the University of New Hampshire, which, based on margin of error in the survey, declared a “statistical tie,” with Janoo leading the race 49% to 43%. 
“Public polling has always undervalued the Governor’s support,” Scott’s campaign spokesperson Emma Shouldice wrote in a statement Monday. She added that the Vermont Public poll was “much better” than the UNH survey, but still discounted Scott. 
Among likely voters — the Vermonters polled who said they would “definitely” or “probably vote” — the margin remained 10 points with the incumbent Scott leading 44% to 34%. Sixteen percent of those likely voters remain unsure or have no opinion, according to the poll. 
Vermont Public’s poll also reported former Democratic Lt. Gov. Molly Gray leading Republican incumbent John Rodgers by eight points in the lieutenant governor race. U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. is leading the congressional race against Republican nominee Gerald Malloy, 43% to 28%.
Longtime Vermont political journalist Chris Graff called last week’s UNH poll an “outlier.”
“I think the Vermont Public poll is a little more in line with how those of us who follow this closely see the race, which is that Governor Scott maintains a lead,” he said in an interview Monday. “Amanda Janoo has a strong following but is largely unknown.”
Scott remained the most popular governor in the country as of a July report by the firm Morning Consult. Vermont Public’s polling reported that Scott held a 45% approval rating, a 15-point decline since their last poll in 2022. UNH also reported a 47% approval rating, which had decreased by five points since July.

READ MORE

Graff said that declining approval ratings are to be expected for Scott, but that the drop could be explained by Scott not having “solved the problems that are facing the state of Vermont.” Alternatively, he said, Scott’s ratings could be explained by national sentiment. 
“The national mood is such that if you have an ‘R’ beside your name — even if you’re someone like Phil Scott — that ‘R’ is an anchor,” Graff said. 
Twenty percent is a significant number of uncertain voters this close to the election, Graff said. He expects that debates will “make a difference,” but that Janoo doesn’t have the “money or organization” to reach the “larger number of voters” across the state who are undecided. 
“We haven’t seen (the candidates debate) yet,” Graff said. “She is not yet defined in the public. People haven’t seen her in person, so I think she was able to beat Aly Richards by being the candidate of change, and really electrifying that base, but it was a very narrow win. Now in a general election, you have a far, far larger number of voters you have to reach.”
Scott’s team remains confident that he and Vermonters are on the same page, Shouldice wrote.
“What we are certain of is that Vermonters share the Governor’s frustration on affordability issues and that’s why we’re focused on getting commonsense legislators elected that will work with him to lower property taxes, housing, healthcare and energy costs,” she wrote.
Janoo, an economist, had never run for office and was relatively unknown before her grassroots campaign. She also remains optimistic about November’s election, according to a Monday press release. 
“This is going to be a close race but no matter what,” she wrote, “I’m incredibly proud of the way we’re bringing people together to celebrate the things we love about where we live, to invite people to articulate the Vermont we want for our children and grandchildren and to recognize together, we have everything we need to get there.”

name: WyoFile
title: Out-of-state companies have swallowed up Campbell County housing rentals, records show
description:
Gillette renters’ money is going to landlords likely based outside Wyoming, according to a Gillette News Record analysis of property data.
The post Out-of-state companies have swallowed up Campbell County housing rentals, records show appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
GILLETTE—Gillette renters’ money is going to owners likely outside Wyoming, according to a Gillette News Record analysis of property data.
Long gone are the days of private and local landlords, as parcel data shows that private real estate investment companies hold a significant stake in Campbell County rental property. But this is not unique to Gillette. Rather, it’s part of a nationwide trend.
The latest Campbell County geographic information systems data shows that 39 parcels containing Gillette’s biggest apartment complexes are owned by companies based in other states, some as far away as Maryland, Washington and Minnesota.
And of the 20 of Gillette’s largest apartment complexes, nearly all of them are held by companies outside the state.
South Fork Apartments and The Butte, for example, are respectively owned by companies filed in Chevy Chase, Maryland, and Sioux Falls, South Dakota, according to county records.
That out-of-state ownership trend is typical, as only five of the 20 apartment complexes in town are owned by companies filed in Gillette.
Those apartment complexes include Valley View Apartments, Squaw Valley, Thunder Rock, Foothills Apartments and the Gillette Apartments along South Gillette Avenue.
That doesn’t mean those apartment complex owners are necessarily local though, but that businesses had been filed locally.
Foothills Apartments, for example, are filed under an LLC called Foothills Apartments LLC, which lists a mailing address in the apartment complex.
The listed agent of the apartments, however, is a Gillette woman named Annette Smith.
There doesn’t seem to be a strong theme for ownership for other apartments, though two LLCs based in Washington appear to be run by the same company under different names. Liberty Village and Remington Village are both filed with separate LLC names under the same mailing address in Seattle.
That address is for a private real estate investment company in Seattle called Investors Capital Group, which currently manages almost 100 apartment complexes across 13 states, according to the company’s website.
Liberty Village and Remington Village are Investors Capital Group’s only apartment complexes in Wyoming, according to its website.
A similar strategy can be observed in the ownership of Cottonwood Terrace and The Village at Gillette. Both are owned by separate LLC’s, but are filed under the same mailing address in Enumclaw, Washington.
That mailing address belongs to another private real estate investment company called Preferred Capital Management. Its website touts owning 2,076 apartments in eight states.
Those apartments come from 29 complexes, including ones in Rock Springs, Riverton and Douglas.
“Since the early 1990’s, PCMI has had a long standing history of buying troubled real estate assets well below replacement costs,” its website states. “Our strategy has been to buy at the right time and at the right price.”
The same pattern also follows the ownership of Antelope Ridge and Windridge apartments.
An address in Montvale, New Jersey, can be traced to a company called Broad Management Group, a real-estate investment and management firm.
Its “about section” on its website does not list its Wyoming portfolio, but it does boast owning 74 complexes, predominately in the South.
Those companies fit the mold of private equity where a private group of investors acquire rental properties then build improvements and renovations to apartment complexes such as dog parks, raising the equity of the property itself.
National investigations by ProPublica and the New York Times have reported skyrocketing rents, diminishing safety and litanies of maintenance problems from properties managed by private investment groups, despite the shiny amenities.
The new ownership appears to be part of a national trend, that reporting showed, where private equity companies have gobbled up rentals across the United States by the thousands.
The profits and that equity is shared among each company’s private group of investors. As private companies, each investment group does not have to report investors, so it is unclear if any investors belonging to Investors Capital Group, Preferred Capital Management or Broad Management Group live in Campbell County.
There are few exceptions to the corporate-owned apartment trend in Campbell County.
Registration to the LLC’s that own the South Fork apartments and College Park Townhomes track back to home addresses in Chevy Chase, Maryland, and Shorewood, Wisconsin, respectively.
Gillette’s other apartment complexes owned by companies outside of Wyoming appear to be operated by other real estate investment groups with multiple properties across the United States.
Other properties
Someone hoping to rent in Campbell County isn’t limited to just apartment complexes though, but a somewhat similar story to Campbell County’s apartment complexes can be told about other rental lots and properties around Gillette.
Out-of-state real estate companies operating mobile home parks in Gillette also hold more individual parcels of land than any one local owner.
Gillette Fund 7 MHP LLC, operated by JRB Communities out of Newport Beach, California, owns 155 parcels of Campbell County land, more than any other company or individual in the county, according to the GIS.
Those 155 parcels contain every modular home lot in the Prairie Rose Mobile Home Park.
JRB also owns and operates mobile home parks in Arizona, Maryland, North Dakota and Ohio, according to its website.
RHP Properties based in Farmington Hills, Wisconsin, owns 79 parcels of land encompassing the Park Plaza Mobile Home community off of Clemence Avenue.
It also owns other mobile home communities in 29 other states.
