description: Nandi Gamble tells Jane Brady that constitutional amendments, parental rights and education will remain priorities as Delaware heads toward a new General Assembly DOVER, Del. — With Delaware’s 2026 legislative session over and voters preparing to elect a new General Assembly, Nandi Gamble of the Delaware Family Policy Council says some of the state’s most co[...]
text:
Nandi Gamble tells Jane Brady that constitutional amendments, parental rights and education will remain priorities as Delaware heads toward a new General Assembly
DOVER, Del. — With Delaware’s 2026 legislative session over and voters preparing to elect a new General Assembly, Nandi Gamble of the Delaware Family Policy Council says some of the state’s most contentious debates over abortion, parental rights and education are likely to return when lawmakers reconvene in January.
Gamble, who tracks legislation for the conservative family-policy organization, outlined those priorities during an interview with former Delaware Attorney General Jane Brady on “A Better Discussion,” the weekly webcast produced by A Better Delaware.
Brady introduced Gamble as someone whose job is to follow legislation affecting families and make that information available to the organization’s members and the public. Gamble said hundreds of bills are introduced during Delaware’s two-year legislative sessions, requiring the organization to track measures it believes could affect family policy.
The conversation offered a preview of the issues Gamble expects the organization to focus on after the November election.
Constitutional amendments could return
At the top of Gamble’s list are proposed constitutional amendments dealing with reproductive freedom and individual privacy.
“There’s actually two that I’m really expecting to come back,” Gamble told Brady.
Senate Substitute 1 for Senate Bill 5 proposes adding a fundamental right to reproductive freedom relating to an individual’s pregnancy to the Delaware Constitution. The measure remained pending after advancing from committee during the current General Assembly.
Supporters describe the proposal as a way to protect reproductive rights under Delaware’s Constitution. Gamble and the Family Policy Council oppose it and highlighted language addressing decisions related to pregnancy, including abortion, contraception, sterilization and fertility care.
House Bill 14 would separately add a right of individual privacy to the Delaware Constitution, stating that the right “may not be infringed without a showing of a compelling state interest.” The bill was released from committee in March 2025 and placed on the Ready List.
Its sponsors say the proposal is intended to protect privacy rights that courts have previously recognized in areas including marriage, contraception, family relationships and child-rearing.
Gamble told Brady her organization views the privacy proposal in part through the lens of abortion policy because privacy rights played a role in earlier U.S. Supreme Court rulings involving contraception and abortion. That is the Family Policy Council’s interpretation of the measure; HB 14 itself is written broadly as a privacy amendment.
Parental consent remains a dividing line
Gamble also highlighted House Bill 46, legislation that would have required parental or legal-guardian consent before an abortion could be performed on someone younger than 16.
A substitute for the bill provides exceptions for medical emergencies and allows Family Court to authorize the procedure if a judge determines the minor is mature and well-informed enough to decide independently or that parental consent would not be in the minor’s best interest because of circumstances such as abuse, neglect or coercion. The substitute remained in the House Health & Human Development Committee.
Gamble told Brady the Family Policy Council sees the proposal as part of a larger debate over the role parents should have in major decisions involving their children.
Brady brought a personal perspective to that discussion, recalling a case she prosecuted roughly two decades ago involving a 14-year-old girl who became pregnant after being sexually abused by an adult teacher.
Brady said the teenager obtained an abortion without her parents knowing and under the influence of the adult who was abusing her. The man was later prosecuted and imprisoned, Brady said.
Gamble said the case illustrated why her organization supports parental-consent legislation.
Supporters of abortion rights have argued that consent requirements can create barriers for minors whose home environments are abusive, unsafe or otherwise unsuitable, while supporters of parental-consent laws argue that parents should ordinarily be involved in major medical decisions involving their children.
End-of-life law remains part of the debate
Gamble also pointed to Delaware’s medical aid-in-dying law as an example of how a small number of legislative votes can determine the outcome of major social-policy questions.
The Family Policy Council opposed the measure for years.
Gamble told Brady the debate demonstrated how individual lawmakers can become pivotal when margins in Legislative Hall are narrow.
“Those one or two votes make a very big difference,” she said.
Supporters of medical aid in dying describe it as an additional option for terminally ill adults who meet specific medical and legal requirements. Opponents have raised moral, religious and medical concerns about allowing physicians to participate in the process.
Turning legislative fights into a voter guide
The November election also gives Gamble’s organization another avenue to advance its priorities.
The Delaware Family Policy Action PAC produces an online voter guide that Gamble said includes candidate questionnaires, legislative voting records and research into candidates who do not respond directly.
Candidates received 10 issue statements this year and were asked whether they supported or opposed them, Gamble said. She told Brady that, for the first time, several Democratic candidates also participated.
When candidates do not answer, Gamble said the organization reviews campaign websites, social media and public forums in an attempt to determine their positions. The guide also tracks endorsements from organizations whose policy positions differ from those of the Family Policy Council.
Because the guide is produced through the group’s political-action arm and reflects its policy priorities, voters can compare it with candidate statements, other voter guides and independent reporting when evaluating candidates.
Brady emphasized the broader value of voters understanding candidates beyond their party labels and encouraged viewers to ask candidates directly where they stand on issues important to them.
Schools and parental involvement
Education is another area Gamble expects to remain prominent.
She said the organization supported legislation intended to give parents greater visibility into school curriculum and other classroom material and provides parents with information about opting children out of certain instruction.
Gamble also raised concerns during the webcast about sex-education materials in schools. Her comments reflected the Family Policy Council’s advocacy position and were not accompanied during the program by examples from specific Delaware school districts or curricula.
More broadly, Gamble said parental involvement in schools remains one of the organization’s central issues. She pointed to previous parental-rights proposals that failed to advance and said similar efforts are likely to remain part of the debate.
From teacher to legislative advocate
Gamble’s path to Delaware politics did not begin in Legislative Hall.
She told Brady she originally entered college intending to become a doctor before changing direction and becoming a teacher.
She taught honors and Advanced Placement biology as well as physics in Florida and said her experience with education policy, particularly the implementation of Common Core, helped lead her into public-policy work.
Gamble became involved with the Florida Family Policy Council in 2015 before eventually moving to Delaware, where she has lived for about seven years.
Today, much of her work revolves around monitoring legislation, communicating with parents and churches, and preparing supporters to participate in public-policy debates.
The organization also operates a Church Ambassador Network that Gamble said connects pastors with legislators and community needs. It recently held its annual summit for pastors and other leaders. Gamble said the event typically attracts about 450 to 600 attendees, with a previous gathering drawing roughly 860.
For Gamble, the November election does not represent the end of those debates. It will determine who is sitting in Legislative Hall when they resume.
And judging from the issues she identified in her conversation with Brady — reproductive rights, privacy, parental authority, education and end-of-life policy — several of Delaware’s most divisive legislative questions are likely to remain part of the debate when a new General Assembly takes office in January.
TO GO

What: “A Better Discussion” with Nandi Gamble of the Delaware Family Policy Council
Host: Jane Brady, chair of A Better Delaware and former Delaware attorney general
Key issues: Reproductive-rights and privacy constitutional amendments, parental consent for minors seeking abortions, medical aid in dying, parental rights in education and the 2026 voter guide
Delaware Family Policy Council: delawarefamilies.org
Legislative updates: delawarefamilies.org/updates
Voter guide: devoterguide.com
Why it matters: Gamble says several of the family-policy and social issues debated during the current General Assembly are likely to return after the November election when newly elected lawmakers convene in January.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Suicide prevention means supporting children long before a crisis
description: I remember the feeling of panic that set in years ago when my daughter told me and my husband she had been feeling incredibly sad for an extended period of time and that a friend of hers had been self-harming recently. Even with years of EMS training and experience working directly with young people with […]
text:
A flier seen Sept. 2, 2026, on a bulletin board at the University of Alaska Anchorage campus gives information about the 988 suicide-prevention hotline established in 2022. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)I remember the feeling of panic that set in years ago when my daughter told me and my husband she had been feeling incredibly sad for an extended period of time and that a friend of hers had been self-harming recently. Even with years of EMS training and experience working directly with young people with mental health needs, I felt temporarily paralyzed when it came to my own teen and her close friend.
It’s never easy to acknowledge that a child needs help. But the fact that she felt comfortable opening up to us was the first step. It gave us an opportunity to listen, take her concerns seriously, connect her with support and keep checking in. It reminded me that suicide prevention isn’t only about knowing what to do when a crisis happens. It’s also about creating the relationships and trust that allows young people to speak up when something is wrong.
For families across Alaska, moments like these can carry enormous weight. And the data show just how many young people may be struggling.
In late August, the Alaska Department of Health released new data on youth suicide. Between 2016 and 2025, we lost 174 Alaska children and teens ages 10 to 18 to suicide. Suicides in 2025 were the highest on record over the previous ten years. Alaska’s youth suicide rate runs nearly six times the national average.
The struggle reaches much further than even these losses. In the most recent Youth Risk Behavior Survey data compiled in KIDS COUNT Alaska, nearly 1 in 4 high school students said they had seriously considered attempting suicide in the past year.
Many of Alaska’s kids are struggling, and it’s critical we help before a child or teen reaches the tipping point. Preventing suicide takes work throughout the year, but there’s never been a better time to start helping than during Suicide Prevention Month, which is September.
The science says that young people who feel connected to their school and family report suicidal thoughts at far lower rates. An additional caring adult in a child’s life like an afterschool provider, coach or educator can be an important source of support. So can a welcoming school, strong friendships and access to mental health care.
So, what does prevention look like in everyday life?
It looks like showing up. Eat dinner together. Learn the name of your child’s new friend. Make it to the game, the recital, the fish camp. And, you don’t have to be a parent. Teachers, coaches, neighbors and afterschool professionals send the same message when they take a vested interest in a child: you matter and belong.
It looks like asking. If you’re worried about a young person, ask directly: “Are you thinking about suicide?” Asking does not increase suicidal thoughts or behavior. Listen without judgment, help them connect with support and keep checking in.
It looks like taking a training and finding community. Alaska-based organizations like National Alliance on Mental Illness Alaska and the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention’s Alaska chapters host trainings and family support groups to help Alaskan families and educators. 
It looks like knowing where to turn. Call or text 988 anytime, whether you’re struggling or worried about someone else. Support is free, confidential, and available 24 hours a day. Save the number in your phone and in your kid’s phone. Talk to your child about how asking for help is a sign of strength — and live that message by showing them that you know how to ask for help from others, too.
Preventing child abuse and neglect means supporting families before problems become crises. That’s the focus of Alaska Children’s Trust’s work, and it matters for suicide prevention, too. The supports that keep families strong also protect a young person’s mental health: welcoming afterschool programs, time with caring adults, connection to culture and mental health care families can reach.
For our family, it meant spending more time together, enrolling in therapy and participation in a Mental Health Advocacy Through Storytelling program. Those interventions helped us — but it’s important that each child’s needs are addressed in a way that works for them.
Suicide Prevention Month is a good time to take a first step and check in with a young person in your life. Make time to listen and keep checking in after September ends.
If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988. Help is free, confidential and available 24 hours a day.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Gov. Sherrill vetoes two bills intended to help Jersey City close budget gap
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill vetoed two bills meant to bail Jersey City out of a budget deficit, blasting former city officials as "irresponsible."
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill vetoed two bills meant to bail Jersey City out of a budget deficit, blasting former city officials as "irresponsible." (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill vetoed two bills Monday that would have taxed car rentals in Jersey City and allowed officials there to divert tax dollars intended for open space and historic preservation to other purposes.
The vetoes were Sherrill’s first since she took office in January, and one includes some harsh language about the policymaking of former Mayor Steve Fulop, who ran against Sherrill for governor in last year’s Democratic primary.
“The residents of Jersey City are currently suffering from a fiscal crisis caused largely by the irresponsible decisions made by the City’s prior administration,” Sherrill wrote in her statement vetoing the vehicle-tax bill. “The prior administration’s over-reliance on short-term budget gimmicks and ‘one-shots’ have seriously undermined the City’s long-term stability. Going forward, sustainable revenue growth and structural reforms must be a priority. The proposed legislation is not appropriate at this time.”
That bill would have created a new 5% tax on motor vehicle rentals, increased a surtax on parking tickets, and given the city wider discretion in how to spend both that surtax and a “mass transit access tax” on fees collected at commercial parking lots that’s meant to fund pedestrian access to mass transit.
The nonpartisan Office of Legislative Services estimated that just the new car rental tax could increase the city’s annual revenue by up to $10 million and noted that the mass transit tax brought in over $10 million in 2024.
Fulop did not respond to a request for comment. Jersey City Mayor James Solomon, a Democrat who took office in January, revealed in February that the city had a budget deficit of $250 million he largely blamed on waste and mismanagement by the Fulop administration.
Jersey City spokeswoman Megan Malloy said officials there are grateful to legislators for “standing up for Jersey City every step of the way.”
“We’re disappointed that these bills were vetoed since they would have provided relief for Jersey City at a time when we need every penny,” Malloy said. “We will continue working with the Governor and state legislature at the state level, and our office is committed to using every tool possible to make sure Jersey City is on the right fiscal pathway while providing relief for our citizens.”
Sherrill noted in her veto that the bill passed less than a week after it was introduced during the last week of June, a whirlwind time when lawmakers rush to vote on bills and the state budget before they recess for the summer. During that time, lawmakers also passed two other items intended to help Jersey City’s finances, a $105 million low-interest loan and a $15 million grant.
Sherrill also vetoed a similarly fast-tracked bill introduced the same week that would have allowed Jersey City to take money meant for open space, recreation, and historic preservation and divert it this year to the city’s general fund.
Sherrill noted that the money comes from an annual levy voters in 2016 authorized via referendum that clearly specified that it would be spent exclusively on the acquisition, development, and maintenance of lands for recreation, conservation, and historic purposes.
“The will of the City’s voters should not be set aside in the manner proposed in the bill,” Sherrill wrote.
The levy is expected to generate over $1.2 million this year for Jersey City, according to an April memo from the city’s tax assessor.
Four Democrats whose legislative districts include Jersey City sponsored both of the bills Sherrill vetoed — Sens. Raj Mukherji and Angela McKnight and Assemblymen Jerry Walker and William Sampson. They did not respond to requests for comment.
The bills were passed along party lines in June, with Republicans in both chambers voting against them.
Sherrill also conditionally vetoed a bill meant to expand mental health treatment services, citing oversight concerns. She suggested amendments that, if approved by legislators, would earn her signature and help the measure become law.

title: Delaware cancer doctor helps shape national pancreatic cancer treatment guidelines
description: ChristianaCare radiation oncologist Lindsay Romak helped develop updated recommendations on when and how radiation should be used to treat one of the most difficult cancers WILMINGTON, Del. — A Delaware cancer specialist is helping shape how physicians across the country treat pancreatic cancer, a disease that remains among the most challenging cancers to tr[...]
text:
Images provided by ChristianaCare.
ChristianaCare radiation oncologist Lindsay Romak helped develop updated recommendations on when and how radiation should be used to treat one of the most difficult cancers
WILMINGTON, Del. — A Delaware cancer specialist is helping shape how physicians across the country treat pancreatic cancer, a disease that remains among the most challenging cancers to treat successfully.
Dr. Lindsay Romak, a radiation oncologist at ChristianaCare’s Helen F. Graham Cancer Center & Research Institute, is a co-author of newly updated national clinical practice guidelines from the American Society for Radiation Oncology, or ASTRO.
The guidelines provide physicians with evidence-based r

ecommendations for determining when radiation therapy should be used for adults with pancreatic cancer and how that treatment should be delivered.
Published in the medical journal Practical Radiation Oncology, the recommendations incorporate new clinical evidence and advances in radiation technology that have emerged since ASTRO issued its previous pancreatic cancer guidelines in 2019.
Why the guidelines matter
Pancreatic cancer presents physicians and patients with particularly difficult treatment decisions.
Only about one in five patients is eligible for surgery when the cancer is diagnosed, according to ChristianaCare. For other patients, treatment can involve combinations of chemotherapy and radiation, depending on how far the cancer has progressed and how it responds to treatment.
That makes determining when radiation should be used — and which patients are most likely to benefit — an important part of treatment planning.
“The treatment landscape for pancreatic cancer continues to evolve, and these guidelines help bring greater clarity to difficult treatment decisions,” Romak said. “By incorporating the latest evidence, we can better identify patients who may benefit from radiation therapy and ensure care is tailored to each patient’s unique circumstances.”
The updated guidelines address radiation treatment for patients across a range of circumstances, including cancers that can potentially be removed surgically, locally advanced cancers, recurrent disease, metastatic cancer and treatment intended primarily to relieve symptoms.
Radiation can play different roles
Radiation therapy does not serve the same purpose for every pancreatic cancer patient.
For some patients, radiation may help control a tumor in the pancreas and surrounding area. In certain circumstances, treatment may help make surgery possible. For others, radiation can be used to relieve symptoms caused by the disease, including pain or bleeding.
The new guidelines also address recurrent pancreatic cancer, treating an area with radiation for a second time and the use of radiation in selected patients whose cancer has spread to a limited number of locations or is progressing only in certain areas.
Those distinctions are important because pancreatic cancer treatment increasingly depends on the characteristics and progression of an individual patient’s disease rather than a single treatment approach.
“National guidelines help translate scientific evidence into better patient care,” said Dr. Adam Raben, chair of Radiation Oncology at the Graham Cancer Center. “Dr. Romak’s contributions to these recommendations reflect ChristianaCare’s leadership in radiation oncology and our commitment to ensuring patients with pancreatic cancer benefit from the latest advances in treatment.”
More precise radiation treatment
The recommendations also reflect technological changes that allow physicians to target tumors more precisely while attempting to limit radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.
Those advances include improved image guidance, techniques to account for tumor movement caused by breathing and adaptive radiation therapy, which allows a treatment plan to be adjusted based on changes in a patient’s anatomy.
That precision can be especially important when treating pancreatic cancer because the pancreas is located close to other organs and sensitive structures.
“At ChristianaCare, we are seeing firsthand how innovations such as adaptive radiation therapy can help us personalize treatment and improve precision,” Romak said. “These advances are expanding options for patients and allowing us to deliver care more safely and effectively.”
Delaware expertise contributes to national standards
ASTRO developed the updated guidelines in collaboration with the American Society of Clinical Oncology, the European Society for Radiotherapy and Oncology and the Society of Surgical Oncology.
Romak’s participation puts a physician practicing in Delaware among the specialists helping establish national recommendations that oncologists can use when evaluating treatment options for pancreatic cancer patients.
“It was an honor to work alongside experts from around the world and across the country on these recommendations,” Romak said. “Our shared goal was to provide clear, evidence-based guidance that helps clinicians deliver the highest quality care and ultimately improves outcomes for patients with pancreatic cancer.”
The guidelines are intended to support — rather than replace — individualized decisions by physicians and patients. Treatment can vary based on the stage and location of the cancer, previous treatments, a patient’s overall health and other clinical considerations.
For Delaware patients, the work also means expertise helping establish national pancreatic cancer treatment standards is represented locally at the Graham Cancer Center.
TO GO BOX

What: Updated national guidelines for radiation therapy in pancreatic cancer
Delaware connection: Dr. Lindsay Romak, a radiation oncologist at ChristianaCare’s Helen F. Graham Cancer Center & Research Institute, helped author the new recommendations.
Why it matters: The guidelines help doctors determine which pancreatic cancer patients may benefit from radiation therapy, including treatment to control tumors, potentially make surgery possible or relieve symptoms such as pain and bleeding.
What’s new: Recommendations incorporate advances in image guidance, motion management and adaptive radiation therapy, along with guidance for recurrent and selected metastatic cancers.
More information: ChristianaCare’s Helen F. Graham Cancer Center & Research Institute and the American Society for Radiation Oncology.

title: ‘Dumbfounds us all’: Congress struggles with policies rippling from AI development
text: The challenges and dire threats surrounding the unchecked growth of artificial intelligence appear unlikely to move Congress or President Donald Trump to act as the U.S. Senate enters its last week before the midterms. The rapid emergence of the technology has sparked a host of policy debates, with some warning of an existential threat to humanity, requiring urgent attention. But the only action Congress could plausibly take before November’s elections is a relatively toothless measure aiming to control the massive consumer electricity costs of AI.“A lot of people are afraid of the dark and change is difficult,” said Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va. “The amazement of AI just dumbfounds us all.”The Senate is expected to vote Wednesday on a plan to urge states to protect consumers from paying higher electricity costs from data centers. A lot of Democrats are balking at the legislation, which will need the support of 60 senators, saying the plan is weak. Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson are scheduled to meet with industry leaders  Tuesday at the White House. Trump continues to express wariness of any new AI regulation.Pew Research Center this summer found 71% worried AI will mean job losses over the next 20 years, up 7 percentage points from two years ago.“Worry over job loss has shown up throughout our research about AI, including among workers and even teenagers,” a Pew analysis said. With constituents clamoring for clarity, and midterm elections weeks away, it’s unclear where all this is eventually headed. Lawmakers are still trying to grasp the nature of the problems.The simple reason it’s been hard to set regulations, says Darrell West, senior fellow at Washington’s Brookings Institution, is inertia. The industry has simply never dealt with significant government influence.“They’re dealing with an industry that hasn’t been regulated for 25 years and is now very powerful,” he said. “It’s hard to regulate powerful industries.”‘There is no one AI policy debate’Concern about AI accelerated earlier this month when a former researcher at AI firms Open AI and Anthropic warned that the companies are “gambling with our lives.” An Anthropic colleague then said “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic’s CEO urged AI developers to slow down.Lawmakers were quick to express concern. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., wants a “kill switch” that would require companies to instantly shut off or curb an AI function if things look dangerous.Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, are seeking to pause advanced AI development until the federal government establishes a regulator to assure safe, secure progress.A bipartisan group of senators is pushing hard for export controls, including making it tougher for China and other adversaries to get access to advanced AI.Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo., are seeking a risk evaluation program that would require developers of advanced AI to provide information to the Energy Department before deploying the technology. Hawley is chairing a subcommittee hearing this week on preventing attacks from rogue AI agents. About all that’s getting traction is the Ratepayer Protection Act, which requires state utility commissions to consider ways to curb the electricity costs that data centers can generate.Though it passed overwhelmingly in the House recently, it faces broad opposition from Senate Democrats as not being tough enough.Overall, AI debate is proving to be a set of puzzles no one can solve.“There is no one AI policy debate. There are multiple AI policy debates,” said Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of Chamber of Progress, a center-left trade organization representing tech firms.He listed some of the topics: the existential risks of AI, its impact on jobs, chatbots, impacts on children, copyright, fair use.While little is likely to happen this month, some action is likely in the future. “It wasn’t that long ago people had a positive view about technology,” said West. “Now sentiment has turned against it. The odds of something getting done are going up substantially.”Why is Washington stuck?The stalemate over AI stems from at least three factors:Congress is polarized. For decades, it wasn’t unusual for Congress to take big swings to deal with emerging issues and industries.Most recently, the Dodd-Frank banking law of 2010 provided strong new protections for consumers and helped restrain large financial institutions after the deep recession from 2007 to 2009. In 1996, as cable television began surging, Congress passed the Telecommunications Act to promote competition in the industry.But in recent years, such big deals have become elusive in the House and Senate. “I have often told people as a new senator that if we were healthy as a country, if our politics were healthy, we’d be talking about AI every single day,” said Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., in an interview.State regulations vary from place to place.“The worst case scenario is 50 kinds of state laws. You don’t want to write a different algorithm for different states,” said West. “Tech firms will want one set of rules.”In Maryland last week, Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat, set up a task force to look at new data center plans. In Virginia, where there are more data centers than in any other state, Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger last week took a major step toward tight regulation of data centers, though she did not propose the moratorium many environmental groups had sought.On the federal level, even the simplest initiatives are proving tough. Trump has insisted that efforts to control AI are a “hoax,” and has resisted any bid to regulate the industry.“I’m not going to stifle growth of anything that’s going to be bigger than the industrial revolution,” Trump said last week. He has proposed an AI Force with a top official to lead it, but has offered no specifics.The Ratepayer Protection Act is Congress’ current bid to get companies to pay for the electricity AI generates. While it has strong support, many lawmakers complain that the bill is only a recommendation, not the mandate that’s needed.The bill is a “fraud,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters. “It's voluntary. No company has to do it.”The industry’s Data Center Coalition says consumers won’t get hurt. The coalition ”supports the underlying goal of the Ratepayer Protection Act, and we appreciate the bipartisan effort that brought it to the House floor….we welcome the chance to work with the Senate and the Administration to ensure all large-load customers and stakeholders pay their own costs for grid upgrades and related infrastructure,” said Michele Nellenbach, the group’s vice president of federal affairs.Competition with China is an issue. There’s a risk that if U.S. firms slow development, Chinese technology could surpass them.Sens. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., are pushing the Chip Security Act, which would bar advanced American chips from “falling into the hands of China and other countries of concern.”Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., is among the senators from both parties who are sponsoring a bill that would ban the export of advanced AI chips to China. Sens. Andy Kim, D-N.J., and Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., are seeking assurances that China can’t get the equipment it needs to make the advanced chips.Trump said last week that while he’s open to talks about AI, he’s unworried about any threat from China."We're about maybe a year and a half up on China," Trump told Fox News Sunday. "We're leading, and we're building tremendous, trillions of dollars' worth of places. And why should we give that up?" What’s ahead?People want assurance that AI will be safe, and “they want the United States to continue to be a leader on innovation. The two are not mutually exclusive,” Kim told reporters last week.There is much to learn, said Kennedy. “It is hard to know precisely what to believe about artificial intelligence. There are some things, it seems to me, that we do know,” he said. “We know, for example, that it is a breathtaking technology.”Kennedy tried to get the Senate to vote this month on his kill switch plan. Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., blocked the bill.Their dialogue on the Senate floor illustrated why it’s so difficult to act. Kennedy wanted quick action. Paul wanted reflection.“When approaching something as important as innovation, as AI, I think we should make sure we have as many facts as possible before we dictate rules for the whole economy,” Paul said.Kennedy was frustrated.“We are not going to get up off of our ice-cold, lazy butts and address this anytime soon,” he said. “It is just not going to happen, and we all know that.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Midterm Oklahoma rally signals trouble for Republicans, Trump, experts say
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — President Donald Trump’s unusual decision to hold a midterm rally in a rural part of Oklahoma, a state long considered a Republican stronghold, signals GOP panic that voters may sit out the election as the president’s popularity wanes. Political scientists said Thursday’s campaign rally in Durant, a city of about 21,500 people […]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during an event in the Oval Office on August 6, 2026. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY — President Donald Trump’s unusual decision to hold a midterm rally in a rural part of Oklahoma, a state long considered a Republican stronghold, signals GOP panic that voters may sit out the election as the president’s popularity wanes.
Political scientists said Thursday’s campaign rally in Durant, a city of about 21,500 people located about 2.5 hours southeast of Oklahoma City, also underscores GOP concerns that a Trump endorsement has decreased in value. 
Trump’s first official appearance in the state in six years also comes as a state party leader said Democrats nationally are putting resources into flipping an Oklahoma City-area congressional seat that has been held by Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Stephanie Bice since 2021. 
“I think it’s a signal of how bad things have gotten for the Republicans under Trump,” said Seth McKee, a political science professor at Oklahoma State University.
While Trump won all 77 of the state’s counties two years ago, his approval ratings have dropped across the country, including in Oklahoma, as war with Iran continues and everyday costs continue to rise. 
McKee said Trump has become “toxic” to Republicans seeking office and he might cause more harm in places that have highly competitive races.  
“He doesn’t hurt in Durant, Oklahoma, but he might be a net negative if he went down to Dallas and campaigned for Ken Paxton,” he said. “… So that’s what we’re dealing with here, which is a real problem. I mean, he’s so unpopular that if you put him in any context where a race is super close, he’s not going to help it, he’s going to hurt it.”
Trump set to rally GOP voters, hold midterm election event in Oklahoma

Paxton, a Republican endorsed by Trump, is running in a tight race against Democrat James Talarico for the U.S. Senate seat in Texas. Paxton defeated incumbent U.S. Sen. John Cornyn in the primary runoff.
Trump will campaign in Durant with Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei, who the president has also endorsed, the Republican National Committee said. He’s also attending a a separate rally Friday in Mobile, Alabama.
A Republican strategist familiar with midterm planning said Trump is holding his rally in Durant because it is near the Texas border and the Dallas-Fort Worth media market. 
A visit there allows Trump to boost Texas candidates and Mazzei at the same time, the strategist said. 
But Allyson Shortle, a professor of political science at University of Oklahoma, said there is likely concern that Trump’s endorsement doesn’t carry the weight it once did. Trump’s visit is meant to boost voter participation within the party base. 
Even with the president’s endorsement, Mazzei won the Republican nomination by a little over 2,000 votes. He’s set to face Democrat Cyndi Munson in November. 
“I think it sort of shows that (Trump) is doing damage control on his base,” Shortle said. “He’s going to the deepest red portions to make sure that they are still on his side and that they will in fact come out for the election. He wants that turnout because elections are won due to mobilization.” 
Congressional seat fight
Shortle said the fight for Oklahoma’s Congressional District 5 seat, which encompasses six counties in central Oklahoma, is also garnering unexpected national attention. 
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has invested resources in Democrat Jena Nelson’s campaign in an attempt to unseat Bice, said Erin Brewer, chair of the Oklahoma Democratic Party.
It’s an unusual move because it’s usually considered a “foregone conclusion” that Oklahoma’s congressional seats will go to Republican candidates, Shortle said.
“If you look at that district in particular, there are a lot of Democratic voters, so they must believe that there is a chance that they could mobilize the Democratic base there to at least have a fighting shot,” Shortle said. 
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee did not immediately respond to requests by publication.
Brewer said the national involvement from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is a big deal because the race between Nelson and Bice is “so close.”
A recent poll of 500 voters conducted by GBAO Strategies found that Nelson is trailing Bice by only five percentage points. The Washington D.C.-based organization works largely with Democratic campaigns.
“I think what people are seeing is (in) what have been ‘Republican strongholds,’ people are waking up to the way Republican policies really failed them,” Brewer said. “And so I think there’s some bellwether states here that maybe have been ignored for the last few years that they’re going to have to start paying attention.”
Trump’s visit to Durant also shows the “weakness” and unpopularity of Mazzei as a candidate, she said. 
“If Trump feels he needs to come and stump for a Republican governor’s candidate in Oklahoma, that should tell you the mood of voters in Oklahoma and that things are shifting,” Brewer said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. House panels hear testimony on automatic license plate cameras
description: Amid a growing national backlash against automatic license plate reader technology and its potential for misuse, Pennsylvania lawmakers grilled law enforcement, tech and civil liberties advocates about how to ensure it isn’t abused. Automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) are broadly deployed by law enforcement, parking enforcement and toll collecting agenci[...]
text:
A Flock camera monitors passing traffic on Sept. 2, 2026 in Miami. The state department of transportation said this month it will remove license plate readers, such as Flock cameras, from all state highways, citing an increase in reports of misuse of the systems. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Amid a growing national backlash against automatic license plate reader technology and its potential for misuse, Pennsylvania lawmakers grilled law enforcement, tech and civil liberties advocates about how to ensure it isn’t abused.
Automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) are broadly deployed by law enforcement, parking enforcement and toll collecting agencies in the commonwealth. They collect images of passing vehicles and record the location, time, license plate number and, in some cases, identifying features such as bumper stickers or roof racks. 
In recent years, they’ve been credited with helping police locate stolen vehicles and wanted people and allowing the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission to eliminate toll booths, among other uses, speakers said Monday at a joint hearing of the state House Transportation and Judiciary Committees.
At the same time, proponents of the technology say they share concerns about privacy, data retention, unauthorized access, sharing and selling data and potential misuse. 
Scott Bohn, executive director of the Pennsylvania Chiefs of Police Association, said his members’ position is straightforward. “Pennsylvania should regulate the responsible use of automated license plate reader technology rather than eliminate an effective public safety and investigative tool,” he said.
Civil liberties advocates, on the other hand, called for an outright ban, or, at least, strict constitutional limits on ALPR use, warning that the profusion of cameras photographing every car that passes when combined with artificial intelligence threatens the privacy of everyone who drives.
“AI-driven automatic license plate reader technology allows the government to do something now that it has never been able to do before, and that is to travel back in time and reconstruct where people traveled, whom they saw, and what they did,” said Mitchell Smith, legislative counsel at the Institute for Justice. “And all this information is now available at the click of a button and does not require law enforcement to first obtain a warrant.
Zealous opposition to APLRs has focused largely on one provider of the technology. Flock Safety markets ALPR cameras and other public safety technology including acoustic gunshot detectors in conjunction with software that allows law enforcement to search a nationwide network of databases maintained by law enforcement agencies. 
Flock’s cameras, usually mounted on freestanding roadside poles, have been vandalized as stories about law enforcement abuse of the tech have circulated in the news. In August, The Washington Post published the results of an investigation that found well over 50 cases of officers who have been charged with misusing Flock and similar systems to spy on spouses or intimate partners, exes and their exes’ new partners.
It included the story of a mother from Leechburg, Armstrong County, who said she repeatedly warned police and the district attorney’s office that her police officer husband had used a competitor to Flock to stalk and threaten her. The officer, Michael McSherry, ultimately pleaded guilty to official oppression and served about 11 months in jail, according to the article.
The U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee Crime and Counterterrorism Subcommittee held a hearing last week where senators heard the story of a woman who was wrongly arrested for a fatal car crash after a Flock camera captured her car miles away.
Kevin Kane, director of government relations for Flock Safety, said his company has been taking steps to address concerns about how his company’s product is used. They include tougher controls on when officers can use it, shorter default data retention windows and automatically flagging searches for review if they don’t meet requirements.
“We’ve invested significantly to make sure this technology is used appropriately, and we’re going to keep doing that,” Kane said.
Elizabeth Randol, legislative director at the American Civil Liberties Union of Pennsylvania, said it’s important to distinguish between ALPRs and automatic traffic enforcement devices, such as red light cameras that issue tickets for violations of traffic laws. 
“ALPRs capture the movement of every driver who passes, regardless of whether they are suspected of any crime, creating patterns of behavior,” she said, adding that the images are entered into a database where they’re checked against “hot lists” of license plates to identify vehicles being sought by police. 
“Over time, this data can reveal personal details about our lives, our religious practices, medical visits, political activities, personal relationships, and daily routines. This dragnet surveillance threatens the freedoms the Fourth Amendment was adopted to protect,” Randol said.
She noted that ALPRs have been in use since the late 1990s, but have recently exploded in numbers with the entry of venture capital funding into the industry and with the advancement of artificial intelligence.
With investment in the technology, there’s pressure to sell more cameras, retain more data and share data to generate the profit investors are looking for, Randol said. 
“In other words, ALPR companies are in the business of trading our privacy for profits,” she said.
Proposed laws would limit ALPR use
Several pieces of legislation have been introduced or proposed to regulate ALPR technology, many with bipartisan support.
State Sen. Doug Mastriano (R-Franklin) published a memo seeking cosponsors last month for a bill that would limit permitted uses to stolen vehicles; missing or endangered person alerts; manhunts for “wanted or dangerous” individuals; vehicles “reasonably believed to be connected to a specific criminal investigations”; public safety threats that are “specific and articulable”; warrant searches; and other emergencies with imminent threats to life or safety. 
Sen. Dan Laughlin (R-Erie) would prohibit “networked” ALPR systems that create automatically databases of every passing vehicle, saying they “could reveal where someone works, worships, receives medical care, spends personal time and who they associate with.” 
Rep. Tarik Khan’s (D-Philadelphia) proposal would give private individuals the right to sue and authorize the state attorney general and county district attorneys to investigate violations and bring civil enforcement actions.
Rep. Nathan Davidson (D-Dauphin) is a co-sponsor of Khan’s bill and introduced legislation that would prohibit law enforcement from sharing ALPR information with federal agencies or police in other states for purposes of tracking people who may travel to other states to obtain abortion care or other health care.
Deanna Dyer, a lobbyist representing the Women’s Law Project, pointed to what she called a  “notorious case” in which a Texas sheriff’s office used Flock databases to investigate the travels of a woman who had a self-managed abortion. 
“One officer was able to make one inquiry about one person regarding suspected personal action that’s not a crime, and successfully collected interstate surveillance data on this person from 83,345 cameras across over 6,800 camera networks, Flock networks to be specific,” Dyer said.
She urged lawmakers to consider the issues through the lens of gender equality and justice.
“This increasing reproductive police state under which many Americans are now living impacts the most vulnerable women and girls in our communities,” Dyer added.
Digital rights advocate recommends warrant requirement
The Electronic Frontier Foundation, which advocates for digital rights and civil liberties, has sounded alarms on the harms of ALPRs for years, senior staff attorney Lisa Femia said. The group is suing the city of San Jose, California, over its practice of searching its ALPR database without first obtaining a warrant. 
She said the scope of the ALPR networks and the scale at which the databases are searched by law enforcement around the country make it difficult for agencies to meaningfully review how their data is being used. Thousands of police departments share access to their data and searches by external agencies can number in the millions, Dyer said, amounting to a “serious invasion of privacy.”
“This is why EFF believes that ALPR mass surveillance should not exist and is incompatible with a free society. It’s why we ultimately urge governments to ban ALPRs and cease use of this technology altogether,” she said. “No system configuration or set of legislative guardrails can eliminate the risks inherent in this mass surveillance. But if and when cities do use ALPR surveillance, state legislatures must then impose strict enforceable limitations.”
That means there should be an “ironclad” warrant requirement before police can search for a vehicle in an ALPR database, Dyer said. Searches should be connected with only the most serious crimes, she added.
Legislation should also mandate a rigid data deletion deadline. She noted New Hampshire requires data to be deleted after only three minutes if a license plate is not already on a hotlist. Flock recently changed the default setting in its software to delete data after seven days rather than 30. 
Dyer said there must also be a rigorous audit trail for every search and annual external audits to identify officers who are conducting invalid searches. Dyer added that the audit logs should be accessible to journalists and the public. 
“Public records have often proved the best way to expose the harms and privacy violations of these systems … and Pennsylvania lawmakers should not cut off access to that vital tool for public transparency and oversight,” she said.
Finally, Dyer said, ALPR data should not be shared with out-of-state or federal agencies.
“Pennsylvania has its own laws and values,” she added. “It should not allow its residents’ sensitive data to be accessed and searched based on the laws, policies, or whims of out-of-state and federal agencies.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: NASA astronaut tours Montana campuses encouraging students to register to vote
description: Few men and women in the world have had the opportunity to “be my own little spaceship,” as former NASA astronaut John Harrington describes performing a space walk at the International Space Station. Two decades ago, Harrington, a naval aviator and member of the Chickasaw Nation, became the first enrolled member of a Native American […]
text:
Former NASA astronaut John Harrington is touring college campuses as part of Astronauts for America, encouraging young Americans to register to vote. (Courtesy photo)Few men and women in the world have had the opportunity to “be my own little spaceship,” as former NASA astronaut John Harrington describes performing a space walk at the International Space Station. 
Two decades ago, Harrington, a naval aviator and member of the Chickasaw Nation, became the first enrolled member of a Native American tribe to fly in space as part of the 16th Space Shuttle mission, spending nearly 20 hours doing spacewalks. 
It’s an event that is commemorated on a 2019 edition of the Sacajawea dollar coin, and one Harrington has been recounting to college students around Montana while encouraging them to register to vote in November’s elections. 
“That’s what our responsibility is, as citizens of this great nation, to get people to go out and vote,” Harrington said in an interview with the Daily Montanan. “Not tell them who to vote for, just get out and do your responsibility.”
Harrington visited Blackfoot Community College last week and will be at Montana State University on Monday evening as a member of Astronauts for America, a nonpartisan organization that launched this spring.
More than 100 former NASA astronauts are part of the organization and Harrington, who lives in Marion just west of Kalispell, is a member of the group’s steering committee. 
Harrington said a few of his colleagues first approached him last fall with concerns they had about the country’s increasing divisiveness, and how they could use their experience and platform to make a difference. 
“What can we do as astronauts to use our voice …  to maybe kind of change the dialogue in the nation today, and really focus back on the Constitution, the rule of law, separation powers, all those things that you know this country was founded on,” Harrington said. “Can we bring back a dialogue across the aisle from both sides?”
Astronauts for America says its members are charged with a new mission — getting young Americans to vote. Many have been touring college campuses for weeks — in California, Michigan, Massachusetts, Texas and Montana — with members interacting with students and community members and hosting conversations about the importance of civic engagement. 
Riffing on one of the most iconic statements of the 20th century, the campaign’s message is that “Going to the polls is one small step for you, and one giant leap for our country.” 
Harrington said when he was in college he carried out his responsibility and voted, but wasn’t very engaged in the issues. 
“I believed that the people we elected to national office had it all together,” Harrington said. “As you get older, you realize that it’s not necessarily the case, right?” 
In the last two presidential election cycles, demographic data compiled by Pew Research shows that more than 55% of voters were more than age 50, around 15% were younger than 30. 
Harrington uses this data and tells students: “Don’t let Boomers decide your future.”
“As a student, your vote is your voice,” he said. “If there’s something you want to see your elected representative vote for — things that are going to make your life better, your kids’ life better — don’t believe that people that are much older than you have your best interest in mind. You have your best interest in mind.”
Harrington said that he’d been asked to get involved in politics numerous times, but emphasized that Astronauts for America was founded on nonpartisan ideals, which Harrington says is an easy parallel to make with spaceflight. 
“As an astronaut, I never asked my commander what his politics were or his religion — none of the crew did,” he said. “That’s not what we were concerned about. We’re concerned about our mission and we all played a part. If we didn’t, the mission would fail.
Everyone in America has a mission, he continued, and the mission “is our country.”
“You may not think one vote makes a difference, but if one little part on a space shuttle comes apart, you’re not going to get to orbit. In voting, you’ve got to play your part,” he said. “Don’t expect somebody else to do it for you, because the mission may not turn out the way you want it to.”
Harrington will also be speaking at the University of Idaho, where he completed a doctorate in 2014 on Oct 12.

name: Delaware
title: Katz calls for televised debate with Coons after campaign says UD debates canceled
description: Republican Senate nominee urges Delaware party leaders and news organizations to organize a face-to-face forum WILMINGTON, Del. — Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Katz is calling for a televised debate with Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons after Katz’s campaign said it learned the University of Delaware will not hold its traditional Delaware Debates progr[...]
text:
Republican Senate nominee urges Delaware party leaders and news organizations to organize a face-to-face forum
WILMINGTON, Del. — Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Katz is calling for a televised debate with Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons after Katz’s campaign said it learned the University of Delaware will not hold its traditional Delaware Debates program for the 2026 general election.
The University of Delaware has not publicly announced 2026 debate dates, and Delaware LIVE could not immediately independently confirm that the university has formally canceled this year’s program.
UD’s Center for Political Communication continues to describe Delaware Debates on its website as a biennial program conducted in partnership with Delaware Public Media. The university says the debates are designed to give voters an opportunity to hear directly from candidates for statewide federal and gubernatorial offices. The most recent debates were held in October 2024.
Katz said the absence of a Senate debate would deprive voters of an important opportunity to compare the candidates directly.
“Delaware voters deserve better,” Katz said. “Senator Coons and I are asking Delawareans to entrust one of only 100 United States Senate seats to us. They deserve to see us on the same stage, answering the same difficult questions and defending our records, policies and solutions.”
Katz asks party leaders to help organize debate
Katz called on Delaware Republican Party Chairman Gene Truono and Delaware Democratic Party Chair Evelyn Brady to jointly organize a professionally moderated and televised debate.
“This is an opportunity to put people over party,” Katz said. “I am asking Chairman Truono and Chair Brady to work together and give Delaware voters the debate they deserve.”
Katz proposed inviting television, radio and news organizations to participate and distribute the debate statewide.
Katz won the Republican Senate primary Sept. 15 and will face Coons in the Nov. 3 general election. Delaware Department of Elections records list both candidates as qualified for the ballot.
Coons was first elected to the Senate in a 2010 special election and subsequently won full terms in 2014 and 2020. Katz previously represented the 4th Senate District in the Delaware General Assembly as a Democrat and ran for U.S. Senate as an Independent in 2024.
Long-running Delaware tradition
The University of Delaware launched Delaware Debates in 2010 in partnership with Delaware First Media, now Delaware Public Media.
That inaugural program included debates for Delaware’s U.S. House and Senate seats. The Senate debate between Coons and Republican Christine O’Donnell drew national media attention and was co-moderated by CNN’s Wolf Blitzer and Delaware journalist Nancy Karibjanian.
By 2016, UD described the event as its fourth biennial Delaware Debates. The program continued through subsequent election cycles, including the seventh edition in 2022 and Senate, House and gubernatorial debates in 2024.
UD says the debates traditionally include questions from journalists and university students and are livestreamed or otherwise made available to the public.
As of Sept. 28, the university’s Delaware Debates webpage highlights the 2024 events but does not list a 2026 debate schedule.
Katz: Interviews aren’t the same as a debate
Katz said individual candidate interviews can be useful but argued they do not provide the same comparison as having candidates answer identical questions at the same time.
“Senator Coons has represented Delaware in Washington for nearly 16 years,” Katz said. “Voters are the employers. They deserve a job-performance review of the person who has represented them and a direct comparison with the person asking to replace him.”
Katz, a pediatric critical care anesthesiologist, compared the need for information in elections to decision-making in medicine.
“Patients deserve to understand their choices before making important decisions about their lives, and voters deserve to be fully informed before making an important decision about their government,” Katz said.
He also argued that debates serve as a check on elected officials and political institutions by forcing candidates to answer questions publicly and respond to each other’s positions.
“This is bigger than Mike Katz or Chris Coons,” Katz said. “It is bigger than Republicans and Democrats. This is about accountability and whether Delawareans have a meaningful opportunity to question, compare and scrutinize the people asking to represent them.”
Challenge remains open
Katz said he would participate in a debate hosted by UD, another Delaware college or university, or a coalition of news organizations.
“I am ready to debate Senator Coons anytime, anywhere in Delaware, before a fair and professional moderator,” Katz said. “There is still time.”
Katz closed his challenge by urging organizers to allow voters to make their own comparison.
“Give Delawareans the debate. Give them the facts. Let them see us side-by-side. Then trust the people to decide.”
Delaware LIVE has requested confirmation from the University of Delaware regarding the status of Delaware Debates 2026 and would add its response when received. The Coons campaign should also be given an opportunity to respond to Katz’s debate challenge.
TO GO

What happened: Republican Senate nominee Mike Katz says he has been told the University of Delaware will not conduct Delaware Debates in 2026.
What is confirmed: UD’s website still describes Delaware Debates as a biennial voter-education program, but as of Sept. 28 it does not list a 2026 debate schedule.
What Katz wants: A professionally moderated, televised debate between Katz and Democratic Sen. Chris Coons.
The race: Katz and Coons are qualified candidates for Delaware’s U.S. Senate seat in the Nov. 3 general election.
What remains unanswered: Whether UD has formally canceled the 2026 program and whether Coons will accept Katz’s debate invitation.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Hundreds of nurses at Dane County SSM clinics vote to unionize
description: Hundreds of nurses at 10 SSM Dean Medical Group outpatient clinics in Dane County voted by 71% to form a union last week.  The union drive of the 340 nurses at the SSM Health clinics comes just months after nurses at SSM St. Mary’s Hospital in Madison voted by 89% to start a union in […]
text:
Nurses at St. Mary's Hospital in Madison have petitioned for an election to vote on joining the Service Employees International Union. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Hundreds of nurses at 10 SSM Dean Medical Group outpatient clinics in Dane County voted by 71% to form a union last week. 
The union drive of the 340 nurses at the SSM Health clinics comes just months after nurses at SSM St. Mary’s Hospital in Madison voted by 89% to start a union in June. The St. Louis-based Catholic health system has vehemently opposed the union effort from the St. Mary’s nurses, including by trying to get the National Labor Relations Board to invalidate the union election results. 
The St. Mary’s nurses have filed official charges with the NLRB over SSM administration’s refusal to begin negotiating a contract and undertaking anti-union efforts. 
Nurses at both St. Mary’s and the clinics have said they’re working to unionize to better advocate for their patients as the administration makes cuts that force the nurses to do more. The clinic nurses have also tied their effort directly to the system’s treatment of the St. Mary’s nurses.
“For too long, policies have been handed down from SSM executives in St. Louis that force nurses to do more and more with fewer and fewer resources,” said Kat Doebler, a 30-year nurse who works at the SSM Health Outpatient Surgery Center. “This intense focus of extracting corporate profits out of us has led to burnout and the loss of some of our very best nurses. It’s time for the nurses who actually take care of patients to have a seat at the table in the decisions that affect our jobs and how we provide that care. We are very disappointed that instead of respecting our freedom to form a union, SSM has been waging a campaign to violate our rights. Together with our coworkers at St. Mary’s, we’re calling on SSM to stop breaking federal law and start working with us to make sure our clinics and the hospital are the best places to work and receive care.”   
After the SSM administration fought the recognition of the union at St. Mary’s, the system said in a statement that it “respects” the decision of its clinic nurses. 
“We thank every nurse who participated in the recent National Labor Relations Board election at ten of our SSM Health Dean Medical Group outpatient centers in the Madison area,” SSM spokesperson Lisa Adams said. “While we would have preferred an outcome that allowed us to continue working directly with our nurses, we respect their decision and are committed to working constructively through the process ahead. We are grateful for the dedication of our nurses and the care they provide each day. Together, we will continue supporting our patients, serving our communities, and advancing our Mission of providing exceptional health care services to all.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah lawmakers want a higher bar for ballot initiatives that raise taxes. Will voters sign off?
description: A political issues committee launched a campaign on Monday urging Utah voters to reject a proposed constitutional amendment on their Nov. 3 ballot that would set a higher bar for ballot initiatives that raise taxes.  Utah lawmakers earlier this year approved a resolution to put the proposed amendment to the Utah Constitution before voters, which […]
text:
The Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A political issues committee launched a campaign on Monday urging Utah voters to reject a proposed constitutional amendment on their Nov. 3 ballot that would set a higher bar for ballot initiatives that raise taxes. 
Utah lawmakers earlier this year approved a resolution to put the proposed amendment to the Utah Constitution before voters, which will appear as Amendment B on Utahns’ ballots when they start hitting mailboxes in about two weeks. 
If voters approve Amendment B, it would change the Utah Constitution to require some ballot initiatives to pass not just by a simple majority, but get at least 60% voter support. 
Utah lawmaker wants to ask voters to set higher bar for ballot initiatives that raise taxes

That requirement would apply if the new law enacted by ballot initiative would entail the imposition of a new tax, the expansion or increase of an existing tax or, “for a property tax, a change to the tax rate that causes the tax rate to decrease less than it would under current law.” 
In 2018, when Utah most recently saw a flurry of ballot initiative efforts, none received more than 60% of the vote. That year, voters approved an initiative for full Medicaid expansion with 53.3% of the vote. An initiative to legalize medical marijuana passed with 52.7%. And a Better Boundaries’ initiative to create an independent redistricting commission passed by a slim 50.3%. 
The Medicaid expansion and medical marijuana initiatives both created new tax revenue streams to pay for themselves, so if they were subject to the new 60% threshold in Amendment B, neither would have passed.   
Proponents — including the Utah Taxpayers Association — have argued the change would help protect taxpayer money. The question’s sponsor, Sen. Lincoln Fillmore, R-South Jordan, argued during this year’s legislative session that voters should decide whether to set the higher threshold or not. 
“The question here is very simple. Do the people of Utah want 50.1% of the people in the state to be able to raise taxes on the other 49.9%? Or, when it comes to this type of a question, should there be a broader consensus?” Fillmore said in January when arguing in favor of putting the question on the ballot. “I don’t know what the people will decide … but I’m certainly not afraid to ask.” 
In a prepared statement issued Monday, Fillmore and the question’s House sponsor, Huntsville Republican Rep. Jason Kyle, argued Amendment B “protects the initiative process while recognizing a simple principle: if you want to raise your neighbors’ taxes, you should have broad support from your neighbors.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Utah voters will still decide,” Fillmore and Kyle said. “Amendment B leaves the decision with Utah voters while requiring broader agreement before a statewide initiative can raise taxes on Utah families.”
But to critics, including the group Utahns Protecting Our Constitution, the change to the Utah Constitution would be an “unnecessary and permanent rewrite of Utah’s founding document that would weaken one of the most important tools citizens have to hold government accountable,” the political issues committee said in a news release issued Monday. 
Elizabeth Rasmussen, executive director of Utahns Protecting Our Constitution, is also executive director of the anti-gerrymandering group Better Boundaries — which successfully pursued a 2018 ballot initiative to ban partisan gerrymandering and create an independent redistricting process.
“The initiative process belongs to the people of Utah, not to the politicians it was designed to check,” Rasmussen said in a prepared statement. “Amendment B changes that balance, making it harder for Utah voters to exercise that power.”
Utahns Protecting Our Constitution argues that the Utah Constitution should only be changed when absolutely necessary.
“Amendment B makes an unnecessary, permanent change to our Constitution, taking power away from citizens and giving politicians more control over the rules,” Rasmussen said. 
In coming weeks, the political issues committee will start spreading its “vote no” message through TV ads, mail, canvassing, and digital outreach. It has also launched a website. 
The group has a sizable amount of money to spend on its opposition campaign. According to financial campaign finance disclosures, Utahns Protecting Our Constitution has collected about $593,000 in contributions as of this month.
Utah legislative leaders express regret over Amendment D’s ‘misleading’ ballot language

However, the group may face an uphill battle to bring voters to their side. According to a poll released by Noble Predictive Insights last week, about 50% of Utah voters support the proposed constitutional amendment, while 21% oppose it. However, 23% are unsure. The poll was conducted of 602 registered voters from Sept. 8-12. It has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.99 percentage points. 
Amendment B is one of two proposed constitutional amendments Utah lawmakers have decided to put on Utahns’ ballot this year. 
The other, Amendment A, would change the Utah Constitution to remove its explicit requirement that state officials publish proposed constitutional amendments in “at least one newspaper in every county of the state, where a newspaper is published for two months” immediately before the election. Instead, that Constitution would require they be published “in a manner provided by statute, for 60 calendar days” immediately before the election. 
Utah lawmakers proposed the change after two proposed constitutional amendments were voided from the 2024 ballot amid lawsuits, in part because the courts determined state leaders failed to meet the constitutional publication requirements. 
Proponents have argued that in the digital age, newspapers are becoming more scarce and not the primary way most Utahns get their information anymore. 
Utahns Protecting Our Constitution has not taken a position on Amendment A, Rasmussen said in a text message to Utah News Dispatch on Monday.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont man dies in custody
description:
A 44-year-old man was pronounced deceased at the Springfield correctional facility on Sunday
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont man dies in custody.
text:
The Southern State Correctional Facility in Springfield in Oct. 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

A Vermont man died in custody at the Southern State Correctional Facility in Springfield Sunday.
Trevis Gembarowski, 44, from Newfane, was taken into custody on Saturday, Sep. 26 and died the following day, according to a press release from the Vermont Department of Corrections. He had a medical event on Sunday morning, and correctional and medical staff began emergency medical response procedures, according to the release.
Officials did not release the reason that Gembarowski was detained. 
Gembarowski was pronounced dead later in the day. The release said the death is not considered suspicious. 
When reached over phone and email, Tracy Velazquez at the Department of Corrections declined to comment on the situation.
The Vermont Department of Corrections often houses detained individuals with specific medical needs at the Springfield facility since the facility has a hospice unit and the largest infirmary in the state.
Gembarowski’s death follows two deaths of individuals incarcerated in Vermont two days apart in March. VTDigger found that there were four deaths in custody reported in 2026 as of March 30. Nine people died in custody in Vermont in 2025.
The Vermont State Police and Defender General’s Prisoners’ Rights Office were alerted to the death, the release said, as is required by Vermont state law.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Recent ICE arrests at CT airports draw officials’ ire
description: Elected officials pointed to how public spaces like courthouses, city streets and bus stops that have been targeted by ICE in recent weeks.
text:
Elected officials decried recent Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests at New Haven’s Tweed Airport during a press conference on Monday, drawing attention to the latest example of public spaces like courthouses, city streets and school bus stops that have been targeted by ICE during the Trump administration’s deportation push.
The recent arrests are part of growing operations in Connecticut in recent months, including more than 100 arrests during an operation that centered in Danbury in August. 
Among those arrested at Tweed was Deng Dhieu Kuach Deng, a native of South Sudan and a freshman basketball player known as “Deng Deng,” who attends Southern Connecticut State University. He was arrested on Sept. 4th while traveling domestically in the U.S. and attempting to fly out of New Haven’s Tweed Airport and was released on Sept. 16. An Ecuadorian student who lives in Fairfield County was also arrested this month and released weeks later.
ICE did not return a request for comment about the recent cases.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said that he met with four young people on Monday morning who had been detained by ICE in the last three weeks — two at Tweed, two at Bradley International Airport — including Deng Deng.
“None of them have any criminal record,” Blumenthal said. “They are not citizens of the United States, but they have a legal basis to be in this country.” 
In each case, those detained were released after stays of two to three weeks in ICE detention, according to Glenn Formica, an attorney with The American Immigrant Legal Clinic. 
“What people really need to understand is that it’s not like they get picked up and released. They get picked up and just traumatized,” said Formica, who worked on the recent cases. 
Formica said that such detainees are not entitled to the same rights, such as the right to a court-appointed attorney, as people held under criminal charges. They are kept in “hyper stress” conditions: “They’re sleeping on floors, cement floors with foil blankets for days, broken toilets, dirty water. They have to pay for phone calls,” he said. “It’s just like one horrifying experience after another, and you’re scared at the time.”
At the press conference, Formica called on attorneys across the state to get involved, at a moment when the crush of cases has advocates sounding the alarm about the lack of due process. 
“My call is to every attorney: I don’t care if you do real estate. I don’t care if you do elder law. You need to step up now,” Formica said. “You hold the line here, or there’s no more line. We go over, after 250 years, into an abyss that we have never thought was possible, and the fight is now for attorneys.”
New Haven Mayor Justin Elicker expressed thanks for the support of such attorneys in assuring Deng’s release.
“Thanks to that collective action and advocacy of many people here — and not in this room as well — and at Southern Connecticut State University, the student was released from ICE detention,” Elicker said. “He’s now back on Southern’s campus with his classmates, exactly where he should be, studying and being a productive member of our community.”
Elicker said that he has communicated to the airport authority board that “We do not want the airport to cooperate with ICE beyond what it is legally required to do. Travel should be about bringing people together. It shouldn’t be about tearing people apart.”
Formica advised those visiting the country to exercise caution when using using airlines.
“Even if you have status, you should be very careful or not use the airlines,” he said. “And I would fear for even visitors to this country getting on domestic flights with the way ICE is handling this.” 
Elicker also urged caution: “I think that people need to use their own judgement about anywhere they go right now, because we’ve just seen over and over again ICE changing their tactics and targeting people where they think they can detain them.”
Kica Matos, president of the National Immigration Law Center, described “agents wearing Tweed access badges and parking in private airport lots” conducting arrests. She said that the recent arrests in Connecticut are part of a larger phenomenon of information sharing between the Transportation Security Administration and ICE.
“Because of this, 800 people throughout our nation have been arrested at airports, including people with pending asylum cases, with green card applications, and with work permits,” she said. “Today, one of the most ordinary acts of American life — getting on a plane — has become a trap, even for people following the process.” 
Matos called for four immediate actions: 
“First, we need to end the secret pipeline of passenger data that goes from TSA to ICE. Second, this administration needs to stop the appalling practice of stopping people at airports. Third, Tweed needs to stop being complicit with ICE. That means that Avports, the company that operates Tweed, and the New Haven Airport Authority must do everything possible to honor this city’s proud immigrant stance. Finally, ICE needs to get out. They need to get out of our city, and they need to get out of our state.”
