name: WyoFile
title: When can Wyoming children be treated like adults in court?
description:
Data has shown that Wyoming kids often are treated as adults in the state’s judicial system.
The post When can Wyoming children be treated like adults in court? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A Campbell County court sentenced 16-year-old Michael Frank Seiser to at least 20 years in prison in 2007 for his involvement in murders orchestrated by Kent Proffit, an adult. 
Though Seiser was a minor at the time, the teen was charged in adult court, meaning court proceedings were public, and he wasn’t entitled to protections under Wyoming’s Juvenile Justice Act. Juvenile courts are confidential and offer rehabilitative services specific to youth. 
It’s not unusual for Wyoming kids to be treated as adults in court when the crimes they are charged with are as serious as those in the Proffit cases, as they came to be called. “You’ll recall that one of the victims was strangled to death. It was absolutely a tortured homicide. And the other one was shot to death,” John Perry, the district judge who presided over the case, said. 
But youth charged with lesser offenses can also be funneled through adult courts. 
In 2018, 14-year-old Dale Warner brought a loaded gun with extra bullets to his junior high school in Gillette, planning to shoot students and staff. He was disarmed after a student reported his plans to school officials. 
Warner was charged as an adult and ultimately pleaded guilty to assault and possession of a deadly weapon with unlawful intent. He also pleaded no contest to a count of aggravated assault and battery. 
State public defenders attempted to have Warner’s case transferred to juvenile court, noting that Warner had been in emotional pain after his biological father died just a few days before the incident. But the Campbell County District Court denied the request, and the Wyoming Supreme Court later affirmed that decision.
Young people in Wyoming are also often processed as adults through misdemeanor courts. All in all, data has shown that just a small minority of youth who come into contact with Wyoming’s justice system are served by juvenile courts. 
Data collected by the U.S. Department of Justice shows Wyoming had the highest juvenile incarceration rate in 2021. (Easy Access to the Census of Juveniles in Residential Placement. Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention)
There are a number of downsides for kids to be tried in adult courts. Proceedings in adult court aren’t confidential, so a charge could impact a kid for the rest of their life. Sentences are also generally more severe in adult courts than they are in juvenile courts. More broadly, the goals between the juvenile and adult court systems are different. Whereas juvenile courts focus on treatment, training and rehabilitation, the adult justice system is more focused on punishment and deterrence. 
“The delta between these aims produces greater risks for children forced to navigate the adult system, including fewer procedural safeguards and exponentially higher possible punishments,” Casper attorney Ryan Semerad, who frequently works on cases involving youth, wrote in a petition to move a client’s case to juvenile court. 
Wyoming’s juvenile courts
The Wyoming Legislature created separate juvenile courts in 1947 through the Wyoming Juvenile Justice Act. The law says the purpose of the juvenile court system is, among other things, to provide treatment and rehabilitation to help kids become “functioning and contributing adults.”
But unlike most states, Wyoming lacks a unified juvenile court system, instead taking a county-by-county approach that results in different treatment for youth based on where they live. 
What’s more, because some parts of the state don’t have juvenile courts, many young people are processed through misdemeanor courts, where they don’t have protections under the state’s juvenile justice act, according to a 2010 Wyoming ACLU report. The report estimated that at the time, 10-15% of youth appeared in juvenile court, while the other 85-90% went through adult courts. 
It’s unclear if those numbers still hold true. Such information is difficult to collect because it exists across disparate systems, or isn’t tracked by agencies at all. Legislation that would allow the Department of Family Services to synthesize such data from multiple systems has repeatedly failed to become law. 
Wyoming laws also have a narrow definition of “status offenses,” which ends up funneling more kids into adult courts. These are offenses that are crimes because of a person’s age — underage drinking, for instance. In Wyoming, some common alcohol offenses, for example, aren’t considered status offenses, but crimes, according to a 2017 Wyoming Law Review article. That means kids who are convicted of these offenses are treated as adults in adult court rather than kids in juvenile court who need treatment or rehabilitation. 
Who decides when kids go to adult court?
In most states, cases involving juveniles start out in juvenile court by default, and prosecutors have to then try to move them to adult court, Semerad explained. 
But in Wyoming, a lot of power is given to state prosecutors to decide whether a kid will be treated as an adult in court proceedings — they alone can decide right off the bat whether to charge a kid as an adult. It’s “purely a prosecutorial decision,” Perry said. “So the judges and the judiciary have no control over what gets filed where.” What’s more, judges in circuit or municipal courts don’t have authority to even transfer a child’s case to juvenile court — that authority is given to prosecutors. 
Judge Ronn Jeffrey discusses his career as a juvenile judge for the Cheyenne Municipal Court during a news conference Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025, in Mayor Patrick Collins’ conference room. After retirement, Jeffrey will continue to work as the lead of a new informal juvenile justice task force. The task force will look for solutions to codify some of the best practices regarding juvenile justice. (Ivy Secrest/Wyoming Tribune Eagle)
“Effectively, when we codified our Juvenile Justice Act, we created some mechanisms in there that just shoehorn all of the discretion to the prosecutor,” Semerad said. 
In district court, once a prosecutor decides to charge a kid as an adult, it’s on the defense attorney to ask the judge to transfer the case to juvenile court. When they do that, the proceedings are confidential, because they take place in front of a district court judge who’s sitting in a juvenile court capacity. 
In the case of Warner, the Gillette teen who brought a gun to school, for example, the evidentiary hearing on whether his case should be moved to juvenile court was the only proceeding in the matter that was kept confidential. 
“You can’t get any information about that, because that was a juvenile court proceeding,” Donna Sheen, the former executive director for the Wyoming Children’s Law Center, said. “So all of the wonderful evidence about how stellar the kid was and how this was just a momentary mental health break never got to the public.” 
Petitions to move cases to juvenile court
Wyoming statute provides a kind of “checklist” for attorneys and judges to go through when they’re analyzing whether a case should be in adult or juvenile court, Perry said. That checklist of seven factors asks them to consider, for example, the relative sophistication of the person involved in the crime and the seriousness of the crime. 
“In my experience over many years, the types of cases that usually get sent back [to juvenile court] are generally property crimes, sometimes controlled substance crimes. There’s no real fixed rule as to how those look,” Perry said. 
Steven Titus, a Gillette attorney, said that youth with a violent felony or who have any juvenile delinquency or adult criminal history are more often than not sent to adult court. 
In Semerad’s experience, there are typically two things that kill petitions to move cases involving minors to juvenile courts. If the charge is a violent felony, the seriousness of the crime usually weighs against sending it to juvenile court. Representatives from state agencies also often testify in favor of the prosecutor’s decision, Semerad said. “They always say, ‘We don’t have the resources to deal with someone with this kind of charge.’” 
It’s difficult to move cases to juvenile court, but not unheard of. Titus had a client charged with aggravated vehicular homicide whose case was originally charged in district court then transferred to juvenile court. “It’s not unheard of that a case can stay in the juvenile court for proceedings, but it is extremely rare,” Titus said. 
Semerad recently attempted unsuccessfully to move two of his clients’ cases to juvenile court. One case involved a Casper teen, Eavan Castaner, who shot and killed another youth in a park. Castaner, Semerad wrote, “struggled with mental illness and substance abuse as he ricocheted off close friends, romantic partners, and other avenues to escape his lived experience in a chaotic home.” 
“This is Defendant’s first exposure to the criminal justice system. And the State chose to have him face the most punitive version of that system for kids with the most serious charge available under Wyoming law,” he wrote. 
Another case involved a Casper teen, Gabriella Kathleen Aultman, who stabbed another youth at a Halloween party (the victim survived). Semerad wrote in his petition to move Aultman’s case to juvenile court that she was “navigating the complexities of teenage girlhood against the backdrop of a new and substantial mental health diagnosis, bipolar disorder, newly prescribed psychotropic medications, and an effort to have a fresh start at a new high school.” 
Diversion?
Juvenile courts may provide more youth-centered services, but in an ideal world, Sheen said she would like to see more options for keeping kids out of the court system entirely. 
“Courts aren’t the best avenue for changing behavior or shaping and managing behavior at that age,” she said. 
“I would love to see a statute that says if they commit a misdemeanor, you just divert them … into something that’s helpful. You provide programming. You work with schools to develop strategies for how you’re going to be changing that trajectory of a kid.” 
Although services aren’t uniform across the state, some Wyoming counties provide diversion programs for youth that give them a chance to avoid charges. The Juvenile Diversion Program in Teton County, for example, provides interventions for youth facing Circuit Court charges. The six-month program could involve community service hours, substance use counseling and therapy. Those who finish the program can have their charges dismissed.

title: 1,289-year-old whitebark pine, oldest on record, found in Grand Teton National Park
authors: Christina MacIntosh, Jackson Hole News & Guide
description:
Beetles killed the tree in 2021. It had been growing since 732 A.D.
The post 1,289-year-old whitebark pine, oldest on record, found in Grand Teton National Park appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
JACKSON—When Jared Friedman took a core sample of an incredibly gnarled, spindly and not-very-tall whitebark pine in Paintbrush Canyon, it did not occur to him that the tree might be ancient. It was less than 30 feet tall.
Friedman, a doctoral student in forest ecology at the University of Wyoming, was in Grand Teton National Park studying what kills whitebark pines. He takes core samples of every dead tree he encounters.
He dated the unsuspecting tree at 1,289 years old, making it the oldest recorded whitebark pine tree on record. 
The tree eclipsed the previous record-holding whitebark from Idaho’s Sawtooth Range by 22 years.
“It was a dream-come-true finding for me,” Friedman said.
Whitebark pines are hardy, grizzled trees that eke out a living in mountain environments across an expansive range that stretches from Canada to California. Because they live in places where conditions are harsh, nutrients are limited and soils are poor, they are slow-growing. Some trees are growing by just two cells per year, Friedman said.
Whitebark that get really old are particularly good at playing the long game.
“Life’s not easy, but growing slowly helps,” said Diana Tomback, a biology professor at the University of Colorado Denver.
That makes counting their rings difficult. Friedman used a microscope to date the tree, because its rings were too close together to be seen with the naked eye. He counted 1,275 rings. He used a model that extrapolates how many rings are missing between a core section and the actual center of the tree, which added another 14 years. He dated the tree to have died in 2021, killed by mountain pine beetles, a native insect that is wreaking havoc on whitebark as its population grows and expands due to climate change.
For all their resilience, whitebark pine are facing declines from nonnative blister rust, mountain pine beetles, wildfire and climate change. In 2022, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service listed the species as threatened.
Because whitebark grow in the alpine — in the case of Friedman’s tree, at 9,800 feet — they’re beloved by mountain athletes and enthusiasts. That also puts them in the crosshairs of recreation, including development at Jackson Hole Mountain Resort and the proposed expansion of Grand Targhee Resort.
The tree was considerably older than its peers. The average age of whitebarks sampled in the stand was 400 years old, with most between 300 and 500, Friedman said. There were a couple of trees that were 800 years old and a couple that were about 1,000 years old. The next oldest tree was just over 1,000, Friedman said.
There are probably more really old whitebark than we’re aware of, Tomback said. In the course of her research she has encountered very old looking trees in the southern Wind River Range, by Christina Lake in British Columbia and by Yellowstone Lake.
“The problem is finding ages on these trees is not that easy,” Tomback said. “Most people when they encounter these trees don’t happen to have a tree core with them.”
“I would say trees this old are rare,” she added. “They’re just probably not as rare as the record would indicate.”
Post mortem
Sara Germain, a botany professor at the University of Wyoming and Friedman’s advisor, and Tucker Furniss, an ecosystem science and management professor, established a forest monitoring plot in Grand Teton two years ago. The plot is one of 85 sites across 30 countries as part of a forest health monitoring network managed by the Smithsonian Institute. Scientists contributing to the network are studying how forests are changing in response to a warming climate.
The professors and their students monitor trees at the entire elevational gradient in the Tetons, from cottonwoods by the Snake River to whitebark pine in the alpine. They know where every tree is and track competitive relationships, insect spread, disease spread, growth, regeneration and survival. Every year, they figure out what kills trees when they die.
Peak whitebark death occurred in Paintbrush Canyon about a decade ago, Germain said. Most of the trees in the plot were dead. There’s evidence that trees that died there 30 to 40 years ago were also killed by mountain pine beetles, Friedman said. It’s possible the old tree was never hit by beetles before. It could have been growing in a spot with access to water, which made it more resilient to fending them off.
The tree had some stripped bark, meaning that the tree was killing branches and roots while continuing to grow, Germain said. That’s a sign that it had been dying slowly over time, in some portions and not others. It’s common to see in old trees. The strip-barked parts of the tree could have died hundreds of years ago, Friedman said.
Old trees are often battered and gnarled looking.
“It’s just the effect of all these severe climate conditions on them,” Tomback said. “It’s an indicator that the conditions are just not where you want to take a vacation.”
The tree’s age could have contributed to its susceptibility to mountain pine beetles, Tomback said. Because it was strip-barked, that means things might not have been working well for the tree, compared to a younger tree that is growing more vigorously. It could have been more vulnerable if it had fewer roots with which to take in water.
“I don’t think old trees are less susceptible, they’re at least average if not more susceptible,” Tomback said.
Those who live and those who die
Trees that get the oldest are those that are able to put up with different stressors the longest, Germain said. That’s a product of genetics (like resistance to pests), neighbors — including trees and beneficial fungi — and a little bit of chance, such as germinating in a west-facing spot and not getting clawed by a grizzly bear, burning or being struck by lightning.
“Between genetics, friends and the luck of the draw, those things come together to produce our oldest trees,” Germain said.
Whitebark pine, in general, have the potential to get older than other forest trees, because they’re slow-growing and able to tolerate rough conditions, Tomback said. Under the right circumstances, whitebark can reach ages of 400 to 600 years. It takes a protected situation within harsh conditions to become a millennial tree, Tomback said. That typically is found right below treeline.
“They’re growing very slow as a result of these very harsh conditions,” she said. “That enables them to live long.”

title: Your democracy needs you
authors: Equality State Policy Center board of directors
description:
This election season is a time for all Wyomingites to not only vote, but help strengthen our system to be more inclusive and accessible to all voters, writes the Equality State Policy Center board of directors.
The post Your democracy needs you appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Fall is finally in the air across Wyoming. Along with turning leaves and cooler temperatures come yard signs, social media ads and other electioneering activities as we head into the 2026 general election on Nov. 3. 

Opinion

As board members for the Equality State Policy Center, an organization with a multidecade mission to encourage civic engagement in Wyoming, we firmly believe that our state is stronger when Wyomingites participate in civic life by voting. High voter turnout and robust participation in elections ensure those elected will truly represent the interests and objectives of people from their communities. 
We encourage you to learn the rules via the secretary of state and your local county elections office and to use that knowledge and exercise your democratic franchise by casting your ballot this fall, whether by absentee mail-in ballot, in-person early voting or at the polls on Election Day — Nov. 3. Importantly, for those who may not yet be registered to vote, or for those who may have been removed from registration lists after not voting in a previous election, you can register (or reregister) and vote in person on Election Day at your polling place. But be sure to bring an acceptable means of identification. From school and local government funding to public lands to personal liberties to many other issues, Wyoming has a lot at stake this election year. Our democracy needs all of us to participate, so please become informed on the issues and candidates and vote for the people who will best represent you to create the Wyoming we all need and deserve. 
Creating a thriving democracy in our state will take more than voting this year. We also encourage the newly elected — and returning — legislators and decision-makers to help us refine our voting processes to build a Wyoming where every citizen has the ability and access to cast a vote for the candidates that best represent them. 
This fall’s election demonstrates that Wyoming’s elections are safe and secure, and as opposed to restricting access to voting by creating burdensome and hard-to-implement rules, we need our elected officials to tear down the red tape. Democracy works better for all hardworking Wyomingites when it is inclusive and accessible to all. 
We call on our decision-makers to be open-minded and seek innovative solutions to make systems and processes that encourage our voting-eligible electorate to participate. Our organization has championed policies like ranked-choice voting and preserving ballot drop boxes to return mailed ballots swiftly and securely, while fiercely opposing new restrictions on how and when Wyomingites can register to vote and cast their ballots. 
As we move from this election season to the next, let’s not revisit failed pieces of legislation that further restrict voting access or fumble the accurate checks and balances within the system. Rather, let’s work together to create a Wyoming that is free and fair for all of our people.

title: State legislators make the case for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus in Idaho
description: Editor’s Note: This is the second installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining a proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focused on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho and is available online. The series concludes Tuesday with a closer look at […]
text:
Idaho state Sen. Dave Lent, R-Idaho Falls, makes an announcement from the Senate floor on Jan. 7, 2025, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Phot by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Editor’s Note: This is the second installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining a proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focused on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho and is available online. The series concludes Tuesday with a closer look at the opponents who say they are against bringing the project to the state.
Idaho is in a uniquely strong position to host a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus because of the 75-year track record of research, safety and innovation at Idaho National Laboratory, says state Sen. Dave Lent.
Lent, R-Idaho Falls, is a retired nuclear facility training manager whose career was focused on protecting workers and the environment from radioactive materials at Idaho National Laboratory, or INL for short. 
In nuclear campus talks, Idaho Gov. Brad Little says protecting Snake aquifer is ‘nonnegotiable’ 

But if Idaho is one of the handful of states selected for the federal U.S. Department of Energy project, it would require the state to accept and store spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste.  If three states are selected to host a campus, each state could be responsible for accepting approximately 33,000 tons of the country’s spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste, said state Rep. Monica Church, D-Boise, who opposes the project.
But researchers and engineers at Idaho National Laboratory are already involved in much of the nuclear lifecycle work, such as taking spent nuclear fuel, reprocessing it and turning it into new fuel for a reactor, Lent said.
“If you look at all of the aspects, and that includes the workforce, the location, facilities and expertise, we are a standout (potential host site) there,” Lent said in an interview with the Idaho Capital Sun. “Our challenge is going to be helping our citizenry understand what high level waste is and how it can be handled safely.”
Officials at Idaho National Laboratory declined to be interviewed for this series of articles.
Lent isn’t the only legislator supporting bringing a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Dozens of other lawmakers do, too.
 More than 40 Idaho legislators voice support for nuclear campus

On Aug. 17, 46 of Idaho’s 105 state legislators wrote a letter in support of the innovation campus, telling Idaho Gov. Brad Little and Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke they would help the cause by pursuing bills, funding mechanisms and more.
“We will prioritize legislation needed to strengthen Idaho’s position, including funding mechanisms, permitting authority and workforce investments that keep pace with the timeline DOE has set,” the letter stated. 
The two highest ranking legislators, Senate President Pro Tem Kelly Anthon, R-Rupert, and House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, both signed the letter. Forty of the legislators who signed are Republicans. Two Democrats, Sens. Ali Rabe, D-Boise, and James Ruchti, D-Pocatello, also signed the letter to Little and Bedke. 
“Idaho’s case for hosting this campus rests on decades of preparation,” the letter continued. “The Legislature is committed to matching that preparation with the policy support needed to see this through to a final decision, and to a successful campus if Idaho is selected.” 
“We are probably the best equipped in the country because of our operating experience with spent fuel,” Lent added. 
 Some legislators say Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus would be economic boon to the Gem State

In July, the U.S. Department of Energy announced that Idaho is a finalist to host a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus. 
“The benefit to Idaho is significant,” Lent said, calling the new campus the most secure new revenue source available to the state. “We’re talking about billions of dollars as revenue streaming into our state.”
Rep. Erin Bingham, R-Idaho Falls, makes a comment during the March 16, 2026, House State Affairs Committee meeting at the Idaho Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Rep. Erin Bingham, R-Idaho Falls, also believes the campus would support good-paying jobs for generations of Idahoans to come. In an op-ed, Bingham wrote that her children have grown up in a community positively shaped by the Idaho National Laboratory by having a “hometown identity built partly around being the place where nuclear energy was born.”
“Here’s what I actually want my kids to understand. Used nuclear fuel isn’t the same thing as high-level waste headed for permanent burial,” Bingham wrote. “It still holds most of its original energy value, and the entire point of the research NLIC would support is developing the technology to use that value again, shrinking both the volume of material that needs long-term management and how long it stays hazardous.
“That’s a research and manufacturing mission, not a dumping ground, and conflating the two doesn’t protect my kids. It just confuses them and their neighbors about what our hometown lab is actually being asked to do.”
While the Department of Energy, or DOE for short, says the new campuses would create thousands of jobs and attract financial investment, the states selected to host a campus will be required to accept shipments of radioactive waste and spent nuclear fuel for reprocessing from other states. 
Church, a Boise Democrat, said the risk to the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer and public health is too great to accept. She said Idaho should rely on and be guided by the 1995 Settlement Agreement between the state and the federal government that limits the amount of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste that can be brought into Idaho.
“The thing Idahoans need to understand most is that agreement is not only protecting Idaho writ large, it also is protecting our aquifer,” Church said. “It’s protecting our farmland, and it’s protecting our drinking water,”
Church called on state officials to continue to support Idaho National Laboratory’s overall research and mission while rejecting the DOE’s innovation campus proposal because of the shipments of radioactive waste.
Bingham wrote in her op-ed that residents and legislators should be asking hard questions about how the project would affect eastern Idaho, its environment and its people. But, she wrote, that doesn’t mean that those questions should prevent the state from exploring the benefits that the project could bring to the state.
“That doesn’t mean I think every question about this proposal is settled, and I wouldn’t tell my kids that either,” Bingham wrote. “Asking good questions is something I try to model for my children every day, and I expect our state to do the same here. But there’s a real difference between asking good questions and assuming the worst before the process has even played out, and I think a lot of the recent rhetoric has crossed that line.”
Lent said Idaho National Laboratory has proven it can do hard work safely. 
“Idaho really has the expertise to do this, and we have the location and the facilities,” Lent said. “We would have to build larger facilities, but like I said, we are already doing this now and we really have the place to do it.” 
 Idaho legislator says risk is misunderstood, Idaho has track record of nuclear safety

During his career, Lent led training programs at Idaho National Laboratory and obtained national certifications. He said the risks associated with a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and accepting spent fuel and radioactive waste are misunderstood and sometimes exaggerated by opponents of the proposal. 
“We have an overamplification of the risk in our culture,” Lent said. “Most people don’t realize that every day they are exposed to radiation. There is radioactive material in the air we breathe; it comes from the earth and sky. The body has radioactivity in it naturally. We have an overamplification of risk, and I think it is up to us to help educate folks.”
Lent also said the understanding of nuclear materials and the approach to protecting the environment has evolved in the 30 years since Idaho reached the 1995 Settlement Agreement. 
Lent said regulations are stronger, science has advanced and measurements are much more precise than they were decades ago. 
That’s not to say public safety isn’t Lent’s priority.
This summer, Lent participated in meetings between Department of Energy and Idaho state officials discussing the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus. One meeting was in Chicago in August with the other states in the running to host an innovation campus and another was in Little’s office at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise, Lent said. 
“We had a pretty frank discussion about nonnegotiables and what our expectations were as a state,” Lent said. 
“I usually start every discussion with the fact (that) ‘we have two nonnegotiables when we talk about doing work in Idaho,” Lent said. “The first is absolutely protecting the people of Idaho and their health and the second is protecting the environment in Idaho and keeping it the way it is. Those are nonnegotiable, and where we start all our discussions with.”
On Wednesday, Little told the Idaho Capital Sun that protecting the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer and the health of Idahoans are also nonnegotiable issues for him. 
To legislators like Bingham, exploring the possibility of being a host site to a campus also protects the state’s economic possibilities that could come with more federal investments and funding into nuclear energy.
“My kids are growing up in a community that helped launch the nuclear age and could help lead its next chapter,” Bingham wrote. “I’d rather they grow up believing that’s something to be proud of, backed by real facts, than absorbing fear stirred up by people who don’t have to live with the consequences of getting this conversation wrong.”

title: Rogers, Dobson lay out contrasting plans for Alabama Secretary of State’s office
description: The contest for Alabama Secretary of State features two candidates with contrasting visions for running the office.  The office is responsible for administering the state’s elections, registering voters, registering businesses in Alabama and is the primary record-keeper for the state. The constitutional office has been held by Republicans since 2007. Current[...]
text:
Voters in Alabama will choose between Democrat Wayne Rogers (left) and Republican Caroleene Dobson (right) for Secretary of State. The candidates laid out differing plans for the office, should they be elected. (photos courtesy of candidates; graphic by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The contest for Alabama Secretary of State features two candidates with contrasting visions for running the office. 
The office is responsible for administering the state’s elections, registering voters, registering businesses in Alabama and is the primary record-keeper for the state. The constitutional office has been held by Republicans since 2007. Current Secretary of State Wes Allen was elected in 2022 and did not seek a second term in order to run for lieutenant governor.
Both candidates had relatively smooth primaries. Caroleene Dobson, the Republican nominee for Secretary of State and the 2024 GOP nominee for the 2nd Congressional District.  won the nomination over two other candidates, and after Republican State Auditor Andrew Sorrell withdrew. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Democratic nominee Wayne Rogers, a first-time political candidate, was unopposed in his party’s primary. 
The candidates
Dobson, 39, said in an interview on WFSA in May that her top priorities are secure elections and a strong economy in Alabama, citing her experience in the 2024 race
“It was a tough general election where Republicans were pitted against Democrats, and I witnessed firsthand that while we have some good procedures, some good laws in place when it comes to election integrity,” she said in May. “There’s still a ways to go in ensuring that our elections are 100% secure, that our voter rolls are 100% accurate, that we are shielded from the outside influence of far left activist groups from out of state.”
She also said she hopes to streamline services, reduce fees and increase accessibility to start a business in the state. 
Dobson also said she wants to create an “election integrity and securities” division within the Secretary of State’s Office, if elected, inspired by Florida’s Election Crimes and Security. 
“Currently, we don’t have a dedicated branch of the office to administer these election laws, to serve as a sounding board when folks have questions about election procedure or to investigate election fraud claims of election fraud,” Dobson said. 
Election fraud is extremely rare in Alabama. According to the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, there have been 41 convictions or findings of voting fraud in the state since 2000. Over 2.2 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election in Alabama. 
While Dobson did not explicitly express support for early in-person voting, she did say a working absentee ballot system is necessary for Alabamians who are unable to vote in person on Election Day. 
“We have so many vital workers – our truckers, our healthcare workers throughout the state – that can’t physically be there on Election Day,” Dobson said in May. “I’m committed to making sure that we have an absentee ballot system that works, and that the ballot is the chain of custody between the probate judge and the person voting via absentee ballot, and no one else is involved in that.”
Voting via absentee ballot in Alabama is exclusive to certain groups of voters, including the elderly, those registering in Alabama but living outside the county (like a college student or deployed service member) and those with scheduled shifts longer than 10 hours on Election Day. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the state effectively opened the illness excuse to all eligible voters, leading to a surge in absentee voting that year.. 
Rogers, 64, said in a recent phone interview that his priorities are compiled in what he likes to call the “Alabama Voting Rights Act.” 
“The decisions in Milligan, the decisions in the Louisiana case that were decided back in the spring have ripped the heart out of the national Voting Rights Act,” Rogers said. “Let’s make it a state law that makes it easier for people to vote … I am not talking about letting non-citizens vote.”
The U.S. Supreme Court this Spring weakened Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act (VRA) of 1965 in a case known as Louisiana v. Callais, requiring plaintiffs in any case to show intent to discriminate by lawmakers. Under prior case law, plaintiffs had to show the effect of maps was discriminatory. 
The justices’ decision led to a special session of the Alabama Legislature to create the infrastructure for August’s special primary election under the state’s 2024 congressional maps. Those maps were previously struck down as racially discriminatory multiple times by federal judges and the U.S. Supreme Court before Callais in a case known as Allen v. Milligan. 
In Rogers’ proposed local VRA, the state would re-establish no excuse absentee voting; open polls the Saturday before an election, and allow 16-year-olds to pre-register to vote when they get their driver’s license. Their registration would not go into effect until they turned 18, but Rogers hopes allowing pre-registration would help with Alabama’s registration numbers.
“We would get a lot more young people registering to vote if we would do that,” he said. 
According to the nonprofit Civics Center, 29% of Alabama’s 18-year-olds were registered to vote as of July. Nationally, the group estimates that 45% of 18-year-olds are registered to vote across 39 states that have data available. 
Alabama Democrats have long pushed for early voting, but Republican lawmakers have pushed back claiming it will be too costly. The Secretary of State does not have power to introduce legislation. 
Rogers hopes that just opening the polls for one day before general elections will be a satisfactory compromise. 
“You’ve got two days when you can go into the polls. I think that would make it much more convenient, and we would drive our turnout up by 15 to 20% if we did something like that,” he said. 
Rogers also wants to limit campaign contributions to half of the average Alabamian’s annual salary at $27,000 per campaign cycle.
“Why should anyone, or any corporation, or any union, or any (political action committee) be able to give to a campaign more than six months’ wages than the average Alabamian? I don’t think they should,” he said. 
His proposal also includes eliminating Alabama’s straight-ticket voting, a system that allows voters to choose a party’s entire slate of candidates with a single ballot mark, which Rogers said “perpetuates the party that’s in power.” Alabama is one of six states that uses the voting system, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. 
Eliminating the system is broadly unpopular within both parties, however some prominent Democrats, including gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones, have called for ending straight-voting, which tends to work against Democrats.
According to data from the Alabama Secretary of State’s Office, more than 1.5 million (67.7%) of the 2.2 million ballots cast in the 2024 general election were straight ticket. Of those, more than 1 million (65.1%) were Republican ballots and about 540,000 (34.9%) went to Democrats. About 58.9% of registered voters voted in the 2024 general election.
In the 2022 general election, about 947,000 (66.6%) of 1.4 million ballots cast were straight ticket votes. Of those, almost 299,000 (20.9%) were Democrat ballots and almost 649,0000 (65.1%) were Republican ballots. About 38.6% of registered voters voted in the 2022 general election.
Campaign fundraising
According to the most recent campaign finance filings, Dobson has raised almost $700,000, and loaned her campaign $500,000 at its start. She spent about $724,000 through the end of August. 
Not including Dobson’s personal loan, most of her cash contributions have come from individuals (40.3%), followed by political action committees (PACs) at 36.7% and businesses at 14.4%, according to the reports. 
Rogers has raised about $39,000 and spent about $22,000 through August 31. According to the reports, most of Rogers’ cash donations have come from individuals at 71.5%, followed by businesses at 20.8% and PACs at 7.2%.

Caroleene Dobson


Age: 39 
Party: Republican
Occupation: Real Estate attorney
Residence: Montgomery 
Education: B.A., History and Literature, Harvard College, 2009; J.D., Baylor University School of Law, 2012
Offices sought/held: Republican nominee for Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, 2024
Fundraising: Raised $694,076.11, spent $723,643.09 and has $470,433.02 on hand as of Sept. 2.

Age: 64 
Party: Democratic
Occupation: Executive Assistant to Jefferson County Sheriff; Lawyer
Residence: Birmingham 
Education: B.A., Music, Samford University, 1984; J.D., Samford University Cumberland School of Law, 1988
Offices sought/held: Former chair, Jefferson County Democratic Party; first-time candidate

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Democratic gubernatorial contender Jerri Green talks affordability, Republican supermajority
description: Democrat and Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green stood in Paris, Tennessee’s Eiffel Tower Park Sept. 20 in sweltering heat to tell a crowd of about 300 people why she should be Tennessee’s next governor. Paris is the seat of Henry County, a rural West Tennessee county of about 32,000 people that went 77% for President […]
text:
Memphis Councilmember Jerri Green is the Democratic candidate for governor. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Democrat and Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green stood in Paris, Tennessee’s Eiffel Tower Park Sept. 20 in sweltering heat to tell a crowd of about 300 people why she should be Tennessee’s next governor.
Paris is the seat of Henry County, a rural West Tennessee county of about 32,000 people that went 77% for President Donald Trump in 2024.
Her platform: Use unspent Temporary Assistance for Needy Families funds to erase medical debt, waive housing security deposits and clear childcare waitlists. Issue an executive order to ensure doctors can practice women’s healthcare without fear of prosecution under Tennessee’s anti-abortion laws. End the Tennessee Highway Patrol’s cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Stop state incentives for data centers. Stop renewing private prison contracts. Appoint an education commissioner with classroom experience. Stop giving tax rebates to big businesses and eliminate the grocery tax.
“Part of my plan is to start using the funds that we’re hoarding right now to relieve some pressure on everyday citizens, and then we can talk about that $2 billion rainy day fund, and if that’s how much we actually need … or if we need to consider that it’s Noah’s Ark out there for a lot of the residents and citizens in Tennessee, and we need to be helping them now,” Green told The Lookout in an interview.
In Lawrenceburg, near the Alabama border, 130 people showed up to meet her. In Claiborne County, 125 attended.
At each campaign stop, Green said she meets self-identifying Trump voters looking for a change. She always asks them why.
“They’re tired of the chaos and the culture wars, and they just want somebody who’s going to not gaslight them about grocery prices or gas prices and talk about real solutions,” Green said.
Will it be enough to give her the upper hand in a race that’s gone solidly to Republican candidates since 2010? Green thinks so.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jerri Green said she is not concerned about competition from independent candidates vying for the seat.(Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Outgoing Gov. Bill Lee is term-limited, leaving the state’s top seat open for the first time in eight years.
Green is campaigning against Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, a constant in Tennessee electoral office since 1999 and a Trump loyalist. Also in the field are businessman David Hatley, a conservative-leaning independent who is personally financing his campaign with up to $7 million, and Lauren Pinkston, a former Lipscomb University professor running as an independent with a moderate political bent.
Recent polling suggests Blackburn could claim between 46-51% of registered voters — less than Lee’s margins, which topped 60% in 2018 and 2022. Blackburn’s campaign recently funded a website attacking Hatley for a 1998 felony conviction, indicating she may see him as a threat to her overall support.
Green isn’t concerned about Hatley or Pinkston, the latter of whom she formally called on to drop out of the race on Wednesday. (Pinkston rejected Green’s request.)
“(Hatley) seems to be attacking and pulling from Marsha Blackburn’s voters, so he can continue to dump tens of millions of his own dollars into the race,” she said. “He’s not polling above 10% in any independent statewide poll.”
A mid-September poll of 600 likely voters, paid for by The Progress Fund, a Knoxville-based political action committee supporting Green, put Blackburn at 45%, Green at 36%, Hatley at 10% and Pinkston at 2%.
Green said her campaign has raised more than $1.5 million from all 95 counties, with an average donation of under $50 and 95% of donations coming from within Tennessee. 
The latest campaign finance reports are due Oct. 13. Green’s pre-primary report shows she raised nearly $147,000 in July, on top of nearly $550,000 she previously reported. While she has accepted funds from labor unions, her coffers contain no donations from corporate PACs, pro-voucher groups, “big Pharma” or “big data,” Green said. Green’s largest donation — $15,400 — came from The Progress Fund.
The independent candidates should drop out and support her campaign, she said.
“If they’re really worried about seeing Marsha Blackburn (win), they need to stop vote-splitting, they need to stop doing these vanity projects and actually think about the people in Tennessee and say, ‘We can’t have Marsha Blackburn. I’m asking you to vote for Jerri Green. She’s the only one with a viable path to beat her.’”
Memphis attorney, councilmember takes a swing at governor’s seat
Green, interim Chief Public Defender of Shelby County, holds a law degree from Georgetown University and previously served as Shelby County Mayor Lee Harris’ deputy chief of staff and senior political advisor. Her political tenure is brief compared to Blackburn, who entered elected office as a state senator in 1999, served eight terms in the U.S. House of Representatives and was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 2018. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Green revived the “One Tough Mother” tagline she used in the 2020 race against Mark White to represent District 83 in Tennessee’s house. She lost that race to White, the Republican incumbent, securing 46% of the vote to White’s 54%. She thought that would be her first and last political campaign, Green said.
But in 2023 she returned to the campaign trail in a bid to represent Memphis’ District 2 on city council. While the council is nonpartisan, District 2 was held by Frank Colette, a state Republican committeeman who had represented the district since 2016. He did not run for reelection in 2023. Green clinched the seat in a runoff election by 1.6%. 
“I learned a lot about what it takes to actually flip a seat, and the kind of effort you have to put in,” Green said.
She never planned to run for governor, but after multiple people pitched the idea, she thought of her kids’ futures and decided to give it a go, Green said.
“My youngest is autistic, and they want to dismantle the Department of Education and take money out of our public schools,” she said. “My daughter has less rights than her grandmother. My oldest will be going off to college soon, and I don’t know if he’ll still have a $7.25 an hour job when he gets out.”
“The future is just really bleak out there for a lot of people, and I just kept coming back to the fact that I’ve got to look them in the eye every day and … I wanted them to see their mom actually did everything she could,” Green said.
District 83 matchup features “one tough mother” against five term incumbent

Working alongside a Republican supermajority
If Green does win the race, she’ll be working with a Republican supermajority in the Tennessee General Assembly. 
She plans to model her governorship after Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who also works in a state whose legislature is solidly red. Green posted a video with Beshear on social media earlier this month.
Tennessee legislators have gerrymandered the state so “they’re picking their voters instead of voters picking them, and they represent a lot of extremism because of that,” Green said.
She said she plans to hold lawmakers accountable for voting in ways their constituents don’t agree with — even tiny towns in red districts may not like vouchers, Flock cameras and data centers. She’s ready to host press conferences and town halls and post billboards to put pressure on legislators.
Still, she’d be “happy to work with them” on some issues, giving the legalization of cannabis as an example (Republican legislators have introduced bills that would legalize medical marijuana over the years, but none have passed). 
Green said she’ll use gubernatorial veto power in cases where legislators seek to pass bills that could harm LGBTQ communities, Muslims, immigrants or women, for example.
“I’m not going to continue to do what they’ve been doing, which … is passing more lawsuits than laws,” she said, citing her experience as an attorney.
If she could convince the state legislature to do one thing, it would be to adopt Medicaid coverage expansion under the Affordable Care Act. Tennessee is one of 10 states that haven’t, citing concerns of financial burden on the state’s budget. Accepting the expansion would extend healthcare benefits to about 300,000 uninsured Tennesseans currently in an eligibility gap. 
“The number of people that I have met across this state that have been bankrupted, that are losing their homes, being forced out of retirement, making decisions about cutting medications in half versus having food versus paying their utility bill is terrifying, and there’s no reason for it,” Green said.
Green said she sees New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an example of how to work with President Donald Trump and his administration. 
“You can still speak your truth, which is, I think (Trump) is an authoritarian, I think he’s detrimental to democracy … Mamdani said all that, and he’s also been to the White House and had conversations with them to get investment in public transportation,” Green said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota University System envisions more collaboration, efficiency
description: The leader of the North Dakota University System is pushing for greater collaboration among its 11 higher education institutions.  Commissioner Brent Sanford on Thursday gained the backing of the State Board of Higher Education for what he calls the coordinated network or “One NDUS” model. Sanford’s plan presented to the board would create a network […]
text:
Brent Sanford, commissioner of the North Dakota University System, speaks during a State Board of Higher Education retreat at Bismarck State College on Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The leader of the North Dakota University System is pushing for greater collaboration among its 11 higher education institutions. 
Commissioner Brent Sanford on Thursday gained the backing of the State Board of Higher Education for what he calls the coordinated network or “One NDUS” model.
Sanford’s plan presented to the board would create a network of the state’s two-year schools and a network of the state’s smaller four-year colleges, with the two research institutions — the University of North Dakota and North Dakota State University — operating independently. 
“So this is not a different model. It’s not, but it is a different mindset,” Sanford said during Thursday’s meeting in Minot, emphasizing collaboration instead of competition among the campuses.
North Dakota college enrollment stable

The two-year schools are North Dakota State College of Science in Wahpeton, Lake Region State College in Devils Lake, Dakota College at Bottineau, Williston State College and Bismarck State College, which offers some bachelor’s degree programs as part of its mission as a polytechnic institution. 
The four-year colleges are Dickinson State, Mayville State, Minot State and Valley City State.
Sanford said each campus would retain its own leadership and would be responsible for its own accreditation. 
Sanford’s presentation said schools within the two-year and four-year networks would be expected to collaborate on academic programs, scheduling and student transfers. Each network would coordinate on developing new programs before campuses compete for the same students.
The presentation said the colleges would be expected to expand academic programming while reducing costs, excessive redundancies and unnecessary duplication of efforts.
Sanford said collaboration has already improved in the months since work on a strategic plan began and has the potential to more quickly address workforce needs. 
Bismarck State College, which has energy-related programs, is working with the State College of Science to address the energy training needs of an industry in Wahpeton. 
There would also be a shared services system for non-academic services, such accounting, payroll and financial aid at the University System level.
“We have to provide the support that the smaller campuses need,” Sanford said.
There have been some examples of shared services within the University System, but those have primarily been developed as needed, with a larger college helping a smaller one. 
A recent example would be NDSU taking over the bookkeeping for Dickinson State. 
Kevin Black, chair of the State Board of Higher Education, speaks during a board retreat at Bismarck State College on Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Board Chair Kevin Black called that situation “a launching pad to show us what could be.”
Sanford said the networks would give smaller colleges enough scale to be more efficient, while UND and NDSU are already at that size and would be able to concentrate on their own needs.
The University System started working with a consultant in June 2025. 
Sanford said they looked at other models, such as geographic groupings or a “flagship model” that would shift some responsibilities to UND and NDSU. 
Sanford said planning teams for the network model could launch in October or November and have more solid information for lawmakers when the Legislature meets in January. 
“This is not something that’s a completed playbook with policies intact,” Sanford said. 
Bernell Hirning, president of Williston State, said the plan would help build on existing academic consortiums for fields such as agriculture and nursing. 
“This is really giving the board a tool to put some support behind a lot of things we’re already doing as a system, and I really, really like that,” he said. 
The board, university presidents and system staff also discussed the potential plan at a retreat in August. 
“All the details about the connections and how structures might be built, we’ll get through that in time,” UND President Andrew Armacost said after the retreat. “But right now, I think the most important message is that sense of unity and connection across the 11 schools.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling contributed to this report. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: West Virginia Watch
title: America’s air monitors are disappearing. So is your power to expose polluters.
authors: Ames Alexander, Floodlight, Brad Racino, Floodlight
description: This story is from Floodlight, a nonprofit newsroom that investigates the powers stalling climate action. Sign up for Floodlight’s newsletter here.  Across much of the U.S., people have little way to know when the air they breathe turns dangerous. Over recent decades, federal funding for public air monitoring has declined, the number of monitors has […]
text:
A California official calibrates rooftop air monitoring equipment used to track local air pollution. (Photo courtesy of the California Air Resources Board)This story is from Floodlight, a nonprofit newsroom that investigates the powers stalling climate action. Sign up for Floodlight’s newsletter here. 
Across much of the U.S., people have little way to know when the air they breathe turns dangerous.
Over recent decades, federal funding for public air monitoring has declined, the number of monitors has fallen, and much of the remaining equipment is aging or located far from major polluters.
Now, the stakes are rising: Wildfire smoke is reaching more communities, data centers are adding pollution, and climate-driven heat waves are worsening ozone levels. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has delayed and rolled back requirements meant to hold companies accountable for their emissions.
As the public monitoring system has weakened, communities have increasingly turned to an alternative: low-cost sensors they can use themselves. 
But a Floodlight investigation finds industry is moving to restrict that option, too.
Since 2024, lawmakers in Louisiana, Ohio and Kentucky have passed strikingly similar bills — backed by chemical or manufacturing trade groups — that curb the use of community-collected data in enforcement actions.
The bills share a common thread: They block regulators from using air-quality data for enforcement purposes unless it meets EPA-approved standards. Similar bills in West Virginia have yet to pass. 
In case after case, proponents have made the same argument: Community monitoring isn’t reliable enough for regulatory enforcement. 
Yet when lawmakers in West Virginia offered a version of a bill designed to ensure accuracy, industry resisted. 
The bill “essentially codifies what we are trying to prevent,” an official at the chemical giant Chemours wrote in an internal email.

An early-warning system in decline
Thousands of small, often-unremarkable instruments serve as the nation’s early-warning system for dangerous air — detecting pollution that people can’t always see or smell.
Some sit inside shelters the size of garden sheds. Others are mounted on rooftops or tucked into fenced compounds. Together, these monitors measure pollutants ranging from ozone and carbon monoxide to carcinogens such as benzene and vinyl chloride.
The network grew out of the 1963 Clean Air Act and transformed the way the nation tracked air pollution, giving regulators data they could use to identify dangerous conditions and hold polluters accountable. Since then, air pollution has fallen dramatically across much of the U.S.
But today, the network is “showing its age,” said Chet Wayland, who led EPA’s Air Quality Assessment Division for nearly two decades. “And it’s getting smaller over time.”
For example:

Leaks, termites and ants plague monitoring stations in one state while officials in another have resorted to shopping on eBay for discontinued parts, according to a 2020 congressional watchdog report. 
Adjusted for inflation, federal grants to support the network have fallen more than 35% over the past two decades, while the Trump administration tried unsuccessfully last year to eliminate them entirely — and is trying again this year.
The number of government air monitors nationwide fell by nearly half over the same 20-year period, according to EPA data.

The decline was especially pronounced among air monitors that track toxic chemicals, including those linked to cancer and other serious health effects. 
For example, the network monitoring vinyl chloride — the carcinogen at the center of the 2023 train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio — shrank by more than half from 2004 to 2025. So did the network for chloroprene and benzene.
Floodlight analyzed the largest industrial sources of air pollution in Kentucky, Louisiana, Ohio and West Virginia — where the monitoring legislation was introduced — and compared what each one reported releasing against what public monitors in those states are capable of detecting.
For 71 of the 100 facilities examined, the chemical they release most isn’t measured by any government monitor in the state. 
Hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, methanol — no air monitor currently reporting to the EPA measures those toxic chemicals. 
Nelson Roque, an assistant professor at Penn State, co-authored a 2025 study that found nearly six in 10 U.S. counties have no public air monitor at all.
Such gaps matter most in communities already facing higher risks. Black and low-income people bear a disproportionate share of elevated cancer risks from air toxics, according to the EPA. 
“We’ve realized the value of other infrastructure, and yet not this one,” Roque said. “Last I checked, we all breathe air.”
The shrinking public network has set the stage for another fight: Who gets to measure the air, and whose data counts.
 Louisiana: A monitoring gap, and the fight to keep it
Public air monitors in Louisiana — a national hub for oil, gas and petrochemicals — are often located miles from major industrial polluters and fail to test for some of the most dangerous chemicals, a recent Floodlight investigation found. 
Community groups have tried to fill that gap. A $500,000 grant awarded under the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act would have allowed the Louisiana Environmental Action Network to establish air monitoring in 27 communities it identified as pollution hot spots.
But the group was able to install monitors in only four communities before the Trump administration canceled the grant last year. 
“It’s like having your legs knocked out from under you,” said LEAN executive director Marylee Orr.
In 2024, meanwhile, Louisiana became the first state to restrict the use of community air monitoring data.
The Louisiana Chemistry Association helped draft the Community Air Monitoring Reliability Act (CAMRA), which cites the need for “science-based standards” and bars the use of air pollution data in enforcement or regulatory actions unless it’s captured by EPA-approved monitors. That equipment typically costs tens of thousands of dollars.
In a previous statement to Floodlight, LCA president David Cresson defended the law, saying it ensures “data used to enforce our state’s environmental protection laws complies with minimum U.S. EPA standards” and doesn’t stop residents from monitoring air quality for their own information — only from using unregulated methods for enforcement purposes.
The same period brought other rollbacks, some sought by the chemical industry’s most powerful national lobbying group. The American Chemistry Council — the LCA’s national counterpart — spent more than $22 million lobbying in 2024, ranking 10th among 9,200 organizations tracked by an independent watchdog group. 
The ACC and the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers last year requested a blanket two-year exemption from Biden-era regulations meant to cut certain toxic emissions by nearly 80 percent at roughly 200 chemical manufacturing plants. They didn’t get the blanket exemption — but individual plants that applied did.
So far, President Donald Trump’s EPA has granted more than 60 petrochemical facilities exemptions from the rule, and the agency is now weighing whether to rescind it entirely. 
The ACC also successfully lobbied against federal rules that would have required about two dozen chemical plants to conduct fenceline monitoring for ethylene oxide, a carcinogen that contributes substantially to the elevated cancer risk in Louisiana’s Cancer Alley.
The national trade group did not respond to Floodlight’s questions about its lobbying or its involvement in Louisiana’s CAMRA law. Nor did it explain its role in promoting similar legislation in other states. 
But in an emailed statement, the ACC said it has invested in community air-monitoring projects and “publicly advocated for expanded access to credible air quality information.” It said it supports monitoring that produces reliable, transparent data and gives communities and regulators information they can use to make informed decisions.
Kentucky takes a page from Louisiana 
Odors from Rubbertown, an industrial complex that housed tire and synthetic rubber plants during World War II, have long bothered residents in west Louisville, Ky. So, in the early 2000s, the city’s Air Pollution Control District, the EPA and others launched a study that confirmed what residents had long known: The air had unacceptably high levels of toxic pollutants. 
A plan was enacted, regulations were revised, and the air was continuously tested. More than 15 years later, regulators announced toxic air contaminants in the Louisville metro area were down by almost 80 percent — with the most dangerous chemicals cut by 96 percent.
Despite the success of expanded air monitoring in Louisville, Kentucky lawmakers have moved in the opposite direction. In March 2025, 10 months after Louisiana’s CAMRA law, they passed House Bill 137, which also restricted how air-monitoring data can be used in enforcement actions. 
Lloyd “Rusty” Cress, executive director of the Kentucky Chemical Council, told the Kentucky Lantern that the bill was similar to Louisiana’s community air monitoring legislation.  The law says air needs to be tested with “scientifically defensible” methods — echoing a phrase used in an ACC blog post in 2023.
The ACC, the American Petroleum Institute, Dow Chemical and Chemours all lobbied for it.
Jess Loizeaux, a Chemours spokesperson, said the company doesn’t object to community air monitoring. “We object to community air monitoring results being used for enforcement decisions without first verifying the validity and accuracy of the data through official tests performed by trained technicians at the appropriate regulatory authority,” she told Floodlight.
Kentucky’s political push unfolded against a backdrop of major gaps in public air monitoring. Only one of the state’s 25 largest air polluters is close to an air monitoring station that measures the top toxic chemical it emits.
Fewer than a quarter of the state’s counties have an air monitoring station. 
Ohio’s restrictions meet with legal challenge 
Ohio’s new air monitoring rule was tucked into last year’s budget bill with no named sponsor.  It, too, stops regulators from acting on air-monitoring data collected by community groups. 
“When we take away the ability for those folks to have a reasonably priced monitor … for their own protection, we’ve just taken any tool they had right out of their hands,” said Miranda Leppla, an attorney who sued the state over the new rules last year on behalf of environmental groups.
The lawsuit also challenges another provision in the budget bill that instructs state regulators to remove Ohio’s “air nuisance rule,” which allowed citizens to take legal action against companies whose emissions endanger public health.
One of the plaintiffs, Donna Ballinger, lives in Middletown, Ohio, hundreds of feet from a steel manufacturing plant that frequently rains down black, white and gray particles onto her house and yard, she said. Fumes sometimes burn her eyes and throat, she said, and she often holds her nose when walking between her house and car. 
“My fear is cancer,” Ballinger told Floodlight.
She has an air monitor mounted in her front yard. But Ohio’s new requirement has made it impossible to use the data such monitors collect “as evidence of the nuisance conditions,” the lawsuit says.
The Ohio Chemistry Technology Council backed the measure. The group did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview.
Tony Long, general counsel for the Ohio Chamber of Commerce, said businesses are concerned that uncalibrated air monitors will spread misinformation.
“Given our litigious nature in this state, we think that the guardrails make sense,” he told Floodlight. “You don’t want to be stopped for speeding on an uncalibrated speed gun.”
With more than 90 public air monitoring stations, Ohio has a more robust air monitoring network than some states. Yet none of Ohio’s 25 largest air polluters are within 20 miles of a public air monitoring station that measures its top toxic emission. In fact, no air monitor in the U.S. measures the chemical that 10 of them release most.
Ohio’s Syensqo Specialty Polymers plant, which makes a resin used in plastics, released more than 130 tons of volatile organic compounds into the air last year, according to Ohio regulators.
The nearest air monitoring station is about four miles away — in West Virginia — and doesn’t measure VOCs. 
Industry resistance stalls West Virginia efforts 
West Virginia’s Department of Environmental Protection runs just 14 monitoring sites in 12 counties. The other 43 counties have no state monitoring stations at all.
None of West Virginia’s 25 largest air polluters has a public air monitor within 25 miles that measures the pollutant it releases most. For 17 of the facilities, no air monitor anywhere in the U.S. measures their top toxic emission.
In 2024, a state bill backed by the West Virginia Manufacturers Association would have barred community air monitoring data from use in regulation, enforcement and lawsuits; it passed the House but died in the Senate — partly because industry couldn’t agree on what to include.
A compromise version of the 2024 bill, drafted to address the concerns of some lawmakers, would have let regulators use community data if the monitors met manufacturer standards. Industry refused to support it. 
In emailed comments about the compromise bill, West Virginia Manufacturers Association Bill Bissett said it “neuters” the measure and was “now toothless.” Chemours’ Jeff Fritz wrote, “I do not like this draft,” and said the bill “essentially codifies what we are trying to prevent,” according to emails obtained by Mountain State Spotlight. Neither Bissett nor Fritz responded to requests for comment.
Subsequent bills, introduced in 2025 and 2026, also failed.
 Why monitoring matters 
Evidence shows that better monitoring can reduce pollution — and potentially save lives. 
In 2018, the EPA made refineries begin monitoring benzene along their fencelines, and within five years, the number of refineries above EPA’s benzene action level dropped by half, according to a report by the Environmental Integrity Project.
A scientist discusses an air-monitoring car with Louisiana Environmental Action Network staff. The Trump administration canceled the group’s air monitoring grant last year. (Zachary Kanzler for the Louisiana Environmental Action Network)
While some states have made it difficult to know what’s in the air, others have been proactive: 

California is funding equipment and training for residents in fenceline communities to monitor for things like pesticides, hexavalent chromium and other toxic chemicals. From 2017 to 2025, the state budgeted $1.4 billion to help communities that have historically been overburdened with air pollution.
Colorado required four industrial plants to install fenceline monitors that measure hydrogen sulfide, benzene and hydrogen cyanide in real time. The state also bought two mobile vans that regularly sample the same pollutants in surrounding neighborhoods. 
The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and its contractors operate 33 automated gas chromatographs — sophisticated equipment that collects air samples every hour and provides near real-time readings of volatile organic compounds. 

But in much of the U.S, those who live near industrial plants still have little way to know what they’re breathing.
An unanswered question
Reonda Victor lives in Louisiana’s heavily industrialized corridor between Baton Rouge and New Orleans, where flares from industrial plants often illuminate the night sky. 
Her mother, grandmother and sister all had breast cancer. Concerned about her own risk, she underwent genetic testing, which showed no predisposition to the disease, she said.
The closest public air monitoring station to her home — which lies in an area where air pollution poses one of the highest cancer risks in the country — tests only for lead. 
Did industrial pollution cause the illnesses that struck her family members? She can’t say. But proper air monitoring could help answer that question, she said.
“Without information, we don’t know.”
Kentucky Public Radio contributed to this investigation.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Cap on state revenue collection would rise under Colorado ballot measure
description: Coloradans will again vote on a long list of statewide ballot measures in 2026 — but unlike in previous years, the state Legislature had hardly anything to do with it. Proposition NN, which asks voters to raise the cap on the amount of tax revenue the state is allowed to keep each year, is the […]
text:
A close-up view of the sign at George Washington High School in Denver, March 25, 2024. (Photo by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Coloradans will again vote on a long list of statewide ballot measures in 2026 — but unlike in previous years, the state Legislature had hardly anything to do with it.
Proposition NN, which asks voters to raise the cap on the amount of tax revenue the state is allowed to keep each year, is the only legislatively referred measure on Colorado’s ballot this year. Democratic majorities in the General Assembly referred it to voters in May.
That’s a departure from the recent trend. Lawmakers referred seven questions to the ballot in 2024, and have averaged about five in every even-year election since 2016.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Legislature’s lone referendum this year comes amid a flood of initiatives that were placed on the ballot by citizen groups who gathered the required number of petition signatures. Proposition NN will appear on ballots sandwiched between 13 initiated constitutional amendments and statutory propositions — including six from Advance Colorado, a right-wing “dark money” group that doesn’t disclose its donors.
14 measures will appear on Colorado’s statewide ballot in 2026

If approved, Proposition NN would raise the revenue cap established by the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights, a 1992 constitutional amendment that placed strict limits on the state’s taxing and spending authority. Nonpartisan state analysts estimate the higher cap would increase funding for K-12 education by about $500 million a year. Depending on trends in revenue growth in future years, it could reduce the amount returned to taxpayers as TABOR refunds.
The measure sailed through the Legislature this year on mostly party-line votes, with nearly all Democrats in favor and Republicans unanimously opposed. It’s backed by the Colorado Education Association, the state’s top teachers union.
“Colorado’s public schools have been underfunded for decades because we are operating under an outdated revenue cap written more than 30 years ago,” CEA president Kevin Vick said earlier this year. “This measure does not raise taxes or ask Coloradans to pay a dollar more. It simply allows the state to use the revenue it already collects to support students, educators, and communities across Colorado.”
Yes For Colorado Kids, an issue committee registered in support of Proposition NN, had reported just under $2 million in campaign contributions as of Sept. 1. About half of that total came from Gary Advocacy, an arm of philanthropic group Gary Community Ventures, with the other half coming from a CEA-associated nonprofit and local Colorado teachers unions.
Two other tax measures
Proposition NN is one of three tax-related measures on the 2026 ballot — and if two or more of those measures are approved, things might get complicated.
The Protect Colorado’s Future campaign, led by liberal advocacy groups including the Bell Policy Center and the Colorado Fiscal Institute, is behind Amendment 87, a graduated income tax measure. The amendment asks voters to approve a new tiered income tax system, under which Coloradans earning over $500,000 a year — the top 3% of earners — would pay higher rates, with those in lower brackets receiving a slight tax cut.



Quotation







Colorado’s public schools have been underfunded for decades because we are operating under an outdated revenue cap written more than 30 years ago.


– Kevin Vick, CEA president


Dozens of liberal and progressive groups have endorsed both Amendment 87 and Proposition NN. The passage of both measures would represent by far the biggest set of changes to TABOR in the 34 years since Colorado voters approved it.
A long list of pro-TABOR conservative groups, meanwhile, are opposed to both measures. Advance Colorado says Proposition NN “undermines the purpose of TABOR, which was designed to limit government growth,” and it questions the need for additional K-12 education funding amid declining enrollment.
“This proposed measure is yet another route the Legislature has taken to circumvent TABOR and retain revenue for their own spending purposes,” the Advance Colorado Institute wrote in a report earlier this year. “TABOR refunds are a unique feature of Colorado that have historically provided significant relief to households across the state, and voters continue to strongly support these safeguards.”
Advance Colorado is also bankrolling a counter-proposal to block the graduated income tax: Proposition 136, which would cap income tax rates and prevent Amendment 87’s higher rates on higher incomes from going into effect.
Under Colorado law, any potential conflicts between two or more enacted ballot measures are resolved according to which measure got the most yes votes.
At least four campaign committees — Let’s Go Colorado, Brighter Colorado, Affordable Colorado and Don’t Price Us Out — have registered in opposition to both Proposition NN and Amendment 87. As of Sept. 1, Brighter Colorado had reported about $275,000 in donations, nearly all of which came from Advance Colorado and another conservative “dark money” group, Common Sense America.
Ballots will be mailed to Colorado voters beginning Oct. 2.

 Catching Our Eye

Billionaire Les Wexner has long been a magnet for political campaigns seeking contributions — especially in his native Ohio, where the retail tycoon directed a generous portion of his giving to candidates from both parties. Then came the Epstein files.
