name: Tennessee Lookout
title: After a fight for equality in the 1980s, Chattanooga civil rights activists prepare for new effort
description: CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. — Afternoon light slipped through the curtains of a dimly lit room on Martin Luther King Boulevard in Chattanooga. Black residents, clergy members and activists gathered in early May to organize opposition to Tennessee state lawmakers’ congressional redistricting effort, aimed at eliminating the last Democratic-held seat in the state. The[...]
text:
"They're trying to take away the vote we had," says Fran Pierce of the Louisiana v. Callais decision. Pierce stands in front of a mural of her father, Leamon Pierce, a longtime member of Chattanooga City Council. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. — Afternoon light slipped through the curtains of a dimly lit room on Martin Luther King Boulevard in Chattanooga. Black residents, clergy members and activists gathered in early May to organize opposition to Tennessee state lawmakers’ congressional redistricting effort, aimed at eliminating the last Democratic-held seat in the state.
The rapid redistricting effort in May by Republican state lawmakers came in response to a major U.S. Supreme Court decision, Louisiana v. Calais in late April carving out Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, a cornerstone of the Civil Rights Movement.
During a meeting hosted by the Hamilton County Branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, NAACP, Chattanooga resident Fran Pierce stood in front of the podium. She apologized to the crowd, sitting in folding chairs, for arriving late. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“They are trying to take away the vote we have. I think about the things my dad endured before I was even born. My dad Leamon Pierce went to Selma, Alabama for the march, sat in a church with Martin Luther King. They gathered to go make a change,” Pierce said. “Where are we at? Because it’s our voices that need to be heard, our vote that they’re trying to take away.”
Her father, Leamon Pierce, was a plaintiff in the 1989 case Brown v. Board of Commissioners of the City of Chattanooga, where a federal court found Chattanooga’s system of government violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act by diluting Black voting power and depriving Black residents of meaningful representation. 
Leamon Pierce went on to become one of Chattanooga’s first Black and longest-serving council members.
In late May, Fran Pierce sat in a small office at Liberty Bonding Company, tucked away just off Martin Luther King Boulevard in Chattanooga. Her father started the business in 1974, as one of the first black-run bail bondsmen.
Pierce, who has continued to run the operation after her father’s death, gestures to the wall behind her where a portrait of Leamon Pierce attached to a city council plaque hangs on the wall.  
“I realized I can’t keep sitting down, I gotta stand up,” Pierce said. “As I was growing up, I didn’t see it, didn’t understand it, but I know my dad was preparing me for something much bigger than me, and that I got to be ready to move.” 
Pierce said she was in her early 20s when Brown v. Chattanooga went to trial, and her father’s involvement in the case and its impact on voting rights for Black Chattanoogans hadn’t fully registered until now. 
Now, decades after the civil rights case, Brown V. Chattanooga, forced an overhaul of city government to ensure greater Black representation, the strength of the Voting Rights Act that underpinned that decision has been weakened.  
Lorenzo Kom’boa Ervin, 79, was a plaintiff and championed the class action lawsuit.
It’s likely the most important civil rights decision ever in East Tennessee, Ervin said. 
Lorenzo Kom’boa Ervin, a plaintiff in Brown v. Board of Commissioners of the City of Chattanooga, the 1987 lawsuit alleging the city’s at-large city council system violated the civil rights of Black Chattanoogans, photographed on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
“The decision was that they had to completely change this government. So it was revolutionary in that sense,” said Ervin.
 A judge ruled that the adopted structure had discriminatory intent to curb Black political influence and impaired the ability of Black voters. He ordered it be changed, creating three council districts with a majority Black population to ensure greater representation in Chattanooga.
Before the ruling, local government existed as a board of commissioners whose members were elected at-large. The top five vote getters, regardless of location, served on the board.  
 A Black person was not elected to the commission until 1971. Black people made up nearly 32% of Chattanooga’s population in 1980, according to court documents. 
“Of course, it (the lawsuit) wasn’t appreciated by the authorities, and even by some elements in the Black community it wasn’t appreciated, but they had to acknowledge that it was going to happen, with or without their say so. So they realized they couldn’t stop it,” Ervin said. “There’s no way to stop it. That was the power of the Voting Rights Act.”
From 1982 to 2024, nearly two-thirds of the more than 450 challenges invoking Section 2 involved local government practices, according to a study by the University of Michigan Voting Rights Initiative. Ten of the cases were brought in Tennessee, including six targeting local government bodies. 
Before the Callais decision, in cases like Brown v. Chattanooga, plaintiffs could prove racial discrimination in the way district maps were drawn by showing consistent lack of representation. Now, a legal challenge of a map must prove districts were intentionally drawn to disadvantage a racial group, which dissenting judges said is nearly impossible. 
The ruling prevents intentionally considering race as a factor when drawing a district, which directly contradicts the previous practice of purposefully drawing districts to have a majority black or minority population as a way to ensure representation for populations that have been historically disenfranchised in the U.S. 
“I think state leaders will look more closely at local maps than perhaps we did in the past,” said Sen. Bo Watson, a Hixson Republican, of the potential for redistricting city councils and local boards. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
The Callais ruling allowed Tennessee Republican lawmakers to swiftly pass redrawn congressional district maps in May, three months before primary elections, cracking the majority Black Congressional district of around Memphis into three. 
But the ruling is not limited to congressional districts; it applies to all electoral maps, including state House and Senate district maps as well as county and city districts. 
Up till now, state Sen. Bo Watson, a Chattanooga Republican, said to his knowledge the Hamilton County state delegation hasn’t been involved with local redistricting, but he expects that to change. 
“I think state leaders will look more closely at local maps than perhaps we did in the past, only because there’s a heightened awareness to it, not necessarily because of any desire to do anything outside what the locals might want to do,” Watson said by phone. “Certainly I think state leaders are going to be more interested in how local leaders are drawing their maps than perhaps we have in the past.”
Local offices could draw redistricting effort 
Every 10 years, based on new census data, city and county governments are required to meet and decide whether to redistrict. New maps are drawn and voted on by local elected officials. All district maps for city and counties must comply with both state and federal laws and if they are in violation they can be challenged in court.  
Watson said he is not currently focusing on redistricting efforts before the 2030 cycle, but he won’t be surprised if there is a legislative push in the next session.
Democratic state lawmakers Sen. Charlane Oliver of Nashville and Rep. Yusuf Hakeem, the only Democratic state lawmaker representing Hamilton County, both said in interviews that they are prepared for Republican state lawmakers to make a play for control of local redistricting
“I would not be surprised if we had some Republicans try to redistrict county government and school board, city council,” Hakeem said in an interview. “I think the reality of it is this has awoken the coinsciouness of people that have been misused and abused by the Jim Crow.”



Quotation







Our representation is thin, to say the least, but my concern is that it will totally be eviscerated with time.


– Rev. Ernest Reid, Second Missionary Baptist Church


Existing state laws already exist for the creation of new local districts. 
Watson said he is proud that in the three times since 2010 Republican state lawmakers have passed new maps, including the most recent congressional one, they have withstood legal challenges.
“So at least the time that we’ve [Republicans] been drawing the maps, we have drawn them within the requirements of the law,” Watson said. “Whether you like them or not, that’s a different question. But the fact of the matter is, we draw them within what the law requires us to do.”
For decades, Councilmember Ron Elliot said the city has maintained three majority minority districts honoring the directive made in the Brown v. Chattanooga decision. 
“I would not be surprised if we had some Republicans try to redistrict county government and school board, city council,” says Rep. Yusuf Hakeem, a Chattanooga Democrat. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
“But there’s a lot of concern. It’s a lot of unease. We see it at the congressional level. I’ve heard some whispers months ago about our state looking at local redistricting and particularly partisan races, and cross your fingers and hope like, hey, hopefully that stops at some point,” Elliot said.
Rev. Ernest Reid of Chattanooga’s Second Missionary Baptist Church, a voting rights activist, said in an interview directly after the Callais decision that he had grave concerns about the future of the local majority-minority districts. 
Reid said he is particularly wary about Hamilton County Commission districts.
County commission maps, which also define school board districts, passed ahead of the 2022 election cycle and maintained two majority-minority districts, currently represented by two Black men. 
What if the commission, currently majority Republican and white, aims to merge the two districts, he said, or racially gerrymander them? If those seats are drawn out, Black people will likely have no representation in county governance, Reid said.
And now there will be few options for legal recourse if that happens, he said.
“Our representation is thin, to say the least, but my concern is that it will totally be eviscerated with time,” Reid said
A lawsuit was the  only path to progress
In the 80s, Ervin said legal action felt like the only path to progress. 
The legal case against the city’s government was not won easily, Ervin said; other attempts to rectify mistreatment of Chattanooga’s Black community and address representation were futile. 
In the years leading up to the lawsuit, Ervin said he worked with an activist group, Concerned Citizens for Justice, and held protests at city hall, attended meetings, brought experts and met with the mayor in an effort to compel the city to address issues afflicting the Black community in Chattanooga.
None of it, Ervin said, brought about change. 
“We were able to put together the case based around the long history of racial discrimination in the electoral process itself, but also years of racial animosity, created by the local government and local officials against the Black population,” Ervin said. 
Ervin, along with members of the Concerned Citizens for Justice, spent more than three years combing the city’s libraries and state records to document Chattanooga’s police brutality, the disproportionate number of Black people killed by police and racial discrimination in housing, employment and public benefit programs before any legal representation agreed to take on the case. 
Some 20,000 exhibits were compiled for the case, Ervin said, which went to trial after another two years of preparation in 1989. 








Fran Pierce says the Louisiana v. Callais decision and move by the Tennessee Legislature to redraw congressional districts spurred a new understanding of her father's work as a Chattanooga civil rights leader. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









Fran Pierce, who plans to run for Chattanooga City Council, with memorabilia honoring her father, Leamon Pierce, who was a plaintiff in a suit to establish majority minority city council districts. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









"Our role in this period is to not accept unjust authority, to not accept a return back to the outright racism and white supremacy that ran this country, ran the South especially, back in the 1960s and 50s," says Lorenzo Kom'boa Ervin, photographed in the Eastgate Branch, Chattanooga Public Library, on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)






“The lawsuit changed this place in a lot of ways,” Ervin said about Chattanooga. “We brought an end to a certain kind of racial segregation where black people couldn’t run for office, it’s just amazing. I think about it sometimes that all the people that are in office now, and practically all the ones who came before and after them, were as a result of that lawsuit.”
Pierce said the precedent set by the court case is reflected in her late father’s legacy on Chattanooga City Council. 
Pierce said after the Supreme Court decision and subsequent redistricting effort spurred a new understanding of her father’s work she plans to take action to protect his contributions and defend Black civil rights.  
Since May, Pierce said she has been driving around and handing out voter registration forms. Pierce plans to run for city council. She said she wants to stand up as her father did. 
“My goal is to get the next generation, we got to reach the community, the ones that don’t know, like I didn’t know back then,” Pierce said. “Let’s get out, because you got a voice and if you don’t use your voice, it’s going to be taken away.”
Ervin credited the power of the Voting Rights Act for forcing change in Chattanooga but said it was the preceding protest movement that made the case possible.
“It was the people in the streets. It was especially working class black people in Alabama and Georgia and Mississippi, and everywhere else that created this movement that couldn’t be stopped, and that ultimately led to the stage of they created the Voting Rights Act,” Ervin said.
Ervin said creating a movement is the only way to push back.
“So, our role in this period is to not accept unjust authority, to not accept a return back to the outright racism and white supremacy that ran this country, ran the South especially, back in the 1960s and 50s,” Ervin said “So in that sense, I’m not afraid of what the Supreme Court does or whatever, because the Supreme Court ever only responded to what the people have done, if the people are willing to stand up and to fight back against these unjust conditions, as as happened back in the 60s and has happened before that, then they can stop anything.”

title: Bill by US Sen. John Boozman of Arkansas would require deeper look at care for women veterans
description: A bill recently introduced by Republican Sen. John Boozman of Arkansas and Democratic Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois would require more detailed reporting of the services provided to women veterans. The two lawmakers last week introduced the proposed Veterans’ Outcomes, Inclusion, Care and Experience for Women Veterans Act. The legislation, also known as t[...]
text:
(Getty Images)A bill recently introduced by Republican Sen. John Boozman of Arkansas and Democratic Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois would require more detailed reporting of the services provided to women veterans.
The two lawmakers last week introduced the proposed Veterans’ Outcomes, Inclusion, Care and Experience for Women Veterans Act. The legislation, also known as the VOICE for Women Veterans Act, would modernize an annual report provided by the federal Department of Veterans Affairs.
The legislation is aimed at helping policymakers identify areas where care for women veterans can be improved, the lawmakers said in a news release.
“As we look to improve the quality of care for women veterans in Arkansas and across the country, we must ensure the VA gathers the data and information necessary to identify gaps, address challenges and improve health outcomes,” Boozman said. “This bipartisan legislation will help strengthen accountability and ensure women veterans receive the care and support they are owed.” 
Duckworth, a retired U.S. Army National Guard and former Department of Veterans Affairs assistant secretary, said the legislation would require the agency to “take a deep look at how well female veterans are actually being served and how we can improve health outcomes.”
“As the primary health care home for veterans, this comprehensive review at the VA is long overdue to better care for the fastest growing veteran group in the country,” Duckworth said. 
The bill is supported by the Wounded Warrior Project, Disabled American Veterans and Paralyzed Veterans of America.
Women are the fastest growing group of veterans, according to the VA, with more than 2.1 million women veterans in the U.S. By 2040, they are projected to make up 18% of all veterans, the department said.

title: UNC online program serving adult learners grows 54%
description: Project Kitty Hawk is serving 2,889 adult learners in online degree programs this fall, a 54% increase from last fall, according to the UNC system.   The General Assembly created the program in 2021 to help more working adults earn college degrees and credentials. It launched its first degree offerings in October 2023.  The system […]
text:
Soon-to-be graduates pose for a photo at the University of North Carolina on May 1, 2024, in Chapel Hill, N.C. The University of North Carolina is one of six Southern public university systems that formed a new accreditation agency this summer, a move that shook the national evaluation model that higher education has relied on for decades. (Photo by Sean Rayford/Getty Images)Project Kitty Hawk is serving 2,889 adult learners in online degree programs this fall, a 54% increase from last fall, according to the UNC system.  
The General Assembly created the program in 2021 to help more working adults earn college degrees and credentials. It launched its first degree offerings in October 2023. 
The system said 766 new students enrolled this fall. Since its launch, 4,385 students have started work toward a degree from the program.. There are now 25 degree programs offered across six universities. 
Winston-Salem State University and UNC Wilmington joined the program this fall. WSSU launched three programs, while UNC Wilmington launched two. 
North Carolina Central University, East Carolina University and Appalachian State University, the program’s original partners, each had more than 850 Project Kitty Hawk students this fall. ECU became the first partner to exceed 1,000 students, according to the system. 
UNC Board of Governors warned about financial sustainability of university athletics 

Project Kitty Hawk was initially funded with $97 million in federal COVID relief funds appropriated by the General Assembly. The program had spent $91.2 million as of January 2026, according to a March report to the General Assembly. As of January, fewer than 100 students had completed an online degree, but that number now stands at 249 students, according to UNC. 
The report said university partners had generated $24.8 million in tuition receipts as of January, and projected that figure would reach $35.2 million by the end of the 2025-26 fiscal year. 
The system said 75% of Project Kitty Hawk students work full time and more than 80% are North Carolina residents. The average student is 32 years old. 
The system also reported a 90% term-to-term retention rate among Project Kitty Hawk students.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Ag commissioner challenger highlights data centers; incumbent calls move ‘grandstanding’
description: Vern Thompson is challenging Doug Goehring for North Dakota agriculture commissioner, but has been most vocal about controversial data center plans in the state.  Thompson, a Democrat, said he is running in part because the ag commissioner is one of three members of North Dakota’s Industrial Commission, which has committed to supporting a natural gas […]
text:
Vern Thompson, left, a Democratic-NPL candidate for agriculture commissioner, and Republican Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, speak during legislative committee hearings. (Photos by Michael Achterling and Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)Vern Thompson is challenging Doug Goehring for North Dakota agriculture commissioner, but has been most vocal about controversial data center plans in the state. 
Thompson, a Democrat, said he is running in part because the ag commissioner is one of three members of North Dakota’s Industrial Commission, which has committed to supporting a natural gas pipeline that Thompson said will ultimately benefit data centers. 
But many residents are apprehensive about those data centers, Thompson says. 
Thompson has led a series of meetings on data centers, with attendees concerned about health effects, using up prime farmland and the state being overwhelmed by demand for electricity and water.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Goehring, a Republican, called the data center discussions “political grandstanding.”
“He’s running for the wrong office,” Goehring said. He said Thompson should be running for the Legislature, which is considering regulations on artificial intelligence and listening to data center concerns. 
Thompson has previously served in the Legislature and originally announced a run for North Dakota’s only U.S. House seat. After Trygve Hammer earned the Democratic-NPL endorsement for the congressional office, Thompson turned to challenging Goehring. 
Thompson points to the state’s financial guarantee of up to $500 million for the WBI Energy natural gas pipeline and loans to Minnkota Power and Reliant Carbon Capture and Storage for Project Tundra as bad public policy. 
“People are tired of the corporate welfare,” Thompson said. 
Goehring said the money to support a pipeline to bring natural gas to eastern North Dakota was appropriated by the Legislature. He said the Industrial Commission’s job was to evaluate the proposed projects to ensure viability. 
He said the state’s backing should help get the project moving and attract other customers, with little chance that the state money will be needed. 
The WBI Bakken East Pipeline needs approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The project’s customers have not been made public. State officials have said customers could potentially include utilities, industrial users and others such as data center developers.  
Energy company eyes adding data center west of Fargo

Goehring, who farms and ranches with his family near Menoken, has been ag commissioner since 2009, when North Dakota was on the verge of a major oil boom. He points to positives from the Industrial Commission, such as reducing the footprint of oil development by encouraging grouping oil wells together. He also points to a pipeline reclamation program and projects and loans to improve water supply and housing in the state.
The Industrial Commission oversees the Bank of North Dakota, which has implemented a loan program to help ranchers rebuild their cattle herds, help farmers repair or replace storm-damaged storage facilities and loans to help ag producers through difficult financial times. 
As an energy-rich state, Goehring said it is important to encourage pipeline and transmission line development, which the Industrial Commission has done. 
He also has worked to develop export markets for North Dakota ag commodities. 
“We’re a state that exports commodities because we have an abundance, but we also have an abundance of energy. So taking and developing those resources is a big deal,” Goehring said.
Thompson said North Dakota residents are feeling run over by those projects. 
He pointed to rural roads rutted by construction traffic, property owners being threatened with eminent domain and industrial development changing the rural landscape. 
Thompson runs a trucking company in Fargo but has a farm background in Benson County.
Thompson said one priority for him is to address food affordability by pushing for a meat processing cooperative in the state. 
He said consumers are paying for the high transportation costs of North Dakota beef going to out-of-state processing and then having the processed meat come back into the state. 
He said limited competition among the “big four” meat packers keeps meat prices high. 
“Farmers and ranchers aren’t the problem when it comes to the high cost of food,” Thompson said. “When it comes to the high cost of beef in the grocery store, it’s the meat packers.”
Goehring said he doesn’t have a list of priorities for the next four years, if reelected, but said he would continue to support ag research and opening up trade opportunities. 
But he said he mostly takes direction from the Legislature, executing their directives. 
North Dakota livestock relief program funds 470 projects as most of state remains in drought

“My vision and plan is: How can we continue to be responsive and accountable? How can we make sure that we’re doing a good job in providing regulatory oversight?” Goehring said.
He said he hears from people that get frustrated by rules on a variety of topics that his agency doesn’t set, from federal food aid eligibility requirements, to diesel fuel regulations and meat inspection and sales. 
“A lot of times we’re just fielding questions about that, trying to help people understand,” he said of the Ag Department.
He said the agency is limited in what it can do by state statute. 
“You just don’t venture out into things that you don’t have the authority to do,” Goehring said.

title: Michigan Data Centers: The Weekly Download
description: Brighton Township joins other Livingston County communities in instituting a moratorium on data center development as the planning commission drafts an ordinance around the facilities, Livingston Daily’s Tess Ware reports. Port Huron Township has also hit the pause on data center development, according to Andy Jeffrey of the Port Huron Times Herald. The mora[...]
text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments

Brighton Township joins other Livingston County communities in instituting a moratorium on data center development as the planning commission drafts an ordinance around the facilities, Livingston Daily’s Tess Ware reports.
Port Huron Township has also hit the pause on data center development, according to Andy Jeffrey of the Port Huron Times Herald. The moratorium will remain in effect for 12 months, with an option for the township board to extend the pause if it needs more time to develop regulations around data centers and other high resource-demand facilities.
Members of Dearborn City Council have also given final approval to a six-month data center moratorium, MLive’s Fuad Shalhout reports.
City officials in Charlevoix will meet to discuss data center regulations on Oct. 12, Kaitlyn Devitt reports for Up North Live News. Jonathan Scheele, Charlevoix’s director of planning and zoning, told Up North Live the city is looking to set up early regulations, as it would be much harder to put limits in place after a developer comes to town.
The City of Sterling Heights is inviting residents to a data center open house at 6:30 p.m. on Monday, Sept. 28 at Velocity, featuring a brief presentation on the city’s moratorium, followed by a panel discussion.

Updates

Residents of Dowagiac living near the Hyperscale Data Inc. data center are receiving a brief reprieve from the facility’s noisy operations, as the company retools the data center for artificial intelligence computing, Chad Livengood of The Detroit News reports.
The State Boundary Commission has scheduled a review for a request to annex land in Vevay Township into the city of Mason for Oct. 7.  WKAR’s Andrew Roth explains that the annexation could lay the groundwork for a potential data center development, as it would enable the facility to connect to Mason City utilities.

Legislative Action

Members of the Sierra Club’s Michigan Chapter, alongside Clean Water Action, Michigan Climate Action Network, Michigan Environmental Justice Coalition and Voters Not Politicians continue to pressure lawmakers to take action on proposals to regulate data centers and institute a statewide moratorium on their development.

News of Note

A newly released survey from the University of Michigan Center for Local, State and Urban policy found that 46% of local government officials disagree that the benefits of data centers are worth the cost, compared to 18% who say the positives outweigh the negatives. Additionally, 55% of local leaders say their residents would strongly oppose a data center development near their community.
Another survey from the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research of Michigan State University found 70% of respondents within the state opposed the construction of data centers in their community, with 83% saying local governments should have a say in permitting data centers.
Lori Jane Gliha and Brittany Freeman of Scripps News detail threats faced by local officials in communities in Michigan and in other states prompted by opposition to data center development.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Republicans may have a Tommy Tuberville problem
description: So, Republicans: what’s the plan for Tommy Tuberville? The question may puzzle you. To use the GOP standard-bearer’s preferred metaphor, your team has what seems to be a 35-point lead with time winding down. Your quarterback can hand the ball off and manage the clock until time expires. But that guy under center is throwing […]
text:
U.S. Sen. and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaks at the Alabama Republican Party's Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. Tuberville last week delivered a speech on the U.S. Senate floor calling for the arrests of physicians who provide gender-affirming care and the involuntary committment of transgender individuals. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)So, Republicans: what’s the plan for Tommy Tuberville?
The question may puzzle you. To use the GOP standard-bearer’s preferred metaphor, your team has what seems to be a 35-point lead with time winding down. Your quarterback can hand the ball off and manage the clock until time expires.
But that guy under center is throwing deep and getting picked off. And he’s keeping the opponents in the game.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Let’s go back to last Tuesday. Tuberville spoke with CNN, who asked him whether high gas prices — $4.09 a gallon in Alabama as of Saturday, up from $2.79 last year — hurt his constituents.
There was a simple answer to this question: Yes. Tuberville opted for a convoluted one. He said that gas prices “go up and down” and agreed with a statement that Alabamians were willing to pay higher prices at the pump because of the state’s prior support for Donald Trump.
Tuberville also took the floor on Tuesday to deliver a nearly 20-minute speech attacking transgender Americans. There was the usual nonsense of pretending that doctors providing gender-affirming care, an intensely vetted process, actually hand out hormones and surgeries like juice cups at a day care center. There were much graver threats to violate the civil rights of transgender Americans and physicians who serve them.
And then, standing next to an emoji of a pregnant man, Alabama’s senior U.S. senator delivered a discourse on furries.
“Many airline pilots, flight attendants and air traffic controllers are part of the furry community,” he said. “Lord help us. It’s terrifying when you think about this. When you walk onto a commercial flight, it’s possible the pilot flying your plane could have a deranged fetish of dressing up like an animal.”
So: Empty your wallet for Trump, and our planes are full of furries. Tuberville 2026.
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones’ campaign almost instantly turned his gas price comments into a clip. Jones said little about the furry speech because he doesn’t need to. Social media is doing that.
This came after Tuberville’s weeks-long fumbling on the data center issue and his no-one-asked-for-it declaration that Social Security is a “scam.” It quickly crowded out focus on a new Tuberville ad outlining his education priorities.
“No problem,” the GOP says. “Tuberville has the money. We’ll just bury the Democrats in ads bought during college football.”
But Tuberville’s repeated stumbling could neutralize that advantage. An ad with a risky embrace of the divisive CHOOSE Act, the state’s effective voucher program, now competes with furry memes and videos mocking your candidate. At a minimum, Tuberville has made it harder to reach persuadable voters. It won’t help Republicans in tight races in the Huntsville area.
Maybe it won’t matter. Straight-ticket voting has saved many a Republican in the past, even if Tuberville seems to be running an experiment to see how far a conservative Alabamian can go without losing its protection.
But then, what’s the plan with a Gov. Tuberville?
Tuberville has ideas. At one point, he floated the abolition of the state income tax. Tuberville also says he wants to expand the CHOOSE Act. This despite the real possibility that the state’s education budget could be squeezed next year. 
In Alabama’s government, the Legislature has the power. Dumping the income tax would be a disaster for public education, but it’s a decision for the Legislature, not the governor. Legislators also have the final word on the budgets. The Legislature’s two education budget chairs have tried to play down the chance that CHOOSE Act spending could increase.
But do they think they can keep Tuberville on script? If not, their lives will become rather difficult. And if so, what in Tuberville’s campaign has persuaded them of that? The man who threatened transgender people on Tuesday was on Monday awkwardly trying to downplay his earlier, vile comments about Muslims.
The senator’s ledger includes other awful statements about Black Americans, immigrants, and people in cities. Nearly all were delivered to some right-wing outlet, the only constituency he seems to care for (besides Donald Trump). Conservative media always seek a new something to rile up its audience, whatever they feared yesterday. And those who chase conservative media approval, like Tuberville, seem more interested in provocation than constancy.
This may sit well with Republican leaders if a Gov. Tuberville attacks “liberals.” It will be a lot less fun if he makes flip remarks about abolishing income taxes or expanding the CHOOSE Act, empowering people on the right edge of the Republican legislative caucus who think all budgets should be blown up. If there’s anything constant about far-right diehards, it’s their belief that they’ve been betrayed or will soon be betrayed by GOP leadership. A Gov. Tuberville could give them reasons to think that.
So, Republican leaders: Are you ready for this?
If your gubernatorial nominee doesn’t throw away the lead this fall, you may struggle to keep him in line next year. And that could upset all your plans.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: FAFO: Flock around and find out
description: As we descend into the panopticon era of technofascism, one of the biggest proponents of this descent is the installation of the Flock cameras we’re seeing in our communities.
text:
A Flock camera is seen in a parking lot in Morgantown, West Virginia on Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)As we descend into the panopticon era of technofascism, one of the biggest proponents of this descent is the installation of the Flock cameras we’re seeing in our communities. 
I’ve been waiting for a report that shows us the data that is needed to decide whether these Flock cameras reduce crime and increase crime clearance rates; the true measure of their efficacy. Recently, such a report was released, where people used the FBI Crime Data Explorer tool for a closer look at the numbers. According to findings, despite nearly an eight-fold increase in the number of cameras in Atlanta, Flock didn’t significantly decrease crime or increase clearance rates as promised. 
According to the ATLPressCollective, Connect Atlanta’s website updated amounts of 28,626 integrated and 17,314 registered cameras as July this year. All these cameras and no significant reduction in crime or increase in clearance rates. Really makes one question about how these cameras were pitched to the individuals who signed off on it. Part of what frustrates me the most is that these cameras in a lot of cases were signed off by one individual, with little to no community input. This was learned from my public record requests to Fairmont and Marion County, West Virginia. Something that affects everyone should be voted on and decided on by everyone. Outsourcing local police to work for a private corporation such as this is a serious sign of incompetence, laziness, and naivety. 
To disarm a couple of counter points I hear; Flock is being sold as “having a police officer on every street,” however we never have had officers on every street, and there’s no need to. Also, to those parroting the, “you shouldn’t worry if you don’t have anything to hide” line, dismissing privacy rights because one has “nothing to hide” is equivalent to dismissing free speech because one has “nothing to say,” as former National Security Agency contractor and classified documents leaker Edward Snowden said.
Another angle I want to direct attention to, is what could have been instead? My record requests showed the city of Fairmont allotted over $30,000 for their purchase of five Flock cameras, and equipment; while Marion County has allotted $238,600 for its purchase of roughly 36 cameras and equipment. 
Given the report showing no significant decrease in crime in places using Flock; that nearly $260,000 could have been put to better use. There are data driven, tested and researched ways to reduce crime such as afterschool programs, trades programs, community centers, rehab centers, etc. Why did we not put any money towards these programs instead? They all are by far more effective at reducing crime than Flock cameras. 
Flock cameras are incredibly anti-community. By installing a “cop of every street” you are essentially removing the “community” out of community policing. Many residents are acquainted and friendly with the officers where they live due to the nature of small communities. Studies have shown that policing is more effective when the officer is from or reflects the community in which they serve. This separation of community from policing will only further weaken the relationships between the police and the communities they serve. 
What good do they really serve? Showing one instance where the cameras helped solve a crime or bring up an anecdote of a past crime that they would’ve been helping on does not justify their purchase or use. Given how many incredible amounts of documented and prosecuted cases of abuse by officers using Flock; it is near comical that a person could hold up one or two examples of usefulness, while a growing laundry list of over 200 abuses exist, and claim any sort of justification to keep them. Also worth mentioning is that Flock Safety is on the federal government’s National Institute of Standards and Technology National Vulnerabilities Database, due to the number of hacks they have been the target of. The Institute for Justice created a database to track and log the number of Flock abuses across the country.
What’s to be done? We organize, educate, and apply pressure. A new batch of public records requests I’ve sent will hopefully provide some answers to the questions mentioned above; however, in the meantime, it is important for people to find out who the decision makers are. Completing a public records request for the flock contracts is the first step to find the decision makers approving and signing Flock contracts. After finding out who signed the contracts, you will know who to direct your questions and concerns too. Technofascism is on the rise and spreading like a virus; I believe that Flock and similar entities’ usage of Automated License Plate Readers cameras are just the first step in trying to bring this dystopian future to fruition.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: KY film credits boost economy, officials and film experts say. Not everyone is convinced.
description: Kentucky towns are serving as the backdrop of holiday movies, thrillers and “Ethan Almighty,” an upcoming film about the dog who inspired the passage of a Kentucky law criminalizing abuse of dogs and cats.  The bump in film production in the commonwealth can be attributed to Kentucky lawmakers building up the state’s film incentives in […]
text:
Ethan Almighty, based on a true story in Kentucky, is a film currently in post-production. (Photo courtesy McClure Films)Kentucky towns are serving as the backdrop of holiday movies, thrillers and “Ethan Almighty,” an upcoming film about the dog who inspired the passage of a Kentucky law criminalizing abuse of dogs and cats. 
The bump in film production in the commonwealth can be attributed to Kentucky lawmakers building up the state’s film incentives in recent years. Yet, some criticize the program for providing state funds to private companies with little return on investment. 
Senate President Robert Stivers, R-Manchester, told the Kentucky Lantern in a recent interview the state has an opportunity to become a destination for movie and television filming. He pointed to places that have seen a boost in tourism because they were featured in a movie or TV show, like Scotland showcasing film locations shown in the “Outlander” series, which he heard about from parliament members while visiting the area. 
“You create tourism destinations and iconic points through movies, through TV series,” Stivers said.
Senate President Robert Stivers speaks with reporters over coffee at Goodwood in downtown Frankfort. March 26, 2025. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)
Not only that, boosting a new industry “would be great to diversify our economy,” Stivers said.  Some major productions have moved out of traditional film hubs like California as other states began offering lucrative tax credits. 
Kentucky has had iterations of tax credits within the last couple of decades, but has put more backing into the program and subsidies in recent years. In 2025, the General Assembly approved Senate Bill 1 to establish the Kentucky Film Office, overseen by the Kentucky Film Leadership Council, within the Cabinet for Economic Development. 
One southern state that has captured film productions is Georgia, which has no cap on the tax subsidies the state can offer. Kentucky’s annual cap is $75 million. 
“Can we be like Georgia? Yes, we can, but we’re really just kind of in our infancy, so we need to basically crawl, then walk, then run,” Stivers said. 
Andrew McNeill, the president and senior policy fellow at the Kentucky Forum for Rights, Economics & Education, isn’t so convinced. The film incentives, which differ from a traditional economic development incentive in that they give direct subsidies from the state to the companies, are for “temporary job creation that doesn’t leave nearly anything in state or in the communities as permanent fixed investment,” he said. He called it “a sugar fix” for small communities, and argued that those state dollars could go to “far more important and impactful investments,” like aging water systems and sewer connections. 
Ethan the dog splooting on the floor in a hallway of the Capitol Annex on March 25, 2026. His life is being turned into a feature film. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)
“Yes, I’d love to see a nice feel-good story come out from ‘Ethan Almighty.’ I’d love to see it be a hit,” McNeill said. “Is that going to turn into major capital investment in studio space and a recurring employment amongst a talented class of people involved in the industry? I don’t see that happening.”
‘Asset to a community’
Kentucky film incentives began under former Democratic Gov. Steve Beshear’s administration, but former Republican Gov. Matt Bevin called for axing the incentives. That made it extra newsy in September when Bevin was arrested on a warrant for contempt of court while working as an extra on a Christmas movie being filmed in Bourbon County. The movie was not listed as receiving film incentives this year. 
Bevin removing the incentive “decimated” growth of the film industry in Kentucky,” said Meg Fister, the executive director of the Kentucky Film Office. When it was brought back under Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear’s administration, “it has slowly increased, and I would say it has astronomically increased since having someone actually out there marketing this program,” she added. 
Fister was named as director earlier this year and focuses on bringing productions to Kentucky in her role. Stivers said not having “structure around the incentive program” was the biggest problem with film incentives in the past, and praised Fister’s work so far. She has more than 20 years of experience in television, film and nonprofit leadership and has had senior roles at Quinn’s House Productions at NBC, Universal and Warner Bros.
On the economic front, Fister said the Cabinet for Economic Development has tracked that more than 300 productions generated more than $800 million in spending in Kentucky since 2022. Film projects are “like an octopus,” she said, as they spread throughout the communities they are in as companies spend dollars. She also pointed to a global trend of fans of movies and shows visiting film locations. 
“They’re connecting to them emotionally, and they’re wanting to visit them,” Fister said. “And so that’s such an asset to a community, just to get that kind of spotlight on it and to really showcase it on the big screen.” 
One Kentucky town that has seen a few entertainment projects in recent years is Paducah. A Broadway show tour, a feature-length film and a television show in McCracken County are on this year’s list of approvals for tax incentives of about $2.2 million. 
Paducah’s historic downtown has been popular with filmmakers, advocates say. (Kentucky Tourism)
Alyssa Phares, the president and CEO of the Paducah Convention and Visitors Bureau, said Kentucky’s variety in landscapes is appealing to filmmakers in towns like Paducah. 
“You can get that sort of small community-city feel, but then also go just 40 minutes and be at Kentucky Lake and have these beautiful natural landscapes,” she said. 
Phares said a recent production that was in town for about four to six weeks brought some attention to the area and noted the production used local companies for things like catering, drivers and more. 
“Several of the actors and actresses posted pictures of the Paducah area and just kind of talked about how nice it was to get out of maybe L.A. or New York or wherever they lived and come to a place that had a different pace of life,” Phares said. 
‘Doesn’t pass the smell test’
In a review by the Lantern of this year’s approvals and business licenses available online, Kentucky Film Leadership Council members Misdee Wrigley Miller and Jeremy Winton had connections to projects approved for potential tax credits. Companies with a connection to Miller are set to get a potential of $6.5 million in tax incentives, while those with a connection with Winton are set to get $1.8 million. 
Meeting minutes show they recuse themselves from voting on those projects. The council has seven board members. 
But McNeill said the situation “doesn’t pass the smell test.” He argued that council members’ companies should not receive tax incentives as a “trade-off” for being on the council. 
Andrew McNeill of Kentucky FREE.
“Their whole vision is tainted by their participation on this commission,” McNeill said. “If they really cared about the integrity of building this industry in the state, they should resign.”
Miller, who owns Wrigley Media Group, said she does not personally receive any incentive funds. 
“My involvement has been to provide deficit financing — essentially advancing funds against the anticipated incentive — to help small productions that otherwise have difficulty securing financing get their projects made in Kentucky. Without that bridge financing, some of these productions would not have been able to move forward,” she said in an email, adding that she does not take a salary for this work. 
Asked about McNeill’s “trade-off” idea, Miller told the Lantern she brings experience to the board as someone in the industry and is committed to growing film production in Kentucky. 
“Hopefully there’s going to be a lot more me’s in the future, but when we first put this thing together, there weren’t too many me’s,” she added. 
Winton, an attorney and a producer, said in an email that he is “proud to be an active member of the film industry in Kentucky, especially as our firm focuses on production work throughout western Kentucky, helping to create jobs for Kentuckians and offering training and work experiences for those wishing to enter this exciting profession.” 
He added when a project is considered that he has any involvement or financial engagement in, “I fully recuse myself from any voting and making any comments and physically remove myself from the meeting while the project is being considered.”
Stivers said he’s discussed the appearance of conflicts of interest with Fister and board members, saying “they’ve got to be careful about that because that would be one thing that I believe would be detrimental and possibly terminate the program.” Stivers did argue, though, that he views the current board members as “some of the most knowledgeable about what should or should not be done because they’re in the industry.” 
“Do you put people on the Kentucky Racing Commission for horse races that raise cattle? No, you don’t,” Stivers said. “You put people who know the racing industry and are involved in the racing industry. You just got to put people in place with guardrails to make sure you protect against self dealing or conflicts of interest.”
As for the future of Kentucky’s film incentives, Fister and Stivers both said increasing the $75 million cap or removing it could aid in growing the state’s film industry. Kentucky is probably going to reach the current cap for the first time this year, Fister said. 
In addition to Georgia, some states like Illinois, Connecticut and Maine do not have a limit on their annual tax incentives. California’s is $750 million annually. 
“I think the caps are always concerning to especially large studios and major movie budgets, and they’re concerning to me running the film office because my goal is for this program to be effective for Kentucky and for constituents of Kentucky,” Fister said. “And so, if a major Marvel feature wanted to shoot in January and took almost all of the incentive, then I wouldn’t have people working all year long, and I don’t want to do that.” 
Stivers said if “a good return on investment” is shown from the tax incentives, “I think people would believe that we could expand the program.” 
“But we have again, we have to do the foundational things to make sure we can grow it with a good return on investment, because if we don’t, then what’s the purpose of having it?” he continued. 
Miller called Kentucky’s film incentives “one of the best subsidies in the country.” 
“I’ve spent a lot of time in California talking to studio heads, and they said, especially with all the consolidation in the industry right now, that the bottom line is driving all of their decisions right now,” she added. “So if there are great incentives to be had, that’s where they’re going to go.”
Expanding the tax incentive is “a terrible idea,” McNeill said, pointing out that recent film projects have not just gone to other states, but moved out of the country. Some of that is in part of other countries backing their own film subsidies. McNeill argued that doubling Kentucky’s cap to $150 million would “not going to build an industry that’s comparable to what you see in Georgia, what remains in California, what Texas could possibly do if they get seriously in the game.”  
“What it’s going to do is just direct more tax dollars to the Wrigley Medias of the state,” he said. 
However, if state lawmakers like Stivers want to invest, McNeill encourages them to debate the issue publicly. McNeil noted that 2025’s Senate Bill 1 was filed on the last day to introduce bills in the chamber. 
“If Sen. Stivers believes that this is something that can create an impactful, transformative industry for the state, then bring it in front of the public,” McNeil said. “Bring it in front of the interim legislative process. Bring it in front of public scrutiny, and let’s have that debate.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: 50 years later: How people and place continue to shape Appalachia’s future
description: My connection to Appalachia didn’t begin when I became a community development professional; it began generations ago. Like many Appalachians, my story is woven into the history of our mountains and the communities that call them home. I chose to spend my career serving Eastern Kentucky because I believe in the people and places that […]
text:
Pine Mountain State Resort Park in October 2023. (photo by Sarah Ladd)My connection to Appalachia didn’t begin when I became a community development professional; it began generations ago. Like many Appalachians, my story is woven into the history of our mountains and the communities that call them home. I chose to spend my career serving Eastern Kentucky because I believe in the people and places that shaped me.
As Mountain Association marks its 50th anniversary, I’m reminded of a truth that has endured through every economic shift and challenge our region has faced: Appalachia’s future has always been shaped by people willing to invest their time, talent, and resources in the places they call home. 
Fifty years ago, the leaders of eight community development organizations came together around a simple but powerful idea that the people of Appalachia were never the barrier to a resilient economic future. Too often, our people and communities lacked the voice, capital and resources, and opportunities needed to turn local ideas into local prosperity. 
That belief became five decades of impact. Since 1976, Mountain Association has been a partner, investor, and catalyst for economic growth throughout Central Appalachia. We’ve invested nearly $95 million across Eastern Kentucky since 2000, provided 66,190 hours of business expertise to 4,628 entrepreneurs since 2013, and facilitated more than 380 energy savings projects. This work has supported small businesses, communities, and nonprofits, and helped launch enterprises that continue to shape the region today.
These numbers reflect meaningful impact, but they tell only part of the story. Over the past five decades, we have watched entrepreneurs build businesses in towns many had written off. We have seen local leaders develop solutions to challenges ranging from food access and childcare to housing and workforce development. We have witnessed communities respond to economic change and natural disasters not by giving up, but by coming together. Those experiences reinforced the belief that resilience is not something communities discover in a crisis. It is something they build every day.
When coal employment declined, communities across Eastern Kentucky created new opportunities in manufacturing, agriculture, tourism, healthcare, arts and culture, and technology. More recently, devastating weather disasters have tested our communities once again. Neighbors help neighbors, local organizations step forward, and towns rebuild.
 
But resilience requires recovery and persistence. It means preparing for what’s next by strengthening local systems, investing in critical infrastructure, and building the capacity to navigate future challenges. This is why resilience has become central to Mountain Association’s work. Whether we’re helping businesses manage energy costs or supporting solar investments, financing equipment that creates affordable housing, revitalizing downtowns, or investing in people who turn ideas into action, our vision remains the same: helping people, places, and local economies prosper and thrive through change.
As I look across Appalachia today, I see reasons for optimism. Historic buildings are coming back to life, entrepreneurs are creating new opportunities, and community leaders are rallying neighbors around shared visions. These are more than signs of economic progress; they are the foundation of communities where people can build a life, feel welcome, and envision a future. Most importantly, I see people choosing to build their futures here. 
Appalachia has often been defined by what it lacks. Those of us who call it home know a different story. We are creative, determined, ingenious, and generous. We are innovators and problem-solvers, workers, and builders. Above all, we are neighbors, bound together by a deep commitment to one another and to this place. The challenges facing our region are real. But Mountain Association was founded on a belief that remains just as powerful today as it was in 1976: local people, equipped with the right resources and opportunities, can build stronger communities and a more prosperous future. 
If the last 50 years have taught us anything, it’s that investments in people and place matter most. When we trust local leadership, support local ownership, and strengthen communities, we create conditions for lasting prosperity. By investing in our people and strengthening our communities, we are writing the next chapter of the story of Eastern Kentucky together. Appalachia’s greatest asset has never been what can be taken from the region; it is what can be built here. The same mountains that shaped my story generations ago now challenge us to leave something of lasting value for future generations. And I believe our best chapter is still ahead.
To learn more about the Mountain Association, visit MtAssociation.org/Fifty.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Luria and Kiggans rematch in Va.’s 2nd Congressional District among most-watched races in nation
description: Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District has emerged as one of the most competitive in the country ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election, with incumbent U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, working to hold her seat against Democrat and former representative Elaine Luria, whom Kiggans ousted in 2022.  Two independent candidates, Matt Baker and Bishop Staten,[...]
text:
From left to right: U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, Democrat Elaine Luria, and independents Bishop Staten and Matt Baker. (Photos courtesy campaigns)Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District has emerged as one of the most competitive in the country ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election, with incumbent U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach, working to hold her seat against Democrat and former representative Elaine Luria, whom Kiggans ousted in 2022. 
Two independent candidates, Matt Baker and Bishop Staten, are also on the ballot to lead the district, which U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson said  “will determine the fate of the country,” as Republicans vie to maintain their slim majority in Congress. 
The Virginia Beach-anchored district oscillates between partisan control and contains the state’s largest concentration of military personnel.
The 2nd District backed Democrat Abigail Spanberger by 53% in the governor’s race last year, which could signal a shift in the sentiments of voters who first elected Republican Kiggans to represent them four years ago.
The district spans the Eastern Shore, Virginia Beach and reaches through Suffolk, Isle of Wight County, Franklin and parts of Chesapeake. Over 593,000 registered voters live there.
 In seeking reelection, Kiggans defends healthcare record, Iran war support 

Kiggans, a former Navy pilot who then became a nurse practitioner, is vying for her third term in the House. She also previously served as a state senator in Virginia’s General Assembly. 
Her 2022 bid for Congress came a year after Republican Glenn Youngkin won the Virginia governorship on a “Parents Matter” platform. While still in the state senate, she carried unsuccessful bills to ban “inherently divisive concepts” and a bill to bar transgender girls from joining girls’ sports teams.
In 2024, she was reelected as President Donald Trump reclaimed the White House. 
In the past year, Kiggans and other republicans have also had to defend their healthcare votes in what may be a litmus test for this year’s elections. 
H.R. 1, a Trump-backed federal spending bill passed last summer, puts 300,000 Virginians at risk of losing Medicaid next year, with 5,800 lawful immigrants set to lose it next month. 
Expiring Affordable Care Act subsidies have also spurred nearly 100,000 Virginians to drop that form of insurance. 
Ahead of the passage of H.R. 1, Kiggans joined an open letter opposing aspects of it but ultimately voted to support it. She also signed a letter backing ACA credits extension, before voting to let them expire. 
Kiggans answered questions by email earlier in the summer but did not follow through on an interview request by the time of publication. 
She previously wrote that her H.R. 1 vote helped protect Medicaid “for those who truly need” it and framed her ACA subsidies vote as an action against “waste, fraud and abuse.” 
The Virginia’s Attorney General office has prosecuted seven Medicaid fraud cases and settled two civil cases over the past year, resulting in millions in restitution paid to the state, the Virginia Medicaid Fraud Control Unit’s 2025-2026 annual report stated. 
Vice President J.D. Vance announced on Sep. 22 that at least 750,000 people nationwide have been kicked off ACA due to fraud. It’s unclear how many Virginians are included in that total. 
Kiggans has also strongly supported the war in Iran, which President Donald Trump launched without congressional approval in February.  
Amid rising gas and grocery prices in the eighth month of the conflict, Kiggans acknowledged the war’s factor in higher prices at the pump and told the John Fredericks Show this summer that gas prices “need to come down before the midterms.”
Luria, Baker and Staten counter that Congress needs to do more to address rising costs and balance the president’s power.
Alongside Kiggans, US House Speaker says Va.’s 2nd District ‘will determine the fate of the country’

Despite siding with her party on contentious votes more recently, Kiggans was once ranked 19th in Georgetown University’s  Lugar Center’s 2023 Bipartisan Index. 
Kiggans this year co-sponsored the latest legislative attempt to curb congressional stock trading. 
The incumbent’s campaign released an ad this month that accused Luria of leaving Congress $21 million richer than she entered due to stock trading.
The allegation is not supported by publicly disclosed trading records, though Luria was not always on board with efforts to ban congressional stock trading. 
The most recent Federal Election Commission filings indicate Kiggans has nearly $3.4 million in cash on hand for her campaign. 
 Luria plans a comeback, touts affordability agenda

Luria, a retired Navy commander, was first elected to Congress in 2018’s “blue wave,” where Democrats nationwide regained control of the House during the midpoint of Trump’s first presidency. 
Like Kiggans, Luria went on to defend her seat for a second term before losing it. 
While in Congress, Luria helped pass the PACT Act, which expanded healthcare and benefits to veterans exposed to toxic chemicals in their line of duty. She also supported Chesapeake Bay environmental protections.
Primary focus points for Luria — and many Democrats’ campaigns this year — are addressing healthcare affordability and access issues and finding ways to curb inflation, she outlined in an interview. 
Aside from restoring the expired ACA subsidies, Luria said that Congress should also “allow Medicare to negotiate costs for more prescription drugs, and invest in medical training, technology, and facilities so that no family has to choose between putting a roof over their head and paying for the care that they need.”
Both Kiggans and Luria have been supportive of Virginia’s offshore wind project — which Trump  has repeatedly tried to thwart and which proponents believe can help drive down energy costs and help the state lower its carbon footprint. 
Though Congress passed a bipartisan housing bill this year aimed at addressing supply and affordability challenges, Luria said that Trump’s tariffs “have led the cost of construction to skyrocket.” 
Luria’s most recent ranking in the bipartisan index before leaving Congress was 28th. She said she was proud to have found “areas of compromise” with her colleagues and would bring that perspective back if elected. 
Dark money in politics — when political action committees or special nonprofit entities exploit loopholes to donate undisclosed amounts to candidates or causes — has had too much sway for too long, Luria said. 
She co-sponsored legislation to curb dark money donations while in Congress and plans to champion the effort again. 
“I do not believe the Republican Party or the Democratic Party are doing nearly enough to clamp down on this culture that rewards those who are well-off and well-connected while leaving working people behind,” she said. 
As of late-September, Luria’s campaign had $3.5 million in cash on hand. 
 Independents Matt Baker and Bishop Stanton give voters another option 

Retired U.S. Marine Corps Col. Matt Baker, one of two independents in the race, aligns with Luria on supporting campaign finance reform. 
His political persuasion would also enable him to act as a “conduit” between Republicans and Democrats, he said. 
As Congress has failed to pass its annual budgets on time and had a downward trend in productivity in recent years, Baker hopes to help ease the gridlock. 
He would also advocate for the U.S. to conclude its war in Iran. 
“We’ve got to figure out a way to extricate ourselves,” he said. “That’s the nature of war, you don’t want to stay in one.” 
He also said that “the federal government has been ignoring the problem” of regulating data centers and artificial intelligence, leaving too much of the burden on states and localities. 
Like Baker, independent candidate Geral “Bishop” Staten said he would help facilitate productive conversations across the aisle. Though not running under a party umbrella, he said that his political alignment skews Democratic Socialist. 
A history of pro-Trump social media posts during the president’s first term, reported by Virginia Scope, has called his stances into question. 
Luria’s campaign filed a suit alleging Staten lacked the signatures to qualify for the ballot but said they dropped it earlier this month. 
In an interview with The Mercury, Staten explained that he doesn’t currently support Trump and that he has typically voted for Democrats. He said that he voted in the 2024 GOP primary for Nikki Haley in an attempt to keep Trump from advancing. 
“This (Make America Great Again) administration got into office and they’ve done everything outside of what we want as people,” he said. 
If he were to join Congress, Staten said he would vote “a hard yes” on extending the ACA subsidies. 
He would also support legislation mandating stronger pricing and billing transparency from healthcare providers and would advocate for more transportation funding.
Staten, Baker and Luria told The Mercury that they are critical of Trump’s immigration policies and would support streamlining citizenship processes for certain immigrants, like non-violent people whose only crime was entering illegally, or children of immigrants. 
Kiggans voted to increase immigration enforcement funding and has visited the U.S.-Mexico border wall that was a key goal of Trump’s first term. 
With early voting under way, Election Day is Nov. 3. Read The Mercury’s voter guide to learn more about Virginia’s congressional districts, candidates and the stakes of the races.

title: Youth advocates warn higher marijuana fine could deepen racial disparities
description: Youth advocates are urging Virginia lawmakers to reconsider stiffer penalties for public marijuana use before the state opens its legal adult-use market next summer, warning that the changes could place a disproportionate burden on young people, their families and Black communities. The maximum civil penalty for consuming or offering marijuana in public is s[...]
text:
Virginia lawmakers are weighing how increased penalties for public marijuana consumption could affect young people as the state prepares to launch legal retail sales in July 2027. (Photo Illustration by Mario Tama/Getty Images)Youth advocates are urging Virginia lawmakers to reconsider stiffer penalties for public marijuana use before the state opens its legal adult-use market next summer, warning that the changes could place a disproportionate burden on young people, their families and Black communities.
The maximum civil penalty for consuming or offering marijuana in public is set to rise from $25 to $250 on July 1, 2027, the same day retail sales are scheduled to begin. A second offense also carries a $250 fine and requires substance-use education or treatment, or both, if available, while a third or subsequent offense is a Class 4 misdemeanor. 
Valerie Slater, executive director of RISE for Youth, told the Joint Commission to Oversee the Transition of the Commonwealth into a Cannabis Retail Market earlier last week that the higher fine would take effect as marijuana enforcement involving young people increasingly begins in schools. 
“What’s really troubling is how increasingly the enforcement has moved into the schoolhouse while we are also looking at an increased impact on Black adults,” Slater said. 
Her presentation was one part of a broader commission meeting that also examined marijuana offense trends and plans for enforcing the new market. 
The Virginia Cannabis Control Authority is expected to lead that work, with temporary assistance from the Virginia Alcohol Beverage Control Authority while the cannabis agency builds its enforcement staff. 
 Complaints shift towards schools

Marijuana-related juvenile intake complaints fell 30% between fiscal 2019 and fiscal 2024, from about 2,700 to 1,904, according to Virginia Department of Juvenile Justice data cited by RISE for Youth. But the share originating in schools rose from 17% to 54%, while the share involving 16- and 17-year-olds fell from 68% to 48%, indicating a shift toward younger adolescents. 
Girls also grew from 25% to 30% of the youth involved in marijuana-related complaints, although the decline in total complaints means the figures do not necessarily show an increase in the number of girls referred. 
“We did not stop enforcing, just where we went with it changed,” Slater said. “We stopped looking at the community, and we started looking at schools.”
Current Virginia law separately imposes a civil penalty of up to $25 and mandatory education or treatment for underage marijuana possession or consumption. Possessing or consuming marijuana on public school grounds during school hours or activities can be charged as a Class 2 misdemeanor. 
Slater warned that a young person could face several consequences from the same incident, including school discipline, juvenile intake, the underage penalty and the higher public-consumption fine. Whether those provisions could overlap would depend on the circumstances and how authorities decide to charge the case. 
“It’s not going to be that middle schooler who’s going to be paying for it,” Slater said. “It’s going to be their family. That’s who’s going to shoulder that burden.”
Slater also noted Black Virginians make up about 19% of the state’s population but accounted for 47.7% of public-use citations in data analyzed by RISE for Youth.
“If Black Virginians only make up 19%, how is it that they are 47.7% of those who are receiving the citations?” she said. “If indeed 47.7% of all of the public-consumption citations are against Black Americans, then we move now to $250 as the amount that is being assessed against Virginians, I can promise you, that’s a whole lot of money.”
RISE for Youth’s written report also pointed to disparities throughout Virginia’s juvenile justice system. In fiscal 2025, Black Youth represented 44.2% of intake cases, 53.4% of detainments and 70.9% of direct-care placements, according to DJJ data cited in the report.
The figures measure different groups at separate stages of the system and do not establish that marijuana enforcement caused the disparities. Slater argued, however, that they show the risks of increasing penalties within a system where Black youths already experience disproportionate outcomes. 
Del. Cia Price, D-Newport News, said the presentation placed firm numbers alongside experiences long described by affected communities. 
“It does not come as any surprise based on what was happening to the adults, but it is sickening and disheartening to see that it is following our youth,” Price said. 
 Advocates seek changes before the market opens

Slater asked lawmakers to leave the public-consumption fine at $25. If the increase remains, she said, minors should be explicitly exempted. 
RISE for Youth also wants lawmakers to eliminate criminal penalties and delinquency treatment for youth marijuana possession and consumption, adopt a cannabis education curriculum developed by Stanford Medicine and dedicate 30% of retail marijauna tax revenue to youth education, treatment and other services administered by the Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Services. 
“Why are children using, not how can we get money out of our families?” Slater said. “Why are children using, and what should we be doing to ensure that they are not using?”
Del. Paul Krizek, D-Fairfax, who sponsored the cannabis retail legislation in the House, said lawmakers should focus on changing behavior rather than increasing a penalty that has not been shown to work.
“Having data that shows $25 doesn’t work, $250 is just going to double down on something that’s not working,” Krizek said. 
He also raised concerns that unpaid fines could be sent to collection agencies, potentially damaging young people’s credit before they turn 18 or leaving their families responsible for the debt. 
“It’s a bad cycle, and we all know it is, and so we need to figure out what we can do that will change that,” Krizek said. He added that revenue from legal sales could support educational programs for young people. 
Separate data presented by the Virginia Criminal Sentencing Commission showed that marijuana possession charges under the state’s former criminal statute have nearly disappeared, falling from 31,837 in fiscal 2018 to three in fiscal 2026. 
The commission’s principal measure of marijuana distribution charges also declined from 5,439 in fiscal 2019 to 1,342 in fiscal 2026. The figures do not include Fairfax Circuit Court or juvenile court data.
