title: Virginia DMV wait times plummet to record lows after major reforms
description: Motor vehicle office wait times in the commonwealth fell to 8.3 minutes in 2026 from about 37 minutes in 2019, according to the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles, making access to essential government services faster and more convenient for drivers. Virginia lawmakers previously directed analysts from the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, th[...]
text:
The customer service center at the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles Headquarters in Richmond. (Photo courtesy of the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles)Motor vehicle office wait times in the commonwealth fell to 8.3 minutes in 2026 from about 37 minutes in 2019, according to the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles, making access to essential government services faster and more convenient for drivers.
Virginia lawmakers previously directed analysts from the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, the state’s monitor for government agencies, to assess DMV performance. Analysts found that the DMV’s average wait time at its high-volume offices was around 34 minutes in fiscal year 2014, compared with the DMV’s 20-minute target.
As a result, analysts recommended that the DMV develop a plan to reduce wait times at high-volume customer service centers and also reduce telephone and call center wait times. 
House Transportation Committee Chair Karrie Delaney, D-Fairfax, said the reduction is a positive development for the commonwealth, as it streamlines processes and benefits those who require DMV services.
“I think it’s pretty good—great news for everyone in the commonwealth,” said Delaney. “I know that, for many of us, when we have an administrative task that requires a trip to the DMV, it’s often met with a groan … but to know that the people of the commonwealth are going to be able to get in quickly, get out, and conduct their business—I think that’s something we hope to raise awareness of, since it’s such great news for everybody.”
The department has reduced wait times by nearly 80% since 2019, following the 2023 launch of the Perfect 10 initiative, which aimed to keep waits to 10 minutes or less.
“While we’ve seen great success with the implementation of ‘Perfect 10,’ customers with appointments experience even shorter wait times,” said Camila Knight, a DMV spokeswoman. 
Knight said the agency improved customer flow through redesigned lobby layouts, separate appointment and walk-in lines, employee guidance tools and center-specific solutions. Expanded appointment availability at 74 centers statewide also improves the experience, with Virginia drivers praising the improved flow online.
Jake Steinman posted online that his visit to a DMV office in Charlottesville was “impossibly fast” two months ago.
“I have waited half a day at DMVs even with an appointment scheduled,” he wrote. “Very lucky to live in a (place) that has an efficient DMV and friendly staff.”
As a result of the work and other customer service tweaks, Knight said the agency received the 2026 Best Strategic Business Transformation Program award at the Business Transformation World Summit. Knight said wait times have remained below 10 minutes since last year, with some variation across centers.
The winning entry, entitled “Transforming a 100-Year-Old Agency,” illustrated that the Virginia DMV’s changes resulted in $15 million in savings, a cut in customer wait times, an 8% reduction in employee turnover from fiscal year 2024 to 2025, strong customer satisfaction ratings statewide, and a record low wait time of 5.9 minutes in October 2025.
Knight says the department continues to reduce wait times. To help, visitors should make appointments on the agency’s website by searching “appointments.”

title: When Virginia’s congressional candidates don’t debate, voters get sound bites instead of substance
description: The day after the Aug. 4 Democratic primary to choose a congressional candidate in Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, the Williamsburg area chapter of the Virginia League of Women Voters invited Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman and Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor to a joint appearance at a candidate forum. Taylor’s campaign declined, said[...]
text:
Basic civic literacy, which debates and candidate forums promote, is not even an afterthought for many political candidates in Virginia and other states, columnist Jim Spencer writes. It is given no thought at all.  (Getty illustration by John Schreiner)
The day after the Aug. 4 Democratic primary to choose a congressional candidate in Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, the Williamsburg area chapter of the Virginia League of Women Voters invited Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman and Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor to a joint appearance at a candidate forum.
Taylor’s campaign declined, said Denise Koch, co-chair of the local league’s voter services committee. Wittman’s campaign acknowledged getting the invitation, Koch added, but never provided an answer.
With US House control hanging in the balance, Wittman faces Taylor in contentious VA-01 race

You might think, as I did, that face-to-face appearances would be mandatory to win voters’ support in a campaign deemed critical to control of the U.S. House of Representatives at a pivotal moment in American history.
If so, like me, you would be wrong.
The League of Women Voters wasn’t the only Virginia organization to be turned down. The Chamber of Commerce for the Richmond metro area, ChamberRVA, is not doing a candidates debate or forum because it was “unable to get any traction with the candidates,” said vice president for government affairs Demas Boudreaux. 
I asked the Taylor and Wittman campaigns whether their respective candidates would be willing to debate face-to-face. I asked the same thing of the campaigns of incumbent 2nd Congressional District U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, a Republican, and Democrat Elaine Luria in another Virginia race of national importance. 
No one bothered to answer me.
Incumbents usually have more to lose than to gain in appearing face-to-face in debates, William & Mary professor and political expert John McGlenon told me.
In this election, Wittman and Kiggans risk much more than usual because they have aligned themselves with President Donald Trump, whose approval ratings are in the toilet. 
In a recent telephone rally the president endorsed Wittman and Kiggans as “spectacular warriors.”  No questions were taken from listeners and the program appeared tightly scripted.
In a public forum, Wittman and Kiggans could be asked about the unpopular war with Iran, which sucks up $3 billion taxpayer dollars a month and has led to $4-a-gallon gasoline and $6-a-gallon diesel fuel.
They could be asked about tariffs imposed by Trump that have been passed along to American consumers and inflation that has raised grocery prices and made home mortgages and car loans more expensive.
They could be asked to explain the federal budget cuts that cost 6,300 federal civilian jobs in Hampton Roads in 2025, where Kiggans’ district is anchored.
Taylor and Luria face nothing as serious. But to beat incumbents in districts gerrymandered to favor Republicans, challengers must control their narratives. With both races being neck-and-neck, it is easier to do so without hostile questions in debates or forums. 
As a result, the 1st and 2nd Congressional District campaigns in this high-stakes election season have devolved into self-serving platitudes on candidate websites, curated social media posts and attack ads. 
With traditional journalism stretched thin by the decline of local news outlets and personnel, interviews have turned into platforms for candidate talking points that often go unchallenged. 
Basic civic literacy, much less the kind of education the League of Women Voters and Chamber of Commerce try to promote with candidate forums, is not even an afterthought. It is given no thought at all.
“It used to be that candidates expected to participate in multiple debates,” Larry Sabato, founder of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, told me.  “All that’s gone. All people have to judge on are TV ads and little sound bites from the media that’s left.”
This is not simply an indictment of power-hungry political parties and greedy politicians. It reflects Americans’ dangerous indifference to the representative democracy that has protected their ability to speak their mind and make a decent living. 
Politicians need a reason to self-regulate. An educated electorate can provide both the carrot and the stick. An uneducated electorate, one that can’t – or won’t – demand enough information to separate lies from truth, has no one but itself to blame for its exploitation. 
Even when the public demanded candidate debates, not many people watched them, Sabato said.
Meanwhile, Federal Election Commission records on the four candidates in the 1st and 2nd Districts show they have collectively spent millions of dollars to craft their narratives in ways meant not to educate or inform constituents, but to favor individual candidates.
Those candidates will spend millions more in the run-up to the Nov. 3 vote. Virtually none of that money will go to educate voters. Too little of it will be used to try to change minds. 
Donald Trump created an “us v. them” mentality among Americans in 2016 when he won the presidency. Americans started alienating each other more after the Jan. 6, 2021 attack at the Capitol by Trump supporters who tried to overturn Trump’s 2020 loss to Joe Biden, who won the presidential election that year. 
The estrangement deepened when Trump pardoned 1,500 of those traitors upon his return to office in 2025. Since then, Trump’s increasingly autocratic and megalomaniacal behavior and his disastrous policies have driven the wedge deeper. 
At this point, Sabato and McGlennon agreed, too few voters look at candidates’ policy ideas and philosophies, only at the letter behind their names.   
It is hard to make anyone change their mind about Trump, George Mason University political science professor Jeremy Mayer told me. Lines have been drawn. 
“The hate is so deep,” he said. “Why bother to have a debate?”
The congressional elections in Virginia’s 1st and 2nd Districts and others  across the country will be a referendum on Trump. And the winners will be determined by an enthusiasm gap.
“We are so polarized,” said Mayer, “the facts don’t matter.”      
Early voting is underway and Election Day is Nov. 3. Read The Mercury’s voter guide to learn more about the congressional candidates and stakes of the races. Take our reader survey to share the issues that will motivate you to vote this fall and inform our elections reporting.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island study links sustained arts education — especially music — to lower chronic absenteeism
description: The students in Danielle Trial Lucini’s concert band class were charging through the White Stripes’ “Seven Nation Army” during first period on a Thursday morning at Mount Pleasant High School in Providence. Lucini let them finish before offering her review: It was enthusiastic, but too fast. “I need to hear the space between the notes,” […]
text:
Music teacher Danielle Trial Lucini accompanies students on the trumpet during her first-period Concert Band class at Mount Pleasant High School in Providence on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The students in Danielle Trial Lucini’s concert band class were charging through the White Stripes’ “Seven Nation Army” during first period on a Thursday morning at Mount Pleasant High School in Providence.
Lucini let them finish before offering her review: It was enthusiastic, but too fast. 
“I need to hear the space between the notes,” Lucini told them.
For more than an hour, 14 students ran through riffs, motifs and abbreviated band and pop standards. Their teacher often took up an instrument herself to demonstrate or sometimes ceded conducting duties to one of her students. She also sang and played alongside them. 
Students often tell Lucini she’s their “strictest teacher.” But Lucini — who was awarded Providence Teacher of the Year in June — expects them to not only show up to class, but to participate. 
“You can come to band class and sit with your instrument in your lap,” she told Rhode Island Current in an interview. “That doesn’t help anybody.”
Continuous high school participation in arts classes — especially music — was associated with better school attendance in a new study conducted by Quadrant Research and commissioned by the Rhode Island State Council on the Arts. 
The Sept. 17 report’s primary question: “Do arts students have lower chronic absenteeism rates than non-arts students?”
To answer it, researchers looked at state education department data spanning 2018 through 2025. The arts council believes the report’s findings could have implications for how the state deals with chronic absenteeism, which is defined as missing at least 10% of the days in a school year during which students are enrolled. 
Reducing chronic absenteeism has been a signature priority of the Rhode Island Department of Education under Gov. Dan McKee. The governor has promoted the Attendance Matters RI campaign, which uses public dashboards, school-level data tools and family outreach to track and reduce absences. In August, McKee celebrated the fourth consecutive year of decline in chronic absenteeism rates, which are now down 14.4 percentage points from a pandemic-era peak.
After accounting for student demographics, year-to-year differences and school district, researchers estimated 25.4% of four-year music students were chronically absent, compared with 37.3% of students without four consecutive years of music. 
The gap was not nearly as large, however, when researchers looked at four-year participation across all arts classes — music, visual arts, theater, dance, and media arts — the chronic absenteeism gap between four-year arts students and those who lacked four consecutive years of art was only 1.9 percentage points. 
The study shows a correlation, Robert Morrison, a co-author of the report and founder of Quadrant Research, cautioned in an interview.
While data may show a relationship between art classes and better school attendance, it can’t actually prove that art classes are what made students show up, Morrison said. “‘Prove’ is pretty strong language,” he added.
Students who stick with arts classes for multiple, consecutive years may differ in ways the data can’t fully capture, Morrison said. The report notes that individual motivation, academic skill or family circumstances which encourage better attendance may keep students more engaged in the classroom. In the case of music, previous experience or lessons outside school can also help.
“What this study shined a light on through the data is something that many of our music and arts educators have known all along,” Morrison said.
Mount Pleasant High School music teacher Danielle Trial Lucini demonstrates on the drums beside senior Sidney Feliz during first-period Concert Band class in Providence on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Sustained engagement matters
Students who took at least one arts course in each of all four high school years had slightly lower chronic absenteeism rates than students who did not sustain arts participation for all four years, the report showed. The difference was much larger among students who took music all four years.
The same attendance-arts correlation was not observed in all students who took art classes. In fact, the data from 2023 through 2025 showed that high school students taking any arts course had chronic absenteeism rates a smidgen higher than students taking none.
“If you’re just taking it one year, if you’re just getting … an exposure course or like a general course that you’re taking to meet a graduation requirement, that’s not the same thing as sustained engagement,” Morrison said.
Lucini described a current junior who, when she taught him as a freshman taking band for an elective, missed 110 days of school and failed multiple classes. The next year, he asked to try band again, saying he hadn’t given it a fair shot.
In his second year with band, he was absent about 15 school days — still around the state’s definition of chronically absent — but he earned an A in band class. He continues to take band and even volunteered to perform with the band in the most recent PVDFest parade, Lucini said. 
“For some kids, it’s the thing that draws them in and gives them a reason,” Lucini said.
Nicole Simpson, Providence Public Schools’ director of fine arts, said it’s important that students have a choice in arts education. They get to make decisions and work toward their own desired final product.
Danielle Trial Lucini conducts her first-period Concert Band class at Mount Pleasant High School in Providence on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
“That level of choice and voice is not present in any other content area,” Simpson said. “Especially in urban education, where all of our teachers are given a curriculum that says, ‘You’re on this page this week, this day, doing this lesson, and here’s how you’re teaching it.’” 
For Lucini, it’s all about choice — and the punctuality, teamwork and structure band class requires only serves to reinforce students’ autonomy, rather than weaken it. She doesn’t force beginning band students to play an instrument they don’t like.
“I’m not sticking a trumpet in your hand,” Lucini said. “I want you to pick something that you like the sound of, that you’re drawn to.”
That individual choice ends up affecting the collective responsibility of the band, which Lucini called “the biggest group project you’ll ever have.” Whether practicing or performing for an audience, the players have to listen to themselves and to one another — something they can only do if everyone shows up. 
Performance, she said, illustrates well the adage that if you’re on time, you’re late, but if you’re early, you’re on time. A 5:30 p.m. gig means arriving at 5 to assemble instruments and warm up. 
“If one person is late, then everyone is late,” Lucini said.
One of Lucini’s senior band students is Sidney Feliz — a drummer and singer who has taken part in band and chorus during all four of her years at Mount Pleasant. She said Mount Pleasant’s music program drew her to the school, and it was her top choice for a high school. (Providence students get some choice in where they go to high school and can shortlist their preferred schools before being assigned.)
“Since I’ve been out the womb, I’ve been totally interested in music,” Feliz said. “I’ve been singing, playing stuff, but once I came here, I started taking drum super serious.”
Feliz credited Lucini with keeping her on beat when her motivation waned during sophomore and junior year. 
“She kind of led me back in,” Feliz said of her band teacher. “And I don’t think I would be doing what I do today without her.” 
For Feliz, the sense of direction was difficult to find elsewhere in her school day. 
“I’m able to push myself to work with other classes, but it’s mainly this class where she gives us the greatest push,” Feliz said of Lucini. “We really give it our all to perform.” 
The pushing works even when the students haven’t been playing a dedicated instrument for a long time. Xionangelys Lopez Davila is a sophomore in Lucini’s concert band class who played piano and flute in the past but who only started violin last year. 
“It’s very difficult, but at the end, you start to understand it and love it,” she said, adding that she always shows up to Lucini’s class. 
The report co-author Morrison — who took music classes himself as a teen, and worked in the music and instrument industries for years before becoming an arts education researcher — offered that the arts are worth more than what they might do for attendance. 
“The arts have legitimacy for their intrinsic value in their own right,” Morrison said. 
The attendance finding, he added, is a “bonus.”
Students prepare to rehearse during Danielle Trial Lucini’s first-period Concert Band class at Mount Pleasant High School in Providence on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)

title: Indiana expungement filings rose 52% over a decade. But getting relief still takes time, money
description: More than 10,000 expungement cases were filed in Indiana courts last year, continuing a decade-long rise in the number of people asking judges to restrict access to old arrests and convictions. Courts opened 10,156 expungement cases in 2025, up 52% from 6,660 in 2016, according to state court data obtained by the Indiana Capital Chronicle. […]
text:
Indiana courts opened 10,156 expungement cases in 2025, a 52% increase from 2016. An expungement can restrict public access to qualifying arrest or conviction records. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)More than 10,000 expungement cases were filed in Indiana courts last year, continuing a decade-long rise in the number of people asking judges to restrict access to old arrests and convictions.
Courts opened 10,156 expungement cases in 2025, up 52% from 6,660 in 2016, according to state court data obtained by the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
A pardon offers another path to relief, but few Hoosiers apply for one.
Carrie Hagan, who directs the Civil Practice Clinic at Indiana University’s McKinney School of Law, said some prospective clients must wait years before they can apply. Others learn that unpaid fines, fees or restitution stand in their way.
director of the Civil Practice Clinic at Indiana University’s McKinney School of Law (Photo courtesy Indiana University)
“People owe hundreds to thousands of dollars — and that’s one of the biggest hurdles for a lot of our clients seeking expungements,” Hagan said. “Time is a really close second. We have folks that hear, ‘Well, you’re not eligible until 2031,’ and then for them, it’s like, ‘Well, what’s the point?’”
The clinic has helped people seek expungements for nearly a decade, including through a partnership with Goodwill of Central and Southern Indiana. Hagan said clients often want a better job or housing, or the chance to volunteer at their children’s schools. Some simply want to put an old case behind them.
“This ability to move on and this ability to kind of free yourself from the shame of making a mistake or a couple, that’s huge for our clients,” she said. “The big thing is that they’re really able to get better jobs.”
In Lake County, attorney Amanda Hires said greater awareness may be one reason more people are filing. Hires, an attorney who works alongside County Clerk Michael Brown, has helped community groups with expungement fairs over the years. Clerk’s office employees are also proactively helping attendees obtain case information and documents.
For convictions, Indiana generally requires a five-year wait before seeking to expunge a misdemeanor. Eligible felonies can require eight or 10 years, depending on the offense and other conditions.
Bringing help directly into the community “can make the process less intimidating,” Hires said.
“I think people become more familiar with the government and not so nervous that way,” she continued. “And that really helps with this (expungement) process.”
A clearer look at outcomes
Data from the Indiana Office of Judicial Administration show that of 27,202 expungement cases disposed of statewide since Jan. 1, 2024, 25,408 were granted. Another 288 were denied, while courts did not record an outcome for 1,506, according to OJA. The cases took an average of 141 days from filing to disposition.
A filing represents an expungement case, not necessarily one person or one conviction. One case can involve multiple convictions, and a person with records in several counties may need to file a case in each county. The outcome figures also cover cases disposed of during the period, including some that may have been filed earlier.



Quotation







This ability to move on and this ability to kind of free yourself from the shame of making a mistake or a couple, that’s huge for our clients.


– Carrie Hagan, director of the Civil Practice Clinic at Indiana University’s McKinney School of Law


Whether a judge must grant an eligible request depends on the kind of record involved. Indiana law generally requires courts to grant expungement of qualifying arrests without convictions, misdemeanors and certain lower-level felonies when the legal conditions are met. Judges have discretion over more serious eligible felonies.
Filings reached a high of 11,309 in 2023, then fell to 10,077 in 2024. They rose by just 79 cases, or less than 1%, in 2025. From January through August of this year, courts recorded 6,336 new filings, down about 11% from the same eight months of 2025.
County figures from the courts’ preliminary annual reports show differences across Indiana.
Marion County had the largest numerical increase between 2016 and 2025, rising from 1,804 filings to 2,472. Lake County rose from 232 to 516, while Clark County went from 71 to 199. Monroe County fell from 565 to 303.
Hires said Lake County’s increase could reflect both outreach and the passage of time. People convicted years ago may now have reached the waiting period required to seek expungement. Her law office has partnered on events with Indiana Legal Services and local groups, while clerk’s office staff have volunteered outside regular hours to help residents find the records they need.
“I think anytime there’s a job fair, there’s really a lot of people talking about expungement,” Hires said.
In her practice, Hires said she most often sees people seeking to expunge alcohol-related driving offenses, thefts and drug convictions.
Marion County Clerk Kate Sweeney Bell said her office has promoted expungement through social media and partnerships with legal aid organizations. She believes more eligible residents are filing as they learn the process is available.
“It’s no guarantee, but it’s not something to fear,” Bell said. “It’s something that can profoundly alter an individual’s life.”
Bell said the additional cases have not created an administrative burden for her office. Dan Goldblatt, director of policy and communications for the Marion County Clerk’s Office, said expungements account for less than 5% of its criminal filings. He noted that people with midlevel felony convictions often don’t realize they could be eligible after the required waiting period.
“It’s not a burden at all,” Bell said of the increased expungement filings. “This is a good thing.”
 What an expungement does — and does not do
Hagan said the process can become complicated when someone has records in multiple counties or convictions that require a judge to weigh their circumstances. Her clinic prepares separate filings for each county and, in discretionary cases, asks clients to explain how their lives have changed and what an expungement would allow them to do.
She said driving offenses and minor drug cases are common among the people her clinic assists. For some, a suspended license makes it harder to work and pay obligations such as child support. Driving anyway can lead to another charge.
Amanda Hires, criminal defense attorney and partner at the Law Office of Weiss, Schmidgall and Hires, P.C., in Merrillville (Photo courtesy of Weiss, Schmidgall and Hires)
Even a successful expungement does not always remove a case from public view. Indiana generally seals qualifying arrests and lower-level convictions from public access, but records of some more serious felonies remain publicly available with an expungement notation.
Hagan said many clients still seek that relief because it matters to them personally, even when the record remains visible. But she questions whether marking a case “expunged” gives people the second chance they expect.
“If we’re going to expunge it, then let’s just expunge it,” she said. “Let’s then move on.”
Hires raised the same concern. In some higher-level felony cases, she said, an employer searching the public court docket can still see the conviction, even though it is marked expunged.
“It’s really a misnomer,” she said, for people hoping the record will no longer affect a job search.
A court order also does not ensure that every criminal history database has been updated.
Hires said a case may move quickly through the Lake County court and clerk’s office, but processing by outside agencies can take longer. In her experience, it could take as long as six months for the relief a person expects to show up in those records.
But even an expungement cannot erase everything someone might find online.
“Sure, you can expunge it legally through the courts,” Hires said, “But unfortunately, Google’s there forever.”
Hagan also said some courts require hearings in cases she believes meet the requirements for mandatory relief. Such hearings can mean taking time off work or traveling back to the county where the case was filed. She described one pending case in which a client who lives four hours from the court was ordered to appear in person, though the prosecutor had not objected.
A narrow change in state law
Lawmakers changed Indiana’s expungement law in 2025, but the amendments did not broadly open the process to people previously unable to apply.
Senate Enrolled Act 281 created a limited path to expunge certain official misconduct convictions with a prosecutor’s consent. It also addressed access to juvenile records, restricted expungement for some firearm and commercial driving offenses, and required an electronic method for sending case information to Indiana State Police after an expungement.
Hagan said the provision on transmitting information to state police could help with the repeated paperwork her clinic prepares for an expungement.
“You are literally retyping everything one more time in a different way,” she said of the paperwork required for state police. Hagan said she hopes the electronic transmission provision will ease that work, though she had not yet seen whether it has changed the process in practice.
Still, Hires said delays can arise after a court grants an expungement as other agencies process the order.
“It gets through the court incredibly quickly. It gets through the clerk’s office very quickly,” she said. “I find that the issue tends to lie within the ancillary entities. … That’s something that could be improved.”
The much rarer pardon route
Expungement is also the first option the Indiana Parole Board asks prospective pardon applicants to consider. The board says the court process is often quicker and provides many of the same benefits.
Pardons, which require a recommendation from the board and a decision by the governor, are uncommon. The board received 53 applications from Jan. 1, 2017, through Aug. 25, 2026, according to parole board figures.

Governors granted eight and denied 15. Ten applications were closed, 11 were found ineligible, seven remained under board review and two are still awaiting a governor’s decision.
One denial went to William Hutson, who sought a pardon for a Marion County conspiracy to commit robbery conviction stemming from a 1990 offense. Court documents show he received a two-year sentence in 1991.
Hutson, now living in North Carolina, said he and his wife later founded a charity that repaired 505 Indiana homes for elderly, disabled and low-income residents. He said he now oversees construction projects for a nonprofit serving veterans.
Gov. Mike Braun denied his application July 27. The Governor’s Office said the Parole Board had unanimously recommended denial, citing several factors that included the circumstances of the offense and Hutson’s presentation to the board. A denial letter Hutson provided to the Capital Chronicle did not explain what information counted against him.
Hutson said the letter left him unsure what more he could show the state.
“I just don’t know what standards they have to get a pardon for a crime committed 36 years ago and it’s the only crime ever committed,” he wrote to the Capital Chronicle, “then turning around and helping so many people while paying for it from my own pocket.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: What’s one of the best public safety tools? A clean record
description: He committed a nonviolent felony 15 years ago: a bad check, a possession charge, a stolen car he was dumb enough to ride in at 22. He served his sentence. He paid his fines. He hasn’t been arrested since. He did exactly what we told him to do. Now he’s 40, and every time he […]
text:
Rhode Island now enables people with criminal records to qualify for expungement of up to four felonies, but only for nonviolent offenses and not until 15 years after they have completed their final sentence. (Getty photo)He committed a nonviolent felony 15 years ago: a bad check, a possession charge, a stolen car he was dumb enough to ride in at 22. He served his sentence. He paid his fines. He hasn’t been arrested since. He did exactly what we told him to do.
Now he’s 40, and every time he applies for a job, there’s a box. Every time he tries to rent an apartment, there’s a background check. 
Fifteen years clean, and the first thing anyone learns about him is the worst day of his life.
So he drifts. Not back to crime because he’s evil. Back to the only world that will still have him. The one place nobody runs his record.
I spent 20 years with the East Providence Police Department. Investigative Services, narcotics, a federal task force with the FBI and DEA. I have arrested people who deserved every minute they got, and I’d do it again tomorrow. So understand me when I say this: Rhode Island’s newly expanded expungement law is a public safety measure, and a cop should be first in line to support it.
Here’s the reentry math, and it isn’t ambiguous. A steady job and a stable place to live both measurably lower the odds someone lands back in trouble. A University of Michigan study that tracked people who cleared their records found their subsequent crime rate was actually lower than the general adult population’s. Within a year, their wages climbed by more than a fifth, mostly because people who couldn’t get hired finally could. Give a person a paycheck and a lease and you’ve done more for public safety than another patrol car ever will.
Now the flip side, the part I watched with my own eyes. 
The revolving door. About 6 in 10 people released from state prison are rearrested within three years. When I was young, I assumed that meant they were incorrigible. It doesn’t. Plenty of them cycle back not out of malice but because every legitimate door is bolted shut. You can’t get an honest job, you can’t get honest housing, and eventually you take the dishonest version because it’s the only one on offer. We build that trap and then act surprised when people fall into it.



Quotation







Rhode Island's newly expanded expungement law is a public safety measure, and a cop should be first in line to support it.


Understand what the new law actually does, because the guardrails are the whole point. Signed by Gov. Dan McKee on June 22, it lets someone with up to four nonviolent felony convictions petition a judge to clear their record, but not until 15 years after they’ve finished their last sentence. Fifteen years. Clean. And it is not automatic. A judge has to find that every condition of the sentence was completed, that every fine and fee was paid, that the person has genuinely rehabilitated, and that clearing the record serves the public interest. Crimes of violence don’t qualify. Neither do child abuse and child endangerment, serious assaults on the elderly, or DUI resulting in death. This is not a jailbreak. It’s a narrow, earned, judge-supervised second chance for people who have already spent a decade and a half proving they’re done.
I know the objection, because once I’d have raised it myself. What about accountability? What about the victims?
Accountability already happened. This is post-sentence: after the time is served, after the debt is paid, after 15 more years of a clean life stacked on top. Nobody is erasing the harm or pretending it didn’t occur. And as for victims: the single best thing we can do for future victims is to keep someone who paid their debt from being shoved back into the only life that manufactures more debts. Expungement doesn’t trade safety for mercy. Done right (and Rhode Island did it right), it delivers both. People who clear their records rarely reoffend. That isn’t sentiment. That’s the data.
I chased the revolving door for 20 years. I watched the same faces come back through booking, not because the system was too soft but because it never let go. A record is supposed to be a consequence. For too many people, it quietly became a second sentence. A life sentence, imposed for a crime that never carried one.
We can keep punishing people forever, long after they’ve earned their way back. Or we can stop manufacturing new victims. Those are the two choices. Pick one.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: A look into the extensive proposed Head Start changes and how they could affect NH
description: When the Trump administration announced this summer that it would seek a rule change to reduce the “federal burden” of Head Start programs nationwide, it was concerning for state officials and childcare providers alike.   “Head Start performance standards really set the bar for high quality care,” said Jessica Carver, who leads the state Bureau of […]
text:
The entrance to the Head Start building on Old Loudon Road in Concord. The Trump administration proposed sweeping rule changes to the program, aiming to cut administrative responsibilities, safety and health practices, and more. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin) When the Trump administration announced this summer that it would seek a rule change to reduce the “federal burden” of Head Start programs nationwide, it was concerning for state officials and childcare providers alike.  
“Head Start performance standards really set the bar for high quality care,” said Jessica Carver, who leads the state Bureau of Child Development and Head Start Collaboration, during a Child Care Advisory Council meeting on Aug. 13. 
August’s bimonthly meeting came a little over a week after the Trump administration announced the proposal. Alex Amaral, the state’s Head Start Collaboration office administrator, had only been able to get through around half of the proposal before the meeting.  
“They want to take 130 pages and mark it down to 13 pages,” she said. 
Most described the proposal as a “sweeping overhaul” of the 61-year-old program. 
Head Start is a federally funded, state-administered early learning and developmental services program that provides comprehensive care to low-income children, often those who are in foster care, have disabilities, or are experiencing homelessness. The program supports children from birth to age 5 and their families in the areas of early learning, health and nutrition, family wellbeing and development with the goal of providing “high-quality services in safe and healthy settings that prepare children for school and life.” 
On Aug. 6, the Trump administration announced a series of rule changes to the program, stating its goal is to restore local flexibility, reduce the regulatory burden and administration costs on the program, remove duplicate regulations and align licensing with state early childhood systems. 
“Head Start began as a bold commitment to the health, dignity and potential of every child,” U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a statement. “We are removing unnecessary bureaucracy, strengthening nutrition and physical health, trusting parents and local communities, and opening Head Start to hundreds of thousands more children.” 
Head Start covers comprehensive child development, health, family engagement and administrative requirements to ensure vulnerable children are prepared for school. 
The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking will eliminate, reduce or deregulate around 80% of the standards that govern the program in an effort to “preserve or expand” Head Start slots nationwide and save $2.2 billion. 
The administration proposes changes to federal regulations that define the baseline quality, service scope and operational rules for Head Start and Early Head Start grantees. While regulatory redundancies are being addressed in the rule change, the proposal also eliminates health and safety, oversight and curriculum rules that benefit families and staff. 
New Hampshire has 35 total programs. Early Head Start programs are for children ages 0-3, and Head Start programs are for children 3-5 years old.
Parent involvement
The administration said the proposed changes to Head Start would recognize “parents as a child’s primary teacher” and preserve the requirement that “programs engage parents and families in children’s learning and development.” However, new rules would cut governance structures that promote parent involvement in the program, increase eligibility requirements for homeless children, deregulate education regulations and more. 
The rule proposal removes regulations from the Head Start Act around parent committees, which were established at each center to advise on local program policies and activities, as well as assist in staff recruitment and screening. It also cuts other oversight committees for the community and parents. 
Additionally, requirements for programs to cover physical health, mental health and family support would be eliminated. Head Start’s capacity to treat both child and parent has been a defining metric of the program. The proposed replacement would have minimal standards. 
Other regulation cuts, changes, or new proposals regarding parental involvement include: 

Requirements for parent activities supporting child learning are removed and/or reduced. 
Requirements about programs providing additional services, such as helping parents of children with disabilities access services, are removed. 

Program curriculum and eligibility 
Head Start serves children from birth to compulsory school age, pregnant women and expectant families. Families who meet federal poverty guidelines and who participate in certain federal programs, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, qualify. Additionally, children in foster care or who are experiencing homelessness qualify, as well as children with disabilities. 
According to the First Five Years Fund, a national childcare organization, more than 60,000 children served in Head Start last year were experiencing homelessness, the highest on record. Families can enroll in the program through self-attestation of their situation and are given a grace period on government documentation. 
Under the rule change proposal, families experiencing homelessness will have a higher burden to prove their qualification for Head Start. Self-attestation would no longer be enough to prove homelessness and therefore eligibility in the program, which could make it more difficult for a population that may lack formal documentation. 
Other regulations on eligibility and enrollment would be cut as well, specifically around how programs select and recruit families, waitlist maintenance, attendance and more. 
The rule change also seeks to eliminate the requirement of dual-language instruction for students who do not speak English. Currently, more than a third of children in Head Start are dual-language learners, and bilingual Head Start instruction is used to bridge the gap between the languages spoken at home and in school. 
According to state Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Jake Leon, the state does not know how many of New Hampshire’s Head Start programs have dual-language instruction because the department does not track it. Leon said the department “will be prepared to do so” if the proposed federal changes get approved and implemented. 
The proposal would require all classroom instruction to be conducted exclusively in English, with no accommodation for children who are still building English proficiency. An exception is made for Indigenous tribes, who can still incorporate their tribal language and heritage into their teachings. 
Head Start has rules about limiting suspension and requiring consultation of a mental health professional before a child could be suspended. The program also prohibited expulsion. 
Those regulations would be cut in favor of narrower requirements on when children with documented behavioral problems get referred to a specialist. The program would also have no general suspension or expulsion policy. 
Some other regulation cuts, additions or changes include: 

Introducing a minimum baseline for physical activity that is aligned with the health secretary’s Make America Healthy Again push. 
Cutting education requirements for home-based Head Start programs, including instructional activities, home visits and curriculum adaptation. 
“Healthy marriage” is now required to be a part of instructional material in a family-engagement context. 
Currently, programs have flexibility to determine their own rules and policies for addressing staff violations of eligibility-determination rules. The proposal, if approved, would require programs to report staff who violate eligibility determination regulations.
Programs would no longer be required to participate in the state Quality Recognition and Improvement Systems program, which is known as Granite Steps for Quality in New Hampshire. Other nationwide program quality measurement metrics would be eliminated. 
Details around helping with kindergarten transition requirements are removed. 

Staff-to-child ratio reductions 
One of the changes in the proposal is for Head Start staff-to-child ratios to match a given state’s childcare licensing standards. 
Staff-to-child ratios determine how many children should legally be allowed with an adult at one time, based on their age. Early education experts use these standards to determine safe care, and make sure that they can adequately meet the needs of young children. 
According to the National Institute for Early Education Research, Head Start ratio standards are based on expert consensus and empirical evidence for high quality and developmentally friendly care that sets “reasonable limits” to the number of young children per staffer in the classroom. Exceeding ratio limits, although they vary by state, could result in unsafe care and faster teacher burnout. 
Currently, only 12 states have childcare licensing standards that meet the 1 to 4 staff-to-child ratio requirement set by Head Start for ages 1-2; four states have the same ratios for two year olds and six states meet them for 3 year olds. 
In New Hampshire, staff-to-child ratios are close to those of Head Start, with the biggest differences being an additional child per adult for 1- and 2-year-olds and an extra two children per adult for 4-year-olds.
New Hampshire’s staff-to-child ratios are somewhat similar to Head Start’s. (Graphic by Maya Mitchell)
State childcare licensing rules recently underwent a long reform process, led by the Child Care Advisory Committee and childcare providers, that ended in 2025. During the reform process, the committee decided to maintain low staffing ratios for safety and development reasons.
At least nine states will have their staff-to-child ratios drastically changed at Head Start facilities if the proposed rules become permanent. Florida, for example, mandates a 1 to 11 ratio for 2-year-olds, 1 to 15 ratio for 3-year-olds and 1 to 25 ratio for children over 5. 
Child safety and other employee practices
In an effort to align Head Start programs with individual state early childhood systems and remove the duplicative regulations that separate federal standards from those of the state, the proposal eliminates a variety of Head Start regulations around child safety and staffing.
Under the rule change, Head Start teachers and staff will have fewer job qualification requirements and less required training. Program volunteers would also have to meet fewer health requirements. Some of the proposed changes include: 

Removal of the requirement for staff to have annual training on recognizing and reporting abuse and neglect. 
Staff health and wellness requirements, including staff breaks and health exams, are removed from the Head Start Act. 
Requirements for programs to screen volunteers for communicable diseases and that prohibit volunteers from being left alone with a child are removed. 

The proposed rule would also bar programs from requiring or favoring postsecondary credentialing in hiring, unless the program can justify the requirement. 
A majority of childcare professionals in New Hampshire, depending on their title, are required to have college or community college credits to be left alone and care for young children. It is unclear if the proposed rule would revert staff qualifications back to state licensing rules, but the requirement could be at odds with existing New Hampshire statute. 
Additionally, the proposed changes would remove vehicle and other transportation requirements for programs. Details around how children should be transported, vehicle operation, annual vehicle safety inspections and pre-trip checks would be removed from Head Start’s rules in favor of state and local transportation laws. Nationwide regulations around safe field trip routing, safety procedures and alternative vehicles adapted for children with disabilities would also be removed in favor of programs relying on state rules. 
Other proposed changes include:

Family childcare Head Start programs are no longer required to have a child development specialist. 
Programs would no longer be required to assist children in daily tooth brushing after meals. 
Definitions of corporal punishment, sexual abuse, emotional abuse, and neglect with behavioral examples that draw from the federal Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act would be removed. 
Federal monitoring requirements on curriculum, financials and program designation renewal would be removed without a proposed replacement. 
Professional development requirements that include social/emotional development, a structured coaching process and an annual training strategy would be removed and replaced with at least 15 hours of professional development. 
Specific disability services and discipline protections would be replaced with general instruction to follow existing state and federal law. 

Administrative work and federal oversight
In an effort to cut program costs to redirect funding to programming, the federal government proposed reducing the administrative spending cap for Head Start programs from 15% of approved program costs to 5%. 
Most larger childcare programs have at least one staff member in charge of managing dollars, government oversight, and vendors, including for food. Administrative costs for Head Start programs include finance staff, human resources, and auditors who run payroll, background checks and financial oversight. The administrative cap will prevent programs from being able to have these positions staffed. 
According to the First Five Years Fund, only about 3.7% of Head Start programs nationwide operate at or below 5% administrative costs. According to Amaral, most New Hampshire programs’ administrative costs sit between 9% and 11%. 
To reach their goal of “reducing compliance-driven activities” that “constrict the early education workforce” the rule-change proposal also includes: 

Cutting regulations around program monitoring communication between local Head Start programs and the federal government.
Removing details in the Head Start Act around grant applicant criteria.
Removing financial regulation descriptions around insurance, facility management and payment (construction/renovation), financial documentation and oversight. 

What’s next?
The proposed rule is open for a 60-day public comment period, which ends on Oct. 6. During this period, anyone can submit formal comments responding to the proposal, and when the comment period ends, the federal government must consider them before finalizing the rule. As of Sept. 24, over 16,700 comments have been submitted. 
After the comments close, the timeline can vary on when a final ruling is published and takes effect. Until then, the current Head Start rules, standards and regulations are in place. 
If the rule proposal is finalized as it stands, Head Start programs around the country will face loads of new rules to follow. However, plenty of existing rules around nutrition, inclusion for children with disabilities, curricula and no cost for parents will continue. 
State Head Start officials told childcare providers in August that New Hampshire is in a better position than most states. All of the state’s programs have childcare licenses and state-level regulations the federal government wants to remove. It could also take years before the new rules are mandated, giving both families and teachers time to transition. 
“Probably, I would say the majority of the Head Start programs will continue to provide that extra quality of care for both families and the children,” Amaral said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Cheniere Energy closing in on $138M tax break for LNG expansion in Cameron Parish
description: A company that’s expanding its liquified natural gas facility in Cameron Parish is one step away from getting a $138 million break on its local property taxes.
text:
A liquified natural gas tanker travels into Calcasieu Lake. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)A company that’s expanding its liquified natural gas facility in Cameron Parish is one step away from getting a $138 million break on its local property taxes.
The Louisiana Board of Commerce and Industry, whose members are appointed by the governor, approved Cheniere Energy’s “mega-project” status application Wednesday for its $6 billion plans to expand the Sabine Pass liquified natural gas export facility, where the fuel is converted for shipping overseas. If Gov. Jeff Landry gives his approval, the company will be exempt from paying 93% of its property taxes over at least the next five years.
With the increased exemption, Cheniere would pay $10.5 million a year in property taxes instead of $29.8 million, according to Louisiana Economic Development calculations. Without ITEP, the company would have owed closer to $150 million over the five-year period.
The mega-project incentive has been part of the Industrial Tax Exemption Program since 2016, when former Gov. John Bel Edwards made substantial changes to one of the state’s most lucrative business incentive programs. Landry has undone most of that policy, but he’s retained the mega-project designation with some changes.
For an investment to receive that distinction under the latest rules, a company must spend more than $500 million in Louisiana or exceed 200% of the average business investment in the parish over 10 years. An applicant can ask for a waiver of between 93% and 100% of their local property taxes.

Cheniere is the second company to receive official mega-project status under the revised ITEP rules. The first was Syrah Resources, whose application was approved in June. The company provides raw materials needed to make batteries for electric vehicles and is investing $587 million in its Concordia Parish facility. Its expansion includes six buildings, three power distribution centers and increased production capacity.
Louisiana Economic Development officials were not available Friday when asked for details on mega-projects approved under the Edwards administration.
The Industrial Tax Exemption Program dates back to 1936, instituted to attract major businesses to Louisiana that otherwise would not have come. The program originally provided a 100% tax exemption on property taxes no matter the investment amount. Companies often exploited loopholes in state law to renew their tax-free status beyond the maximum allowable 10 years.
In 2016, Edwards issued an executive order to require companies either create or maintain jobs in order to qualify for a ITEP break and gave local taxing authorities power to approve or reject applications from companies doing business in their jurisdictions.
Property taxes generally go to local governments to fund things like schools and police departments. It’s one of the reasons locals were given say-so over the projects, because missing out on tax revenue impacts local budgets.
Edwards also reduced the 10-year incentive to five years plus a five-year renewal option and lowered the tax exemption rate to 80% for renewals. In 2018, the Louisiana Legislature set the rate at 80% for all ITEP projects.
In 2024, Landry changed the ITEP rules to no longer require companies to disclose how many jobs they create, keep or eliminate. And instead of local taxing authorities having power over a company’s participation in the program, the Landry administration supported the creation of new parish-level ITEP review boards with appointees from local taxing agencies, typically the school board, sheriff’s office and parish council or police jury.
Jan Moller, CEO for the progressive economic policy nonprofit Invest in Louisiana, said Landry’s ITEP revisions have hurt local agencies that benefitted from the tax dollars collected under the rule changes Edwards made in 2018.
“The big question that we never answer with these projects is the ‘but for’ question,” Moller said. “Would they still come to Louisiana ‘but for’ this lucrative tax break that exists nowhere else but here in Louisiana?” he added.
Moller was a member of the Board of Commerce and Industry under the Edwards administration. He said there was no business impact after local agencies were given say-so over ITEP, and more industry tax dollars flowed to help parishes pay for projects such as new schools, roads and bridges.
“Those reforms did nothing whatsoever to slow down investment in Louisiana industry, and it’s a real shame that those reforms were rolled back and we went back to the status quo,” Moller said.
The Louisiana Association of Business and Industry has said Edwards’ ITEP overhaul resulted in fewer applications for the tax incentive.
However, Together Louisiana, a progressive coalition of civic and church groups, points to numbers showing the industrial tax break was given to more companies after the 2016 executive order than when the 100% tax exemption was available. The group attributes the drop in ITEP applications to an administrative rule change that cut down the amount of paperwork required for renewals.
The Board of Commerce and Industry also approved 26 other ITEP applications at Wednesday’s meeting, under both previous rules and the newest 2025 rules. When combined, the projects represent nearly $7.9 billion in investments and an estimated $135.3 million in tax breaks, according to Louisiana Economic Development. An estimated $19.3 million in local taxes will be collected from these projects.
“That’s a big number,” board member Wesley Wheelis, a West Monroe financial adviser, said at the meeting about the combined project value.
“It is a big number,” added member Jerry Jones, a Baton Rouge attorney, saying that any day a company invests in Louisiana “is a good day.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Advocates may try to extend life of the ‘flush tax’ in 2027
description: Since 2004, Maryland's “flush tax” has raised $2.3 billion for wastewater treatment plant upgrades that have kept hundreds of millions of pounds of nutrients out of the Bay. It could decrease in 2030, but advocates say sewage treatment plants still need the help.
text:
The filtration system at the Back River wastewater treatment plant in Baltimore County. (Photo by Josh Kurtz/Maryland Matters)Since its enactment in 2004, Maryland’s “flush tax” has raised $2.3 billion from property owners, funding pollution-saving upgrades at scores of wastewater treatment plants in the state and keeping hundreds of millions of pounds of nutrients out of the Chesapeake Bay.
The fee for the Bay Restoration Fund is set to be cut in half in 2030, but a group of state legislators and Chesapeake Bay advocates want to step and head that off, possibly making it a subject of discussion in the 2027 legislative session.
“The BRF is arguably one of the single most important successful efforts that the state of Maryland, or really any state that I know of, [has used] to fund major environmental improvements,” said Del. Dylan Behler (D-Anne Arundel), who serves on the House Environment and Transportation Committee.
The fund, established in 2004, has paid for upgraded technology at 66 of the state’s 67 major sewage treatment plants, and another 17 minor plants, according to data from the Maryland Department of the Environment. Sixteen other minor plants are in the planning phase for upgrades.
It’s estimated that the upgrades to the major facilities alone, over a 20-year lifespan, will prevent 200 million pounds of nitrogen and another 10 million pounds of phosphorus from flowing into the bay, where those nutrients spur low-oxygen summer “dead zones” that kill underwater life.
In 2012, lawmakers doubled the fee for many Maryland property owners from $2.50 to $5 per month. But the higher fee is set to sunset in 2030, unless environmentally minded legislators can stop it.
Del. Dylan Behler (D-Anne Arundel) speaks during a March rally on utility spending on gas pipelines. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Since 2009, some 64% of all nitrogen reductions and 61% of all phosphorus reductions achieved by the states surrounding the Chesapeake Bay have come from upgrades to sewage treatment plants.
But some of those “enhanced nutrient removal” upgrades in Maryland are approaching the end of their projected 20-year lifespans. About 20 facilities received upgrades more than 15 years ago, meaning it is time to reevaluate the systems, according to data from the Maryland Department of the Environment. Twenty more facilities will hit that point from 2027 through 2029.
The effort to extend — or eliminate — the 2030 sunset could also provide a good opportunity to refine the fund, said Behler, who said lots of ideas are on the table.
The fund could be used for sewage plant maintenance, in addition to upgrades. Or it could do more to improve septic systems or convert homes to public sewer service. Maybe it could help sewage treatment plants deal with removing harmful “forever chemicals” from water they discharge.
“What I don’t think that we can do is simply just reauthorize it and say, ‘Well, we’re just going to do the same thing that we’ve done for 20 years,” Behler said.
But legislators also must be careful not to overextend the fund, or let it be used for outside purposes, said Sen. Sara Love (D-Montgomery). She serves on the Chesapeake Bay Commission, which consists of lawmakers from states in the bay region.
Legislators enter the 2027 session facing a projected $3 billion structural budget gap. Over the past few years, lawmakers have raided special funds in order to address budget woes in the short-term.
“I can’t tell you how many people have said, ‘Well, maybe we can look at the BRF for funding,’” Love said. “We have to be very careful to make sure that the fund doesn’t get raided for things that are important — no doubt — but maybe somewhat tangential to the bay.”
Matt Stegman, staff attorney at the Chesapeake Bay Program, said there is an argument for increasing what Maryland home and business owners pay into the Bay Restoration Fund, because ever-increasing construction costs have continued to make infrastructure projects more expensive.
“Even having just the same amount of resources available, you’re still shrinking that pie,” Stegman said.
Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery). (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Stegman also wonders if the fund should be deployed to help Maryland cities and counties in their efforts to reduce pollution from stormwater runoff — considered among the fastest growing sources of pollution to the bay.
While upgrades at sewage treatment plants are considered a success, dealing with stormwater and agricultural runoff issues have been more challenging for the bay states. That’s why the region fell short of its 2025 pollution reduction goals, though some states, including Maryland, came close.
“We’re spending all this money on stormwater, but as a whole, because of climate change and additional development, everything else … We’re not keeping pace,” Stegman said.
Another debate could be about, for the first time, allowing Bay Restoration dollars to cover the costs of extending sewer service to new rural locales in the state, said Dominic Butchko, director of intergovernmental relations at the Maryland Association of Counties.
MACo, which represents county governments across the state, said preserving the fund is the “first priority” in 2027, so that counties “can continue maintaining existing systems and planning for future needs.”
“Maryland also needs more water and wastewater capacity to support housing and economic growth,” Butchko said. “The BRF should remain part of that conversation, but counties need certainty that the program itself will continue.”
As Maryland faces a shortage of affordable housing, Behler agreed that the idea must be considered during the ongoing reevaluation of the Bay Restoration Fund.
“It’s important for us to remember the other ongoing needs in the state, and the housing crisis is certainly one of them,” Behler said. “And [we] would be remiss if we did not at least have a conversation about what that might look like.”
Since the last time lawmakers took up the Bay Restoration Fund in 2012, Maryland has also seen maintenance woes undermine progress at some of its largest wastewater treatment plants — and smaller ones, too.
Baltimore City’s two facilities, the largest in Maryland, both saw staffing woes in the wake of the pandemic and maintenance backlogs caused equipment to fall into disrepair. That led to excess pollution entering the Patapsco and Back rivers, and an eventual consent decree for the city.
Smaller plants on the Eastern Shore, where jurisdictions have fewer staff members to run facilities and manage contracts, have also faced struggles, said Matt Pluta, the Choptank Riverkeeper and director of riverkeeper programs at the nonprofit ShoreRivers.
The Back River Wastewater Treatment Plant, as seen from Cox’s Point Park in Essex. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters).
“We have specific examples here on the Eastern Shore, where plants have been upgraded with funds from the BRF, but are being run into the ground,” Pluta said.
He believes that, if lawmakers update the Bay Restoration Fund in 2027, they should consider allowing those jurisdictions to use the money to keep plants in good working order, and prevent excess pollution from entering Eastern Shore rivers.
“It’s one thing for the government to hand out funds and say, ‘Upgrade this plant,’ and it’s another thing for a facility that lacks a town engineer to oversee those contracts,” Pluta said.
Pluta also believes more could be done with the Bay Restoration Fund to transition more of the state away from septic systems and onto wastewater treatment plants.
“We have areas that are low-lying on septic systems that need to be bailed out — figuratively and literally. And that bailout is probably to hook them onto sewer,” Pluta said.
There also ought to be conversations, Stegman said about improving the smaller slice of Bay Restoration funds that pay farmers to plant cover crops during the winter months to slow down harmful runoff. Those funds are currently doled out to farmers who apply on a per acre basis, but there is an argument that the state should target the program more precisely, with more money for cover crops that are most successful at reducing nutrients, he said.
“Is it the time to maybe raise the bar on some of these programs to say, ‘Look, we are going to ask more of you to get this money’?” Stegman said.
Amid all the debate, environmentalists say they see the next legislative session as a good chance to make improvements to a 22-year-old fund.
“To us, it’s an opportunity. We’ve seen the success. Let’s build on it and match it to modern times,” Pluta said.

title: Survey: Floridians sour on prospects for the property insurance market
description: A majority of Florida homeowners say that despite proclamations by lawmakers and rating agencies, they don’t believe the property insurance market is improving in the state, with more than a quarter asserting that the market is getting worse. A majority in that same poll say that, by far, tackling property insurance is more important than […]
text:
U.S. Coast Guard crew members search the flooded Big Bend of Florida area for survivors of Hurricane Helene, via Coast Guard.A majority of Florida homeowners say that despite proclamations by lawmakers and rating agencies, they don’t believe the property insurance market is improving in the state, with more than a quarter asserting that the market is getting worse.
A majority in that same poll say that, by far, tackling property insurance is more important than lowering property taxes.
Those are findings from a survey of 1,511 Florida homeowners conducted last month by the Public Opinion Research Lab at the University of North Florida in conjunction with the Orlando Sentinel and South Florida Sun Sentinel.
When asked which statement is closest to their view, 55% of respondents said they see no signs the homeowners insurance market is improving, 26% think the market is getting worse, and 18% believe the market is improving and rates are likely to come down.
When asked who they feel has benefited most from insurance reforms, a strong majority (69%) said it’s been the insurance industry, with 16% saying consumers have benefited most, and 9% said trial lawyers.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.The poll comes as property insurance becomes a major issue in the Florida gubernatorial race between Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly.
Donalds has gone on the airwaves and campaign trail blasting Jolly’s proposal to create a state catastrophe fund to absorb wind insurance coverage that the Democrat says could reduce insurance rates by up to 60% to 70%.
Donalds contends that would result in a $1,000 “hurricane tax,” citing a recently published study by researchers at Florida State University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Business. However, that study did not review Jolly’s proposal, but instead a plan introduced by two lawmakers in the Florida Legislature in 2024.
(That plan is not publicly available but the Donalds campaign shared it with the Phoenix.)
Donalds has introduced his own plan to lower property insurance rates, which would maintain legislation passed in 2022 and 2023 that has limited homeowners’ right to sue insurance companies. He and other Republicans in  the Legislature have boasted that those laws have reversed the crisis the property insurance market was in at the time.
Jolly has countered that they haven’t done nearly enough to reduce premiums.
AM Best, a ratings agency, released a report this summer finding that Florida’s home insurance market was beginning to stabilize. It reported that personal property insurance companies recorded nearly $1 billion in underwriting gains last year, following a $132 million underwriting loss two years earlier.
An representative of AM Best told WINK TV that profits for insurance companies were “probably creating some space for rates to come down,” although he added, “We haven’t seen that really happen dramatically yet, but I think the expectation is that forward looking there should be some easing now.”
Of the 1,511 Florida homeowners surveyed in the poll, 261 said they had filed a claim against their insurance company in the past five years. Of those 261, 45% said their claims initially were denied; 47% of those people said that their annual insurance premiums had increased by at least 50% in the past five years.
Salience
The survey notes that 19% said their premium increased by that amount in the past year, compared to just 2% nationwide, according to a 2024 national Consumer Reports survey.
“Florida homeowners are overwhelmingly negative in their assessment of not just the property insurance market, but also government efforts to overhaul it,” said Sean Freeder, faculty director of the survey lab and associate professor of political science at UNF.
“Only about one in 10 Democrats and Independents, and one in four Republicans, see signs of improvements, which is remarkable. Plenty of political science research shows that perceptions of the economy are highly influenced by partisanship — the more one’s own party controls government, and therefore economic policy, the stronger the assumption that government policies are effective and the belief that the economy is healthy. For Republicans to break from these assumptions, and from their own’s party’s direct messaging, dissatisfaction with that aspect of policy must be very high and very salient.”
When asked to choose between property taxes or property insurance, 63% of respondents said they are more concerned about insurance, while 36% indicated greater concern about taxes.
“This is remarkable given the amount of attention that has been spent this year discussing property tax reform, especially with Amendment 3 on the ballot,” Freeder said.
“Even in a rhetorical environment that would otherwise prime Floridians to think heavily about property tax, nearly two in three still said property insurance was the greater concern. This sentiment was essentially uniform across partisanship and region of the state.”
The survey’s margin for error is +/- 3.18 percentage points.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Understanding Indiana’s reserves
description: Many smart people have been spending time thinking about how state leaders might invest Indiana’s growing revenue and robust reserves. This is especially of interest as monthly revenue collections continue to outperform forecast estimates (revenues have exceeded estimates for the last ten consecutive months).  We mentioned in our recent Fiscal Year 2026 Clos[...]
text:
Here's what you need to know about Indiana's growing reserve balances. (Getty Images)Many smart people have been spending time thinking about how state leaders might invest Indiana’s growing revenue and robust reserves. This is especially of interest as monthly revenue collections continue to outperform forecast estimates (revenues have exceeded estimates for the last ten consecutive months). 
We mentioned in our recent Fiscal Year 2026 Close-Out Report (ending June 30) that Indiana closed the books with nearly $4 billion in reserves. At that same time, the state estimated reserve levels for fiscal year 2027 — this projection assumes flat revenue growth and projects $5.3 billion in reserves by June 30, 2027, or 22% of revenues. 
Already in the first two months of the current fiscal year, revenue collections have exceeded forecast projections. A positive (growth) revenue forecast in December 2026 could push the state’s structural surplus past even the existing FY 2027 reserve projections. 
Before anyone starts considering how to invest this windfall, there are a few realities that all of us need to contend with: 
Not all reserves are available to spend 
A surplus is the amount of General Fund revenue that exceeds expenditures each year. In fiscal year 2026, that surplus was $1.855 billion. What is known as combined balances includes the general fund surplus plus three other funds that we lump in the larger $3.99 billion reserves. Here are their balances as of June 30: Medicaid Contingency & Reserve Fund: $274.7 million State Tuition Reserve: $739.6 million Rainy Day Fund: $1.12 billion. 
Because each of these funds that are included in the larger “reserves” have dedicated uses, we will have far less than the total amount available if we want to make state investments with reserves. 
Automatic taxpayer refunds are a real possibility
Current state law requires that in odd numbered years (budget crafting years like 2027) if the state determines that there are “excess reserves” of more than $50 million, then state law requires an automatic taxpayer refund. Excess reserves are defined as reserves that exceed 12.5% of the general revenue appropriation for the current state fiscal year. For comparison, in FY 2026, combined balances were 17.2% of the following year’s appropriations. 
That means that without a change to the Automatic Taxpayer Refund law or spending down reserves, Indiana might realize another refund, such as those in 2021 and 2022. 
Gas tax holiday impacts
Despite strong reserves, it is anticipated that over $1.1 billion may be needed to pay back the state highway fund for this summer’s suspension on state gasoline taxes. The Indiana State Board of Finance has been using cash from that fund to reimburse municipalities and counties for their lost revenue during the holiday. It is absolutely critical that the state pay back the fund to ensure that Indiana has the necessary funds to maintain our roads and streets. 
Re-Visiting 2025 budget and programming cuts 
The actual impact of the current state budget (passed in Spring 2025 and covering FY 2026-2027) is that Indiana state government realized an overall 7% reduction in real spending (accounting for cuts, holdbacks, and inflation) as compared to the previous budget. Our analysis of these reductions showed that the cuts differed by program and agency — for example, that the agencies under the purview of the Secretary of Commerce (including the Indiana Economic Development Corporation and Indiana Department of Workforce Development) realized reductions of 40%. 
It is very possible, given the scale of these reductions and the fact that whole programs were eliminated, that state leaders may want to revisit some of these decisions and reverse them while revenues are available. 
A lot can change from December 2026 and April 2027
Budget leaders went into the 2025 budget expecting status quo revenues (based on the December 2024 revenue forecast), when they received an updated revenue forecast in April 2025 that substantially reduced expected revenues. As a result, budget leaders significantly cut spending and added a cigarette tax increase to balance the budget. Even though revenue trends look promising now, any downturn in the economy could severely hamper Indiana’s ability to target expected increased revenues and available reserves on spending that will benefit Hoosiers.
