name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio gets a failing mark on sex education policy from national group
description: Ohio received an “F” for its sex education policy, according to a new report from the Sexuality Information and Education Council of the United States.  This is the second year in a row Ohio has earned an “F” on the report card from SIECUS, a national organization that advocates for comprehensive, medically accurate, and inclusive […]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). Ohio received an “F” for its sex education policy, according to a new report from the Sexuality Information and Education Council of the United States. 
This is the second year in a row Ohio has earned an “F” on the report card from SIECUS, a national organization that advocates for comprehensive, medically accurate, and inclusive sex education. 
“It’s deeply concerning that such an important part of our responsibility to prepare students for life is being so poorly managed,” said Abortion Forward Executive Director Kellie Copeland. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The goal should be to help students be prepared to make decisions about their bodies and their lives, and that’s just not what the Ohio curriculum does at all.”
The grades were determined using two categories — Sex Ed Requirement and Sex Ed Content Requirement. Ohio earned a “D” on the sex ed requirement and an “F” on the sex ed content requirement. 
Nine other states also received an “F” on SIECUS’s report card: Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Indiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, South Dakota, Utah, and Wyoming. 
“What young people are allowed to learn about their bodies is increasingly being determined by politics—not by what they need to be healthy and safe,” Callie Simon, SIECUS Executive Director, said in a statement. 
“This goes beyond the classroom because what young people are allowed to learn today will shape their health, safety, and wellbeing for years to come.”
California, Illinois, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, and Washington each received an “A” on the SIECUS report card. 
A 2021 report from the Journal of Adolescent Health reviewed three decades of research and determined there is strong support for comprehensive sex education.  
“When you have a curriculum that is scientifically accurate, and teaches young people about the emotional, the physical, the social aspects of sexuality in an age-appropriate way, they understand their bodies better. They develop healthy relationships,” Copeland said. 
Ohio’s curriculum stresses abstinence as a general policy and requires some instruction about sexually transmitted infections, according to the Ohio Revised Code. 
Schools are required to “emphasize adoption as an option to unintended pregnancies” and “teach the potential physical, psychological, emotional, and social side effects” of sex outside of marriage, according to Ohio’s law. 
Ohio lawmakers decide curriculum requirements, so the State Board of Education can not require health education standards. Because Ohio lacks comprehensive sex education, it’s ultimately up to each school district on how they decide to teach it. 
The Ohio Department of Education and Workforce is required to conduct an annual audit to ensure school districts are in compliance with the state’s law. 
Every school district completed the 2024-25 audit and all but two school districts were found to be overall compliant. 
Jefferson Township Local School District (Montgomery County) and Ridgewood Local School District (Coshocton County) were non-compliant. 
Both districts were also non-compliant during the 2024-23 audit as well. 
“Many family structures exist today, and all can provide children with a loving and supportive environment,” Ridgewood explained in ODEW’s audit. 
“We have school staff and students who come from single-parent households, same-sex couples, and traditional married-couple families alike. This highlights the importance of recognizing and respecting all family types. Furthermore, sex education should never be used to shame students for their family background.”
Jefferson Township’s district explained there was an “unexpected resignation of our Jr./Sr. High School principal on Feb. 21” who was making arrangements for the sexually transmitted infection education. 
“Our interim building principal was unable to restart/reconnect for the training,” Jefferson Township said in ODEW’s audit. 
“We also lost our Phys. Ed. teacher this year. We have hired a new staff member certified in Health and Phys. Ed. She will be responsible for scheduling the sexually transmitted infection education during the 2025-2026 school year.” 
The Ohio Center for Sex Education is the education arm of Planned Parenthood of Greater Ohio that teaches comprehensive sex education in schools and community organizations using the Get Real comprehensive sex education curriculum for middle and high schools. 
“That curricula focuses a lot on social and emotional learning, so we’re excited that not only do we get to talk about the stereotypical STIs, birth control, pregnancy prevention, but we also talk to folks about how to be members of their community and have proper communication skills and healthy relationships and just think about consent as a whole and and gender as a way that’s affirming,” said Jes Fuller, director of the Ohio Center for Sex Education.
Comprehensive sexual education is developmentally appropriate, she said.
“We want to give information to young people before it becomes incredibly useful because they can have that information for the future,” Fuller said. 
Ohio has a higher teen birth rate than the national average. 
The national birth rate for females 15-19 years old was 12.6 per 1,000 females and Ohio’s teen birth rate was 14.0 per 1,000 females in 2024, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Ohio lawmakers passed a bill over the summer that will soon require schools to teach students to graduate high school, get a job, and get married — in that order — before having a baby. This is known as the success sequence and the law takes effect Oct. 6.
Ohio House Bill 485, also known as the “Enact Baby Olivia Act” would require schools to show either the ‘Baby Olivia’ video or a similar video to students every year starting in fifth grade all the way up through twelfth grade beginning with the 2026-27 school year.
Ohio state Rep. Melanie Miller, R–Ashland, introduced the bill, which the Ohio House passed last year and has had two hearings in the Ohio Senate Education Committee. 
The Ohio lawmakers are currently on break and will come back after the November election. Any bill that does not pass before the two-year General Assembly ends in December would have to be reintroduced.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio economists: Abatements may attract data centers, but is that a good thing?
description: In a recent survey, most economists said Ohio’s tax abatements are an effective way to attract AI data centers to the Buckeye State, but many also questioned the desirability of doing so. They were more split on the economic benefits of making data centers generate their own electricity. There has been a swift, sharp backlash […]
text:
An aerial view shows an Amazon data center last year in Ashburn, Va. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)In a recent survey, most economists said Ohio’s tax abatements are an effective way to attract AI data centers to the Buckeye State, but many also questioned the desirability of doing so.
They were more split on the economic benefits of making data centers generate their own electricity.
There has been a swift, sharp backlash against data centers this year as projects have been rammed through without community input, electricity bills have shot up, and workers fear mass displacement by the technology. And there are worries about how artificial intelligence will reshape the jobs that remain.
As huge and growing numbers of Americans find it harder to simply pay their bills, the backlash has also been directed against a political system in which monied interests seem to have all the power.
In Ohio, anger against data centers built in June when the public learned that former Gov. John Kasich had granted some of the richest tech companies in the world billions in taxpayer incentives that would last 40 years.
Scioto Analysis surveyed 37 Ohio economists about data centers, including asking whether taxpayer incentives are an effective way to attract them. Twenty three said they were — although several expressed doubts about whether that’s a good thing.
“I think that (tax abatements) are effective for attracting the data centers,” Curtis Reynolds of Kent State University wrote in the comment section of the survey. “That does not mean that I think they are a good idea. Tax abatements become a race to the bottom and as communities fight for businesses. In the case of data centers, there will be little employment gains for the local community so the economic benefits of these tax abatements seem dodgy at best.”
Other economists questioned whether such incentives play much of a role in Big Tech’s decision making.
“Data centers locate where the power is, not where the abatement is,” wrote Roman Sheremeta of Case Western Reserve University. “The evidence on tax incentives shows most go to firms that would have come anyway — and hyperscalers are building everywhere they can. Ohio’s $2.3 billion mostly bought what it would have gotten for free.”
One economist said the unpopularity of data centers should make corporate handouts unnecessary.
“Because many communities across the country oppose data centers, Ohio may attract them without additional incentives,” wrote David Lindequist of Miami University. “Tax abatements seem to only provide marginal incentives at best.”
The economists split when asked whether making data centers produce their own electricity would lower Ohioans’ electricity bills. Sixteen said it would, 10 said it wouldn’t and 11 were uncertain.
Casey Boyd-Swan of Kent State University said such “behind-the-meter” generation might reduce electricity bills, but it could come with other costs.
“The idea behind this makes sense,” she wrote. “The biggest economic risk from data centers is cost-shifting, so requiring on-site generation keeps those costs with the data center. In practice, energy costs may not increase as much for Ohio residents, but most on-site generation will be natural gas turbines, which concentrate both air pollution and around-the-clock noise in the communities where data centers are located.”
For his part, Lucas Englehardt of Kent State University argued that on-site power generation might actually increase Ohioans’ power-bills. He said it would make electricity more expensive by adding to the scarcity of the fossil and renewable fuels needed to produce it — and through less-efficient generation.
“This just pushes the demand back a step,” he wrote. “Instead of competing for energy itself — driving energy prices up, they’ll be competing for the resources used to produce the energy — driving up the cost of those resources.”
He added, “In as far as data centers are below-average in energy-production efficiency, this will divert energy-production resources away from high-productivity uses to low-productivity uses, actually driving energy prices up for the end consumer compared to if we just allowed data centers to buy electricity from the grid, and allowed more efficient energy producers to expand production.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio farmers are getting crushed by our politicians’ failure to fight for us
description: I’m Joe Stimmell. I am a lifelong resident of Ashland County and farmer of more than 20 years, where I raise 25 head of beef cattle and farm about 700 acres of corn, soybeans, and small grains with my brother and uncle. I am unaffiliated with any party or candidate. I’ve been through tough times, […]
text:
A farmer harvests corn beside a highway. (Photo by Cami Koons/States Newsroom.)I’m Joe Stimmell. I am a lifelong resident of Ashland County and farmer of more than 20 years, where I raise 25 head of beef cattle and farm about 700 acres of corn, soybeans, and small grains with my brother and uncle. 
I am unaffiliated with any party or candidate. I’ve been through tough times, like the Great Recession and the pandemic, but the reality facing Ohio farmers right now is unsustainable and unlike anything I’ve experienced.
Right now, working people across our state are working harder than ever but feel like we are slipping further behind. Yet if you listen to politicians like Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted and our local Congressman, Max Miller, you’d think the economy is booming. They live in a completely different reality than the rest of us.
Just look around. Thanks to the Iran war our leaders keep voting to prolong, gas prices in Ohio have climbed to about $4.50 a gallon, and diesel recently set a record high of $6.81. 
It is nearly a daily conversation now about what fuel is doing, and whether or not we should top the tanks off or let it ride. Husted has voted 14 times to support the war in Iran. 
Miller has voted for it 7 times, including for a budget framework that would give President Trump $73 billion for the war. 
Every single time they cast those votes, they rubber-stamp a war of choice that’s driving up our bills and making it harder for businesses to operate. That they refuse to change course tells me they either have no clue what we are going through or they simply do not care. 
I saw it firsthand this spring. My brother and I were on our way to meet with the local co-op about fertilizer prices when the war with Iran broke out. By the time we got there, everything was in total disarray. 
Prices for essentials like urea went bonkers, getting dangerously close to $850 a ton on the farm. It’s nearly impossible to plan for the future when our leaders’ actions completely upend the market. You’re just hoping you can survive until things settle down.
On top of foreign policy, our elected officials offer no pushback against the administration’s constant meddling in our markets. 
In the livestock industry, we’ve seen the president’s beef imports take a direct toll on our livelihoods. Since September, live cattle are down roughly 20 cents, or $300 a head. 
Since June, fat cattle have dropped 40 to 50 cents, wiping out nearly 20% of their total value. 
While cattle farming remains profitable for now, these drastic reductions in live cattle prices haven’t led to lower prices for consumers at the grocery store. All it does is make our country more dependent on foreign beef in the long run.
But it’s not just farming and the fallout of the Iran war. 
When you look at the impact of the tariffs, influx of data centers, and healthcare cuts, everything from utility bills to groceries to basic household goods is going up. 
I make significantly more than I did when I started, but I feel no more secure because the cost of living has skyrocketed.
Things have gotten so tough that I know multiple people who are having to finance paying for groceries. That’s hardly indicative of a booming economy.
Husted and Miller are worth millions. Their quality of life is not truly affected by the votes they cast in Washington. But for farmers like myself who have seen input costs skyrocket and cattle values drop, we feel the stress and understand the constant series of tradeoff decisions Ohioans find themselves making. 
Do we spend more on fertilizer to plant corn, or switch to soybeans to save on inputs? Do we buy less meat at the store to save on groceries?
We need leaders who understand the impact their decisions have on the lives of the people they represent — not rubber-stamp politicians who are too scared to stand up for us while Ohio families pay the price.

title: Ohio families are paying the price for the government-induced energy crisis
description: Last month, gas prices hit a record high here in Ohio, and honestly, that tracks: 94% of Ohio voters say energy costs are extremely or somewhat important to them. Whether it’s the gas pump or the AC bill, Ohioans can’t catch a break. And that’s not bad luck. It’s a choice Republican elected officials keep […]
text:
Gas pumps. (File photo by Niki Kelly, States Newsroom.)Last month, gas prices hit a record high here in Ohio, and honestly, that tracks: 94% of Ohio voters say energy costs are extremely or somewhat important to them.
Whether it’s the gas pump or the AC bill, Ohioans can’t catch a break. And that’s not bad luck. It’s a choice Republican elected officials keep making.
Let’s call it what it is: a government-induced energy crisis. Trump promised to cut energy costs in half in his first year.
Instead, household electricity costs in Ohio have gone up more than 25% since he took office. And thanks to his war in Iran — with Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted cheering from the sidelines — we’re paying a dollar more per gallon of gas than we were a year ago.
That’s not incidental for Husted, by the way. He’s voted 14 times for Trump’s war and policies that raised costs for Ohio families on gas, electricity, tariff-affected goods, and ACA coverage.
A Center for American Progress analysis found that in just the first half of 2026, Trump’s and Congress’s policies raised costs for Ohio families by $2,175 per household. The Iran war alone has cost Ohio residents an extra $1.77 billion in gasoline — $365 more per household.
Here’s the part that should really make you mad: none of it seems to bother them.
Trump told reporters “I love the inflation”, and that he’ll “never apologize for $4 gas.”
Husted, for his part, has said the Iran war is going “much better” than expected, and that people living in poverty are “not very experienced at navigating the real world.” Try telling that to a family deciding between groceries and the electric bill.
Husted even used the Iran war as an excuse to skip testifying in person in one of Ohio’s biggest corruption scandals — the FirstEnergy scandal that’s already costing Ohio households $663 more a year on their electric bills. He found time for a fundraiser, though.
Meanwhile, Trump and congressional Republicans have been cutting domestic energy production, not expanding it. Last year, Husted voted for the so-called “Big Beautiful Bill,” which repealed made-in-America energy tax credits that even some Republicans asked Speaker Johnson to protect.
Statewide, that vote put an estimated $10.48 billion in investment and 14,304 good-paying clean energy jobs on the chopping block — many of them recruited by Gov. DeWine himself. That law is now expected to raise Ohio families’ annual energy bills by another $190 a year by 2035 and cost the state 34,000 jobs.
This really isn’t complicated. It’s supply and demand. If you want energy costs to come down, you don’t make it harder to produce more clean energy, which Republicans at the state and federal level have done. That’s especially true right now, with data centers driving up demand across the state, which Husted has been a long-time champion of.
Ohioans are the ones paying for all of this, every month, at every gas station and on every electric bill. Trump built this crisis, and Jon Husted has been right there helping him do it. Ohio deserves leaders who’ll own that and actually fix it — not ones who dismiss our struggles while launching ill-advised wars that make them worse.

text:
In 2019, Gov. Tony Evers issued the first pardons in Wisconsin in nine years. He said that reinstating the pardons process and “offering over 2,000 second chances to folks across our state” has been one of his administration’s most important endeavors. The last deadline to apply for pardons before Evers leaves office is Oct. 5. (Getty Images)The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Gov. Tony Evers announced a deadline of Oct. 5 as the last day for a Wisconsinite to submit an application for a pardon for a crime, before Evers’ second and last term as governor ends in January 2027. 
Distinct from a commutation or a parole order, a pardon restores rights that a person loses if convicted of a felony, including the right to serve on a jury, hold public office and hold certain professional licenses. 
In 2019, Evers issued the first pardons in Wisconsin in nine years. In a press release, he said that reinstating the pardons process and “offering over 2,000 second chances to folks across our state” has been one of his administration’s most important endeavors. 
“I encourage folks who are interested to apply by the deadline and sincerely hope to see this good work continue in earnest in the years ahead,” Evers said. 
To be eligible, a person must be seeking a pardon for a Wisconsin felony conviction and have finished any criminal sentence at least five years ago. Applicants must not have any pending criminal cases or charges in any jurisdiction or be currently required to register as a sex offender. 
Evers’ Pardon Advisory Board held two hearings on Friday; the agendas for the hearings listed 30 applicants for pardons. 
The pardon application and answers to frequently asked questions are on the governor’s website. Each applicant appears before the board for about 10 minutes, giving an introduction and taking questions from the board. The board votes whether or not to recommend a pardon for an applicant; if a majority of the board votes in favor, the application is sent on to Evers for a final decision.

title: A Global Legacy, Built in Mississippi: Corolla Celebrates 60 Years
description: Six Decades of Corolla Since its 1966 debut, the Toyota Corolla has become one of the most recognized and trusted vehicles in automotive history. For 60 years, it has evolved with generations of drivers while remaining synonymous with quality, efficiency and reliability. Today, that global legacy continues in Blue Springs, where Toyota Mississippi team membe[...]
text:
Six Decades of Corolla
Since its 1966 debut, the Toyota Corolla has become one of the most recognized and trusted vehicles in automotive history. For 60 years, it has evolved with generations of drivers while remaining synonymous with quality, efficiency and reliability.
Today, that global legacy continues in Blue Springs, where Toyota Mississippi team members proudly build one of the world’s best-selling car.
Toyota Mississippi joined the Corolla story in 2007, when the Blue Springs plant was announced. Since the first Mississippi-built Corolla rolled off the line, the facility has produced more than 2 million vehicles—connecting Mississippi craftsmanship with drivers nationwide. Today, every gas-powered Corolla sold in the United States is built here, placing Toyota Mississippi at the heart of one of the automotive industry’s greatest success stories.
Powered by Mississippi Team Members
Building the Corolla is both an honor and a responsibility. Each vehicle reflects Toyota’s commitment to quality and the trust millions of customers place in the Corolla name. From stamped steel and body welds to paint, assembly and final inspection, thousands of team members bring skill and dedication to every vehicle.
And every team member of the plant’s 2,400-person crew knows the vehicles they build become part of customers’ daily lives—helping people commute, travel with family and go places not just on the road but in life.
“For our team members, building the Corolla is more than assembling a vehicle—it’s about contributing to a legacy that has earned the trust of millions of customers around the world,” said Aaron Foster, president of Toyota Mississippi. “Every Corolla that leaves our plant represents the passion, skill and dedication of our team. We are incredibly proud to be part of a 60-year history of quality and reliability, and even more excited to help carry that legacy into the future.”

Photo by: Adam Robison
Corolla’s enduring success reflects Toyota’s philosophy of continuous improvement—or kaizen. Across six decades, the vehicle has adapted to customers’ needs without losing the dependability and value that made it a global bestseller. That same commitment guides Toyota Mississippi team members as they improve processes, solve challenges and uphold rigorous safety and quality standards. 

“It’s an incredible feeling to know that something we build here in Mississippi is trusted by millions of people around the world,” said Melissa Roberts, Quality Control Group Leader at Toyota Mississippi. “Every Corolla that leaves our plant represents our hard work, our dedication and the pride of our entire team. Knowing that some families rely on vehicles that I’ve had a part in building gives me a real sense of purpose.”
Toyota Mississippi’s impact reaches beyond the assembly line. Team members mentor students, support local organizations and create career opportunities throughout northeast Mississippi. Since production began, that combination of manufacturing excellence and community investment has made the plant a cornerstone of the region.
Driving the Legacy Forward
To mark Corolla’s 60th anniversary, Toyota Mississippi is inviting the public to celebrate throughout October. From October 1 through October 29, the Toyota Mississippi Experience Center will host “A Lifetime of Legacy,” an exhibit tracing Corolla’s six-decade evolution through models from each generation and highlighting Mississippi’s role in carrying the legacy forward.
Visitors can also attend Corolla 60th Anniversary Evening Tours every Thursday in October from 6:30 to 7:30 p.m. These limited-time tours offer a behind-the-scenes look at the technology, teamwork and craftsmanship behind the world’s best-selling car—and how Mississippi team members bring it to life each day.
As that story continues, Toyota Mississippi is preparing for Corolla’s next chapter. A recent $125 million investment will add hybrid-electric Corolla production, making the plant the first in the United States to assemble electrified Corollas. The milestone advances Toyota’s commitment to innovation and helps ensure Corolla remains a trusted choice for generations to come.
Six decades after its debut, Corolla remains a symbol of reliability, quality and opportunity. Every vehicle built in Blue Springs carries that legacy forward—strengthened by the passion and dedication of Toyota Mississippi team members.
Learn more and reserve your tour today at www.TourToyota.com/MS.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Why I’m a CT YIMBY
description: Many Nutmeggers believe that the built environment in which they live must never be altered. But we should react to change with openness.
text:
I’ve been thinking about the film   I, Robot   recently. Inspired by Isaac Asimov’s anthology, the 2004 Will Smith vehicle is mostly forgotten, but remains a personal favorite of mine. 
Beginning in 2035 Chicago, the film establishes its temporal setting by incorporating computer-generated, “new” skyscrapers among well-known landmarks in the city skyline. This cinematic choice grounded the film’s timeline in a not-so-distant future without cumbersome exposition. The filmmakers anticipated audiences to apprehend that a city’s physical infrastructure changes over the course of decades, and leveraged this universal understanding to get moviegoers up-to-speed quickly.
But is such an understanding, that communities change over time, actually universal? Not in Connecticut. Many Nutmeggers believe that the built environment in which they live must never be altered. Often referred to as NIMBYs (Not-In-My-Backyard), such folks react with unease, even hostility when physical alterations are proposed in their towns. Whether it’s senior housing, solar panels, or bike paths, Connecticut NIMBYs are there to say, “no!”
 I appreciate the instinct for preservation that motivates some NIMBYs, but I believe NIMBYism is a regressive philosophy rooted in exclusionism, incapable of meeting Connecticut’s contemporary challenges. Because I oppose NIMBYism, I identify as a YIMBY (Yes-In-My-Backyard).  
 But if NIMBYism is a philosophy centered around saying, “no,” is YIMBYism simply a double-negative? Not necessarily. I am a YIMBY because I hold specific ideological principles and goals. 
 I am a YIMBY because I am a progressive. I believe that the government should act to improve the conditions of people’s lives, and that one’s identity should not be a barrier to advancement.  
Housing affordability is a major challenge for Connecticut . The best way to lower housing costs is not through complicated equity-through-bureaucracy initiatives, but through simply building more housing. The regions that have managed to control home costs while still experiencing high demand are those where construction is facilitated rather than stifled. 
 In Connecticut, local authorities, dominated by NIMBYs, stonewall new builds through restrictive zoning, labyrinthine permitting and excessive veto-points. If Connecticut leaders are serious about affordability, they need to get serious about supply and demand. That means saying “yes” to new homes. 
 To suggest that town governments relinquish, or merely adjust, their zoning prerogatives invites backlash. It is true that, in principle, local voices should influence local development. But municipal organizations are sometimes run by imperfect people, capable of holding destructive biases.  
America has a sordid record of using race-blind legalism to achieve racist ends. For some, local control is a means through which unwelcome groups can be excluded. NIMBYs sometimes characterize their opposition to housing reform as a desire to preserve something intangible: “character,” or “heritage.” It’s worth asking if the heritage they wish to preserve is one born out of bigotry. 
Additionally, I am a YIMBY because I am an environmentalist. Connecticut must reduce its carbon footprint, and to do so, we must produce more renewable energy. That means building nuclear reactors, solar farms, and wind turbines. The green-energy transition cannot occur without change, but NIMBYs hate change. Consider the furor raised by the Revolution Wind project. 
NIMBYs, maddeningly, cite environmental concerns when they obstruct green infrastructure. I have heard some insist that the energy produced by a turbine will never offset the emissions released as a result of its installation. This statement is false, and those expressing it are sourcing their arguments from a fictional TV show. Others oppose offshore wind due to its impact on marine ecosystems, ignoring the damage caused by burning fossil fuels. Mercifully, others admit that they just think turbines look weird. 
Environmentalism isn’t just about energy generation, it’s also about transmission. As our reliance on renewable energy grows, we need to strengthen our electrical grid. Without robust infrastructure, green energy gets wasted because wires can’t handle the load. Yet Connecticut NIMBYs oppose grid-strengthening on aesthetic grounds.
 Lastly, I am a YIMBY because I am a patriot. Our nation’s history is littered with injustice, but there is progress and honor there too. Many NIMBYs rely on good-old-days rhetoric as an ideological bulwark, but the noble nation for which they wistfully pine was one that said, “yes,” not “no.” Yes, we will break away from foreign tyranny. Yes, we will liberate the enslaved. Yes, we will go to the moon. Yes, we   can.     
YIMBYism isn’t about reflexively greenlighting every proposal, some projects do lack merits. It’s about reacting to change with openness, rather than fear, to promote economic, environmental, and social renewal. 
At the end of I, Robot, Will Smith’s character overcomes his anti-android prejudice, accepting a future in which humankind must coexist alongside newly autonomous robot neighbors. Today, Nutmeggers must do the same…kind of.
 We can embrace uncertainty while rejecting inaction, abandoning old prejudices while striding boldly into the future. Change is scary, but paralysis is fatal. Let’s say, “yes” to better days ahead.  
Matthew Silber lives in Norwalk.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Duplicate billing fix can lower cost of health care
description: Addressing duplicative billing in healthcare is critical for New England’s Medicare beneficiaries -- and for taxpayers.
text:
Patients across New England are struggling to afford care because of rising healthcare costs. This is especially true for seniors living on fixed incomes. There are many factors that contribute to healthcare inflation, some of which are beyond the influence of policymakers. 
However, addressing the waste hidden within routine billing practices is one meaningful way to bring down costs for everyday New Englanders.
Billing codes are used by providers to bill insurers for healthcare services. These codes are often complex, which makes it easy for duplicative billing to go unnoticed. At scale, this is not just costly for patients, but since providers directly bill Medicare and Medicaid, it also wastes taxpayer money. Now, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is taking action to curtail duplicative billing. We believe this is an important step toward making healthcare more affordable.

Haley Director

To better understand how this works, imagine you go to see the dermatologist to have a skin blemish looked at. During the visit, your provider reviews your medical records with you and evaluates the dark spot on your skin, deciding the mole needs to be removed. Rather than scheduling a separate appointment, your dermatologist tells you she can perform the procedure right in the office during that same visit.
As the patient, you might be surprised to realize that this visit would be billed as two separate services under current billing rules. One billing code would correspond to the evaluation at the beginning of the visit, and another for the procedure performed immediately afterward. This ignores the fact that billing for both at the full rate results in Medicare being charged twice for many of the same underlying costs.
This is what a newly proposed CMS rule would address. If the evaluation and the procedure happen on the same day, CMS would pay the full price of the more expensive service and a reduced rate for the second service. This would account for the shared costs between the two services and stop Medicare from overpaying for these types of visits.
Addressing duplicative billing is critical for New England’s Medicare beneficiaries. A single routine visit can cost more than $235 for the evaluation and management fee. The patient would be responsible for nearly $50 of said fee under the Medicare Part B standard co-insurance. Add in the cost of the actual procedure on top of that, and the visit becomes unaffordable for many seniors. 
Recent studies have found that a majority of seniors in the U.S. live on less than $2,000 per month, which means that a medical bill like the one described here would leave a noticeable dent in their monthly budget. Furthermore, research shows that nearly 60% of seniors have skipped an essential medical service or product in the last year due to cost. That is an unacceptable statistic and an important reminder of why reforms are needed.
We encourage CMS to move forward with this proposed rule to help end duplicative billing and bring relief to patients. By taking policy steps like these, we can help turn the tide of rising healthcare costs in New England and across the country.
Dr. Haley Director, PhD, MPH is the Policy Director of Rare New England, a nonprofit organization serving the rare disease community.

name: WyoFile
title: Grand Teton National Ballpark? Visitors call it a field of nightmares.
description:
Park visitors greet news of a potential MLB game in front of the Tetons with disbelief.
The post Grand Teton National Ballpark? Visitors call it a field of nightmares. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
MOOSE, WYOMING—The news shot around Grand Teton National Park’s Jenny Lake on Sunday like the crack of a well-hit baseball echoing off the walls of Cascade Canyon.
The Trump administration and Major League Baseball are scouting the park for a site to play a game?
That was the report in The Washington Post that shook campers and other visitors from their serene surroundings where they had come to escape the mayhem of daily news. The Post story and others that followed chased down a request by Major League Baseball and statements from the White House that the league’s request was not a priority.
“Keep America’s pastime in our baseball parks, not in our national parks,” said David Kelly, an Angels fan from L.A. who was visiting Grand Teton on Sunday. “What are they going to do, cut down a bunch of trees?”
“They would have to build a field?” asked Kristen Kelly. “Not in Yellowstone, not in Yosemite. No!”
“This is our sanctuary,” said Scott Bauer, a visitor from Seattle and a Mariners and Red Sox fan who was at Jenny Lake on Sunday. His bicycling companion Carol Bauer added a few words about President Donald Trump and his building projects: “I don’t need him doing any construction in parks.”
Christiana Rinderle, the former mayor of Durango, Colorado, was visiting Grand Teton on Sunday and called foul. “National Parks are meant for people to enjoy the wildlife and natural beauty,” she said.
“The stadium should be facing the Tetons.”Steven Williams
The Post reported that National Park Service Deputy Director Frank Lands visited three Grand Teton sites including one that was “already disturbed land.” White House statements to news outlets said Lands was not on a baseball scouting mission.
“This is not a Presidential directive, ​nor is it being directed by the White House,” Reuters reported the statement reading. “It’s also not being driven by the Department of Interior. Therefore, this is not a White ​House or Administration priority.”
“I first thought this has to be a joke or an AI spoof,” Joan Anzelmo, former superintendent of Colorado National Monument, said in a statement. “MLB you should know that Grand Teton National Park, home to free ranging wildlife, including grizzly bears, bison, wolves, moose, cougars and elk, is not an appropriate or safe venue for your baseball fantasy,” the valley resident and park advocate said.
Seriously, folks…
Fans describe a towering home run as a ball that would have been hit out of any park but Yellowstone. Well, now maybe …
WyoFile’s examination of Grand Teton on Sunday revealed thousands of acres of sagebrush plain across the 310,000 acre reserve. A baseball field can cover up to about four acres. A stadium can cover 25. A complex, including parking, can cover hundreds of acres.
In Grand Teton, about 10 acres of the sagebrush fields are “already disturbed” — recently bulldozed to expand the Taggart Lake Trailhead parking area.
A sagebrush field in Grand Teton National Park bulldozed for expansion of the Taggart Lake Trailhead parking area.  (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
Steven Williams, a former Jackson Hole resident who now lives outside Steamboat, Colorado, offered advice on how to design a stadium. Williams, (6’2”, 160 pounds, bats right, throws right) tried to walk on as a Chicago White Sox pitcher in 1973.
“The stadium should be facing the Tetons,” he said as he pointed Sunday toward the mountains from Moose. “The fan experience should be the vision of the Tetons.”
Jorge Colon, who played catcher in the Jackson Town League decades ago, disagreed. Fans want home runs, he said, and Williams’ layout would disadvantage the batter.
“You’re against the wind,” Colon said.
Playing baseball at 6,783 feet above sea level near Jenny Lake would, nevertheless, give a batter a boost. At the high-elevation site, a baseball would travel, according to experts’ calculations, 40 feet farther than one hit at sea level.
The Park Service already has an appropriate site for a baseball game at a historic site it oversees in California. A game was recently played at the Manzanar National Historic Site where thousands of Japanese Americans were interned during WWII.
In 2024, the Little Tokyo Giants played the Lodi JACL Templars, the first time the field had been used since the Manzanar camp was closed in 1945.
Grand Teton itself had a ball diamond at Moose years ago in the middle of a park housing complex. But the Park Service converted the open space to additional quarters for park staff in response to Jackson Hole’s worker housing crunch.
Neither the Department of Interior nor Major League Baseball returned emails seeking comment Sunday.

title: Two fraternity members charged with hazing 30 pledges at UW-Madison
description: Two leaders of a fraternity which the University of Wisconsin suspended back in 2015 were taken to the Dane County jail after 30 young men were found filthy, partially clothed and visibly injured in the fraternity’s hot, humid basement. The pledges, most of whom were 18 years old, were apparently being subjected to a hazing […]
text:
The University of Wisconsin's Bascom Hall. (Photo by Ruth Conniff/Wisconsin Examiner)Two leaders of a fraternity which the University of Wisconsin suspended back in 2015 were taken to the Dane County jail after 30 young men were found filthy, partially clothed and visibly injured in the fraternity’s hot, humid basement. The pledges, most of whom were 18 years old, were apparently being subjected to a hazing ritual.
Brayden Klein and Samuel Vane, both 20, were taken to the Dane County jail and charged with hazing and disorderly conduct. Both of them posted $400 bail Thursday morning. The incident is still under investigation. 
Madison police say the pledges were found in the basement on Wednesday night. They were covered in food, condiments, and “other liquids,” police said. The basement’s temperature had been turned up to 81 degrees, making it uncomfortable and humid. A photo of the pledges shows them all confined in an area of the basement shirtless, all wearing black pants and surrounded by trash. 
The fraternity, Alpha Epsilon Pi,  still has a national chapter. Despite its suspension by the UW-Madison over a decade ago, the frat still maintained its campus house where the 30 pledges were found.
Alpha Epsilon Pi was started in 1913 as a Jewish fraternity. It has over 150 chapters open across the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. The fraternity has included seven billionaires among its ranks including Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, as well as the founders of other prominent businesses and politicians.
In a statement, the fraternity condemned the incident and said those responsible will be expelled from the frat. “Hazing is a betrayal of everything our fraternity stands for,” it said in a statement, ABC News reported. There have been nearly 130 deaths due to hazing incidents since the year 2000.

name: VTDigger
title: Grant funded initiative seeks sustainability for regional birthing services
description:
“This grant gives us an important opportunity to take a regional approach to a challenge that no single organization can solve on its own,” said Brattleboro Memorial Hospital co-CEOs Dr. Elizabeth McLarney and Dr. Tony Blofson.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Grant funded initiative seeks sustainability for regional birthing services.
text:
Deidra Razzaque of Brattleboro, whose son was born at Brattleboro Memorial Hospital’s Birthing Center, holds a sign while attending a hospital board meeting on Tuesday, July 14, 2026. File photo from Brattleboro Reformer

BRATTLEBORO — A new grant will help Brattleboro Memorial Hospital and other hospitals, community health organizations, social service providers and other regional partners plan for the future of maternity and newborn care in Southeast Vermont. 
BMH said it received $3.1 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to lead the regional effort to develop “a sustainable model” for delivering the services. Hospitals apply for the federal grant through the states. 
Groups will come together as the Southeast Vermont Perinatal & Newborn Access Network to explore options, according to a news release. The network was proposed as part of the grant application.
“This grant gives us an important opportunity to take a regional approach to a challenge that no single organization can solve on its own,” Dr. Elizabeth McLarney and Dr. Tony Blofson, acting co-CEOs of BMH, said in the news release. “Our goal is to ensure that families throughout Southeast Vermont have reliable access to high-quality maternity and newborn care, while developing a model that is sustainable for the long term.”
BMH said it runs “Southeast Vermont’s only remaining hospital-based birthing center.” A recent plan to close the center due to financial challenges was reversed earlier this month. The BMH Board of Directors affirmed its commitment to continuing obstetric and birthing services, thanks in part to the funding. 
Hospital leadership developed an improvement plan that includes operational efficiencies, staffing changes, increased appointment availability, improved coding and charge capture, and efforts to increase the number of births delivered at BMH, according to the announcement. The hospital also anticipates an increase in expected births in updated fiscal year 2026 projects. 
“The board believes strongly that access to local maternity care is essential to the health and well-being of our community,” Chloe Learey, chairwoman of the BMH Board of Directors, previously said. “We are encouraged by the progress that has been made and by the opportunity to continue improving how we deliver care.”
BMH also plans to continue working with state and federal legislators on payment reform and potential models to strengthen the hospital’s financial stability, including exploration of Critical Access Hospital and Federally Qualified Health Center models.
The grant funded planning initiative will look at “a range of potential models, including shared staffing and services among regional hospitals, coordinated regional birthing services, and community-based prenatal, postpartum, and newborn care,” according to the news release. BMH said the process doesn’t fund direct patient care or provide an operating subsidy for the BMH Birthing Center but will “support regional service and workforce assessments, financial sustainability analysis, referral and transfer planning, transportation-access planning, and development of a future-state care model.”
“We are intentionally not starting with a predetermined answer,” McLarney and Blofson said. “We need to look carefully at the needs of families, the availability of providers, workforce challenges, and the financial realities of rural healthcare. This work will help us determine what model can best serve our region over the long term.”
BMH said the project also will involve collaboration with Cheshire Medical Center/Dartmouth Health in New Hampshire and Baystate Franklin in Massachusetts on regional consultation, referral, and transfer pathways.
Running through July 31, 2027, the 10-month planning initiative is anticipated to culminate in a regional care-model blueprint, financial sustainability analysis and five-year regional implementation plan.
“This is an investment in the future of health care in Southeast Vermont,” McLarney and Blofson said. “We are grateful for the opportunity to work with our regional partners to develop a sustainable system of care for the families we serve.”
Work on the initiative is anticipated to start around Oct. 1.

name: VTDigger
title: Regulators wanted more transparency on Vermont’s medical education. Now they’re getting it.
description:
Budget conditions imposed on the University of Vermont Medical Center require it to collaborate on a new plan for how it funds medical education by the end of this year.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Regulators wanted more transparency on Vermont’s medical education. Now they’re getting it..
text:
Larner Medical School. Photo by Bob LoCicero/VTDigger

When Green Mountain Care Board chair Owen Foster first started to dig into Vermont’s hospitals’ budgets, one question kept surfacing: Where could all the money be going? 
The solvency of the state’s primary commercial insurer was teetering. Vermonters paid some of the highest rates for healthcare in the country. And still, hospitals’ budgets were tight. How could there not be enough money?
Part of the answer, Foster said, lies in the Larner College of Medicine and graduate medical education training at the University of Vermont Medical Center. 
In a late July memo, health policy analyst Nancy Kane, who is a professor at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, determined that it cost UVM Medical Center $161 million to run its medical education programs in 2025. Of that, $82 million came from commercial insurance payers, Kane found — as in, average Vermonters relying on the UVM Health network for care. She estimated that number would be on track to reach $88 million for 2026. 
Now, the care board is asking the medical center to provide more information so the state can better understand Larner’s finances and how the college is serving Vermont’s needs. The medical center is on board.
“I personally see this as an opportunity to do a better job at sharing information with the board about what we’re spending our money on,” said Dr. Ramsey Herrington, who leads UVM Health’s Medical Group. “I think it’s an opportunity for us to also think about what needs we’re meeting in our educational program, and what other needs are out there for Vermonters.”
The care board approved annual budgets for Vermont’s 14 regulated hospitals earlier this month, and the directives for UVM Medical Center’s budget hinged on the medical center and its affiliated medical college improving their financial transparency. 
Vermonters who buy their health insurance through the state’s Affordable Care Act marketplace pay some of the highest premiums in the country. In recent years, the care board’s budget orders have targeted what hospitals charge commercial insurers in an attempt to reign in healthcare spending.
Kane, the health policy analyst, determined that only a few senior leaders at UVM Medical Center, the medical school and the affiliated medical group understood and decided what money moved where. She called the whole process a “black box.”
Now the care board wants to open that black box.  
The Sept. 14 care board order requires the hospital to form a public working group alongside representatives from the medical school, the care board, the office of Vermont’s Health Care Advocate, smaller rural hospitals, federally qualified health centers and other independent stakeholders. 
The group must examine the role, expenses and “measureable benefits” of both the Larner College of Medicine and the medical center’s residency programs. They have until Dec. 15 to prepare a plan for how UVM Medical Center should financially support medical education. 
At that point, the care board has a month to vote on whether or not to approve the proposal. 
Foster said he will be looking for strategies the school can employ to fill gaps that Vermont hospitals have typically filled with expensive traveling nurses or temporary clinicians, called “locums.” 
Herrington, with UVM Health’s Medical Group, said that looking across the state at where there are the longest delays in patient care, where there are the most locums and where Vermonters spend the most money on out-of-state clinicians will be key to identify the gaps that medical education can try to fill. He also pointed to primary care, mental health care and anesthesiology as some of the clearest needs. 
“Our strategy for where we’re going to expand across the entire spectrum of medicine should be meeting the needs of the health system and of the region,” he said. 
Just expanding the number of residents, even if they don’t stay in Vermont, could have its benefits. Residents are some of the most “efficient” parts of the workforce, Herrington said. The federal government contributes money for residents’ salaries and training. That’s a good return on investment for how much a hospital spends on training and paying a resident physician, he said.
Still, Herrington wants learning to be at the core of how UVM spends its medical education funding. 
“It just has the other added benefits of helping take care of our patient population and creating the pipeline,” he said.
Mike Fisher, the state’s healthcare advocate, hopes that the working group can, at the very least, serve as a gathering ground for ideas of how Vermont might be able to get these benefits without relying so heavily on commercial insurance payers to foot the bill. 
“What are the options? What are other states doing? What are other medical schools doing?” he said. “Maybe there are no options, but we should at least kick those tires.”
If the working group’s December plan fails to garner the support of a majority of care board members, it will trigger a series of reporting requirements on the medical center intended to yield similar accountability and transparency as the working group.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico think tank proposes legislative ethics reforms
description: A new report from Think New Mexico proposes nearly a dozen reforms for state legislators, lobbyists and advocacy groups as elements of "modernizing" the state Legislature.
text:
Think New Mexico on Sept. 27, 2026, released a new report and a list of proposed ethics reforms for state legislators, lobbyists and advocacy groups ahead of the 2027 legislative session. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A new report from Think New Mexico proposes nearly a dozen reforms for state legislators, lobbyists and advocacy groups as elements of “modernizing” the state Legislature.
The report, issued Sunday, follows two years of research, according to a news release from Think New Mexico, bolstered by support from BSP Polling, which found that 81% of New Mexico voters “support holding legislators to a higher ethical standard,” and 64% support paying salaries to legislators “if legislators also have to comply with mandatory ethics reform.”
New Mexico voters will have the opportunity to amend the state Constitution on the Nov. 3 general ballot and allow state legislators to collect a salary for the first time in the state’s history.
New Mexico Election 2026: Constitutional Amendment 4

The think tank news release said the organization will be advocating for the reforms in next year’s 60-day legislative session, which begins Jan. 19, 2027.
Reforms for state lawmakers include
• requiring them to disclose direct, financial conflicts of interest with legislation and recuse themselves from votes on those bills;
• “enhance” financial disclosure forms for state legislators, statewide elected officials and heads of state agencies to include more specific information in order to “more effectively identify potential conflicts of interest”; and
• bring New Mexico in line with most other states by creating a two-year period before which state legislators can become paid lobbyists.
Ethics reforms for lobbyists include:
• requiring more detailed information on their expenditure reports that identify which legislators benefited from expenditures; which bills are being lobbied for; and which clients support such expenditures. Efforts to create expanded lobbyist disclosure requirements failed in the last legislative session.
• Require financial reports from lobbyists at the legislative mid-point and shortly after its conclusion versus the current schedule that requires them in May.
• Require lobbyists to disclose which bills they are lobbying for and their positions on such bills. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham vetoed comparable lobbyist disclosure legislation last year.
60 days later, Cicero Institute’s reason for NM lobbying still hidden from public

Finally, Think New Mexico also proposes reforms for advocacy groups aimed at addressing various dark money loopholes in state law, including:
• requiring disclosure of the “true source” of funding used for political or issue ads;
• closing a loophole in state law and requiring out-of-state political action committees to file the same reports as those that operate within the state. New Mexico’s June 2 primary election featured political involvement by both out-of-state PACs and so-called dark money groups.
• Finally, Think New Mexico proposes outlawing “the growing practice of using constituents’ names and emails to send fake emails to elected officials.” Source New Mexico originally reported the appearance of such emails in connection with advocacy for an air-quality permit for the data center Project Jupiter.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s nuclear watchdog has gone quiet
description:
The panel overseeing Vermont Yankee's decommissioning has little to say as a lease deal opens the door to a data center on the contaminated site.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s nuclear watchdog has gone quiet.
text:
This commentary is by Ann Darling, a member of the Citizens Awareness Network, a New England grassroots environmental organization working to end the use of nuclear power and replace it with sustainable, reliable and affordable energy generation.
I could have written this letter any time in the past 10 years. Why now and not then? I suppose I was hoping I wouldn’t need to make my opinions so public, because they are quite critical. But something is happening at the Vermont Yankee nuclear power plant site that leaves me no choice but to speak out. 
First, a little background. The Vermont Yankee nuclear reactor stopped operating at the end of 2014, and it is now almost completely decommissioned. The most significant things remaining are 60 concrete-and-steel casks of extremely radioactive waste, along with electric transmission and railroad infrastructure that can be used for other purposes. Its owner, NorthStar, a decommissioning company, has leased the site to a Texas-based energy development company called PowerTransitions, which is apparently considering options including a small modular nuclear reactor, battery storage or a data center.

READ MORE

Vermont Yankee has an associated Nuclear Decommissioning Citizens Advisory Panel (NDCAP) chartered by the legislature whose job is to advise the governor and the legislature on decommissioning, and to serve as a “conduit for public information and education” and to encourage “open communication and community involvement in matters related to the decommissioning process.” In my opinion, they have failed to fulfill this latter part of their charter. They hold meetings, fewer and fewer over the years, but they do no outreach to attract people to those meetings. I’ve raised this issue repeatedly and gotten nods of agreement to my suggestions — and absolutely no action. Even though they have money donated by Vermont Yankee’s owner, they don’t use it for public education events or media outreach. As a result, they regularly hear from a handful of anti-nukers like me, but they do not hear a peep out of the many people whose lives are impacted by how the site is cleaned up and used. 
Here’s why I’m writing now. There are supposed to be three meetings a year of the NDCAP, and there has been only one so far, with none scheduled. The May 2026 meeting was postponed, ostensibly because they wanted a report on the chemical contamination at the site from the state’s contractor. We know there are PFAS. We don’t know exactly where or how much. 
And then there’s the whole piece about leasing the Vernon site, which has chemical and radiological contamination, along with 60 concrete-and-steel casks of radioactive waste, to an out-of-state power development company. Although we have asked about the lease contents, waste ownership and how plans are being made and with whom, we have received no answers. 
This is all happening in a broader context. Gov. Phil Scott is promoting legislation that would define nuclear power as clean energy so that it can count toward meeting the state’s climate goals. Nuclear power emits ionizing radiation and makes people sick. Its entire fuel chain, from mining to waste management, is a net carbon emitter. It is not clean. The governor is also trying to repeal the statutory requirement that the legislature vote on whether nuclear power could be used again in Vermont, and he has vetoed legislation placing guardrails on data centers.
If the governor, Public Service Department and NDCAP are interested in transparency and building trust with the public, they’ve got me fooled. To me, this looks like they’re hiding something. Is it a really bad report about the PFAS and NorthStar balking at the cost? Is it their attempt to hide plans for a new nuclear reactor or data center in Vernon until it’s too late for the public to stop it? What is going on, really? We all deserve an answer. We deserved it a long time ago. 
Ann Darling, Easthampton, Mass.

name: VTDigger
title: UVM and Middlebury College announce tuition discounts
description:
The University of Vermont is offering discounts to New England students next fall in an effort to boost enrollment. Meanwhile Middlebury College is expanding its free tuition offers.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM and Middlebury College announce tuition discounts.
text:
Williams Hall on the University of Vermont campus in Burlington on Wednesday, September 20, 2023. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Two of Vermont’s leading universities are offering new tuition discounts to attract more students. 
The University of Vermont will offer a more than 35% discount on tuition starting next fall for students from other New England states who study certain majors. And it will offer free tuition for in-state students whose households make less than $125,000. 
For UVM, the discounted tuition is an effort to attract more students to the university’s recently declining ranks and recruit more graduates to join Vermont’s shrinking workforce. The university enrolls some of the most out of state students among state universities. 
“We wanted to tackle affordability head on and if we do that we believe enrollment growth will come,” said Jay Jacobs, vice president of enrollment management at UVM.
Meanwhile Middlebury College similarly announced Wednesday that it will offer free tuition for all students from households that make up to $175,000 annually, starting next fall. 
Both universities say they’re trying to stay competitive in the headwinds of a phenomenon dubbed the “demographic cliff.” Fewer people are projected to attend college in part because Americans started having fewer babies around the start of the Great Recession in late 2007. 
Although Middlebury College, a small and prestigious liberal arts college, hasn’t seen a decline in enrollment so far, it wants to compete for students and attract more people from middle and low-income backgrounds, according to Nicole Curvin, vice president of strategic enrollment. 
The college is following suit with other private universities across the country— which are slashing the prices of tuition and offering discounts to compete with public universities, according to The Wall Street Journal. 
Other universities across the state, including Vermont State University, the Community College of Vermont and Saint Michael’s College also offer tuition discounts based on household income. 
At Vermont’s land grant university, the effort to recruit more students comes amid serious enrollment challenges. This fall UVM’s enrollment of first-year students is down by about 14.5%, according to Jacobs.
Its freshman class is slightly bigger than the university projected last spring, when it warned that declining students would drive a $12 million budget deficit at the university. 
The university was able to close that projected deficit by making cuts in “operational inefficiencies” and nixing vacant staff positions, University President Marlene Tromp said last month.
To attract more students, UVM is offering discounted tuition for students from other New England states who enroll in a major offered within three of the university’s colleges: the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, the College of Education and Social Services and the Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources. 
The university considers the majors — which range from microbiology to social work — to be both high impact areas of study and central to the university’s brand, Jacobs said. 
“We wanted to make sure that those high impact programs where students go out into the workforce and create significant and positive community impact were attractive to students from all over New England,” he said. 
Tuition at UVM typically costs about $46,600 for out-of-state students and about $17,000 for in-state students for the year.
Under the discounted program, out of state students could pay more than $18,000 less, according to Jacobs. 
As UVM tries to recruit enough students to fill its ranks, Middlebury College has been in a different position. 
Enrollment has remained steady for the small college, according to Curvin, although it’s attracted fewer students from within New England. Tuition to attend Middlebury College costs about $72,900 this year. 
While Middlebury hasn’t seen smaller ranks of students, it wants to remain competitive — and be cognizant of how much education costs impact students’ school choice.
“We’ve been thinking about the ways in which we can be supportive of a wider band of students over time,” Curvin said, including students from different income levels and backgrounds. 
The new bar for free tuition is set to offer much more expansive financial aid than the university has offered in the past. 
Typically, the university only offers a financial aid package that amounts to free tuition if a student comes from a household that makes $65,000 or less, Curvin said. And it usually only offers discounted tuition in the form of financial aid for those who come from households that make $80,000 or less, she said. 
“What we’re trying to do is make sure that students are considering Middlebury, given the high cost of education at every institution,” Curvin said.

name: VTDigger
title: 3 decades after sparking a debate about censorship, ‘Daddy’s Roommate’ returns to Rutland
description:
The Rutland Free Library is launching a Freedom to Read Book Club with a pick that spurred local conflict and national coverage in the 1990s — and holds newfound relevance amid fights over the First Amendment today.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  3 decades after sparking a debate about censorship, ‘Daddy’s Roommate’ returns to Rutland.
text:
The children’s book “Daddy’s Roommate,” as pictured at the Rutland Free Library. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

For newcomers, the inaugural selection of the Rutland Free Library’s upcoming Freedom to Read Book Club might seem an unusual choice: an out-of-print 1990s children’s title with only one sentence on each of its 32 pages.
But ask any longtime local: “Daddy’s Roommate” has plenty of backstory.
When leaders at the public library added the picture book to their 76,000-volume collection three decades ago, they hoped to help preschoolers whose fathers had divorced their mothers to move in with another man.
“Mommy says Frank and Daddy are gay,” notes the book’s young narrator, who asks what that means.
“Being gay is just one more kind of love,” the mother responds. “And love is the best kind of happiness.”
A now-deceased Rutland parent disagreed. In the spring of 1995, she shared her concerns with neighbors, conservative groups and national television networks. Two months later, nearly 350 people stood in and outside the library as its governing board reviewed and ultimately rejected calls to limit access to the book.
Today, about half the local population wasn’t alive or around during the debate, according to the census, while the library staff has changed completely. But the question of who should be able to read what lingers, with the American Library Association reporting the highest U.S. rate of book complaints since it began collecting data in 1990.
“Censorship has not been at this level since Joe McCarthy was in the U.S. Senate,” Rutland library director Randal Smathers, rewinding to the 1950s, said in an interview. “There is an organized and politicized attack on what the whole country can read, say and think.”
In response, Rutland’s new Freedom to Read Book Club is inviting the public to meet the first Monday of each month from October through May to learn about specific titles and why they’re sparking debate.
“We’ve seen this proliferate from libraries into mainstream media, public broadcasting, national parks, museums, cultural institutions,” Janique Robillard, a producer of the recent Emmy Award-winning documentary “The Librarians,” said at a library program on the subject last week. “Censorship is trickling into anywhere there is history, documentation, archive, the written word.”
Joy Worland, a consultant with the Vermont Department of Libraries, added it was also spreading to current studies.
“There were more book bans about science and medical things in the last year than there ever have been,” Worland said. “Misinformation is huge right now.”

A Rutland Free Library sign asks about “Daddy’s Roommate.” (The answer is B.) Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Activists increasingly are plugging into artificial intelligence and other technology to push large-scale challenges of library and school books that feature sexual, racial, ethnic or religious diversity, according to a recent report by the nonprofit literary organization PEN America. 
Rutland’s issue started more simply. In the spring of 1995, the local Herald featured front-page headlines about the deadly bombing of an Oklahoma City federal building. Inside, the April 23 edition also noted a local veterans’ fundraiser, an owl show-and-tell and one parent’s call for the Rutland library to segregate “Daddy’s Roommate” from the rest of the children’s collection.
“It doesn’t belong where impressionable 5-year-olds might read it,” the parent was quoted.
June Osowski, the children’s librarian at the time, felt differently.
“We live in a pluralistic society,” the now-late Osowski told the Herald. “Libraries subscribe to the idea of intellectual freedom. Our community is a lot more varied than people think.”
Within a week, the seemingly tucked-away story led to multiple letters to the editor and interest from the Associated Press. Within a month, news crews from CNN and NBC were filming in Rutland. By June, so many people wanted to attend a public hearing on the issue, the 180 people who squeezed into the library were matched by nearly as many waiting outside.
“Under the glare of television lights that heated the already sweltering air to nearly 90 degrees, library trustees heard polarized viewpoints,” the Herald reported of the three-hour session. “In general, the crowd seemed fairly evenly divided.”
Library leaders were not: They went on to retain the book and receive a national award from the American Library Association for “successful mobilization of the community in support of the library’s intellectual freedom policies.”
Today, Vermont isn’t reporting many news-making book controversies, in part because a 2024 state law requires libraries to “protect and promote the principles of free speech, inquiry, discovery and public accommodation” by adopting policies that “comply with the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution and state and federal civil rights and antidiscrimination laws.”
“It’s still possible to challenge a book in Vermont, but it’s very hard to win that,” Worland said. “We have a very strong statute about this topic.”
Rutland’s Freedom to Read Book Club is set to kick off Oct. 5 at 6 p.m. at the library as part of the American Library Association’s Banned Books Week. Meetings will continue on the first Monday of the month, with Ray Bradbury’s 1953 dystopian novel “Fahrenheit 451” selected for November and the Pulitzer Prize-winning graphic novel “Maus” coming in December.
As library director, Smathers acknowledges publicity about the book club could rekindle protests.
“I hope it doesn’t cause antagonism, but we will not shy away from speaking out against censorship,” he said. “Our job is to provide for the whole community. We guarantee our library will have something to please — and offend — everybody.”
